description: Industry ranking per "Industry-Level Investment Parameters & Scoring Architecture": hierarchical category scores (1–5), overall 0–100, evidence coverage reported, three lenses kept separate. DERIVED — regenerate with node tools/build-industry-ranking.mjs.

framework.category_score: Σ(parameter weight × parameter score) ÷ Σ(weights of supported parameters)
framework.overall_score: Σ(category weight × category score ÷ 5) × 100, renormalised over supported categories

scale.1: Very unattractive — materially adverse, structurally weak or unsupported by evidence
scale.2: Below average — weak outlook or economics; meaningful disadvantages
scale.3: Mixed / average — balanced evidence, average economics or material uncertainty
scale.4: Attractive — strong evidence of favourable economics or improving prospects
scale.5: Highly attractive — exceptional, durable advantage supported by robust evidence

parameters.risk_formula_note: Risk-adjusted = structural x (resilience / 5). The risk category is scored on the attractiveness scale, so 5 means MOST resilient / LEAST risk — a higher input raises the adjusted score, which is the correct direction.

value_capture._doc: Component/node value-capture weights, from the Registry Review & Recommendations §4. A separate score from the industry-attractiveness weights above — it answers 'which part of this chain keeps the money'.

industries.title: India 5G / 4G RAN

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: A RAN bill of materials is 4-5% domestic, so Indian assemblers earn integration margin on a product they do not make. Tejas built a ~1 lakh-site BSNL network and then reported FY26 revenue of Rs 1,103 cr against a Rs 909 cr loss once that order ended, on a Rs 2,315 cr order book. Nokia's own read is that locally sourced components cost 20-80% more than Vietnam or China.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: India TANE is $25 bn in FY25 rising to $50 bn by FY32 - a 10.4% nominal CAGR, roughly twice the global pace (NITI Aayog, Aug-2026; KPMG in India, Oct-2026). With 4G/LTE RAN localisation at 4% and 5G RAN at 5%, the substitution gap rather than the growth rate is the opportunity.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: 98% of demand is private operators buying Nokia, Ericsson and Samsung, so Indian OEMs contest one-off state orders. Tejas, ITI, HFCL and Dixon are fragmented at assembly while RF devices and RAN silicon sit in a US/Japan/EU oligopoly with no Indian fab.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Private 5G capex has passed its peak (5.63 lakh BTS installed, Jun-2026). The next triggers are BSNL's Dec-2026 commercial 5G target, the Rs 1,537 cr add-on RAN order to Tejas and 5G-Advanced refreshes - but only 44-46% of sites are fibre-connected, which caps densification.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series exists in the registry. Tejas, ITI and HFCL trade on single-order flows, and a company multiple is not a sector series.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: RF front-end devices, filters, RAN silicon and RAN power supplies are imported with no listed Indian pure-play. What stays is assembly, integration and a rising share of design. ECMS was doubled to Rs 40,000 cr in Budget 2026 and now covers antennas, filters and coils - the first real component policy.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Assembly-level capex is modest - SMT lines, RF test benches and anechoic chambers - but working capital is order-book heavy and lumpy, and the Rs 12,195 cr telecom PLI ends 31-Mar-2027 with its successor still awaiting Cabinet approval.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Open-RAN and vRAN lower the silicon lock-in, and India has a proven indigenous 4G/5G stack (C-DoT, Tejas, TCS) plus a PLI-approved Open-RAN line at Dixon. The RF and silicon frontier remains a generation behind.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Four gates: 52.3% of telecom parts imports by value are Chinese (antennas 69.3%, populated PCBs 55.4%), RAN silicon is YEARS to STRUCTURAL, demand concentrates in two or three buyers, and certification test capacity under MTCTE/ITSAR is itself a queue that gates every launch.

missing_critical: component-level import value by HS code

value_capture.basis: The absolute barrier in the chain: L1-PHY FPGAs, SoCs and ASICs come from AMD/Xilinx, Altera, Marvell and Qualcomm, with no Indian fab, and every RAN sold anywhere pays it.
GaN/LDMOS devices and transceivers from a US/Japan/EU oligopoly; Indian GaN is pilot-stage and 52% of parts imports are Chinese, so the barrier is real and so is the exposure.
The smallest pool today and the highest returns - no fab, no inventory, no freight - and the one layer where Indian design houses and TCS genuinely compete for global work.
The hardest node to localise - the array and the radio are one part, so assembly, calibration and beamforming test must happen together - and the margin is competed away at the assembly step.
A small pool with a genuine process barrier; SAW/BAW and cavity filters are precisely what the doubled ECMS now covers, which makes this the next localisable layer.
Where Indian design is strongest and where the software value sits, but the hardware itself is a board-assembly business with limited pricing power.
The commodity end of the chain: contract-manufactured by ITI and others at thin margin, with the value sitting in the parts it buys rather than in the build.
The largest Indian revenue line and the weakest economics: the TCS-led BSNL integration and the AMC layer are pass-through, with switching costs from site lock-in rather than from margin.

industries.notes: First industry score on this page, 2026-11-06 (Tier-2 backfill). Market size and growth are the NITI Aayog/KPMG TANE series already carried in the digest; valuation stays UNAVAILABLE because no industry series exists. Value capture scored for the first time here, on the page's own tree nodes.

industries.title: India 6G (IMT-2030)

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: There is no revenue pool in India - or globally - before 2030. Today's spending is R&D (Rs 271-542 cr TTDF, Rs 1.0 lakh cr RDI), not product margin, so there are no industry economics to score yet.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: The global 6G pool runs $11.4 bn in 2030 to $110.46 bn in 2036 at a 46.0% CAGR (MarketsandMarkets, Oct-2025). India's domestic revenue is approximately zero before 2030 and Indian forecasts of 35-52% CAGR to 2035 all start from a nil base [CONFLICTING DATA] - a large TAM with no near-term cash flow.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Indian participation is consortia and centres of excellence - Bharat 6G Alliance, C-DoT, the Tejas 6G CoE - while silicon, sub-THz devices and test equipment are foreign oligopolies with no domestic entrant.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Pre-commercial trough: 3GPP Release 21 stage-1 freezes Mar-2027, first specifications Dec-2028, commercial chipsets end-2029. That is three years before a market exists to compete in.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series, and 6G is not a revenue segment for any listed company yet, so there is nothing to value.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Value sits in RFIC and baseband silicon, sub-THz front-ends and test and measurement, all of them imported. India's defensible position is software, integration and optical transport.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Funded by public R&D rather than industry cash flow, and neither sub-THz lines nor the test infrastructure exist domestically at commercial scale, so the capital has not yet been committed.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: The most active technology-policy area in Indian telecom: RIS/ISAC/NTN testbeds, a SAMEER THz facility, a target of 10% of global 6G patents and an active standards push inside 3GPP and ITU-R.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Spectrum stays undecided until WRC-27 (Oct-Nov 2027), the standard is two years out, and every critical input - silicon, sub-THz devices, test equipment - is imported.

value_capture.basis: The node that will hold the pool in 6G exactly as it does in 5G: a handful of foreign vendors, no Indian fab, and every radio pays it.
A near-total import leak with no listed Indian player - and a tollgate, since nothing ships without the measurement capability to certify it.
The 5G barrier carried into 6G at higher frequency; Indian GaN exists only at pilot scale through BEL/GAETEC.
No commercial domestic capability at all and the deepest technical barrier in the chain; whoever qualifies first owns a pool with almost no second source.
Where Indian research is most visible (RIS testbeds, metasurface work) and where the pool grows fastest from a zero base - but the revenue is speculative.
Software-defined and the least capital-intensive node; Jio's in-house stack shows Indian capability exists, but the compute underneath is imported.
The one node where India is already a global exporter (HFCL, Sterlite) - real manufacturing, real export revenue, and it is needed regardless of which air interface wins.
The assembly layer India already does for 5G, carried forward at sub-THz where the calibration burden is heavier and the margin thinner.

industries.notes: First industry score on this page, 2026-11-06 (Tier-2 backfill). Scored as a pre-commercial technology family: economics and valuation are deliberately low or UNAVAILABLE because there is no revenue pool yet, and the opportunity score is held at mixed rather than high because the India base is nil.

industries.title: India Agrochemicals & Crop Protection

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Off-patent technical synthesis earns a 15-20% first-mover registration margin that decays into a commodity spread once competitors register. The durable margin sits in CDMO/CSM innovator contracts, where PI Industries' CSM is ~74% of revenue.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: The industry is $11.2 bn in FY25, up 8.7% yoy, and is forecast to reach $14.5 bn by FY28 at a 9% CAGR (Rubix Data Sciences, Jun-2025). That sits on a base where ~50% of technicals and ~70% of intermediates are imported and use is 0.24-0.27 kg/ha against a 2.4 kg/ha global average.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Fragmented at formulation and distribution, consolidating at CDMO. India is the world's fourth-largest producer and third-largest exporter, but competes against Chinese technical capacity and a post-patent price collapse that took CTPR prices down ~80% after expiry.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Exports fell ~22% in FY24, recovered ~8% in FY25, and FY26 is mixed (PI's agchem exports -15%). Domestic demand remains monsoon-linked, so the cycle is real but shallow.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series exists in the registry; the listed players span a 3x range of multiples depending on CDMO versus formulation mix, which is a company observation, not a sector series.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: A genuine technical and export base rather than an assembly economy, but the middle of the chain - advanced intermediates and key starting materials - is the import leak, and that is exactly where backward integration re-rates.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Batch chemistry capex is moderate and modular, so entry is affordable; but working capital is inventory- and receivable-heavy and environmental compliance capex keeps rising.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Process chemistry and continuous flow are the frontier and India is competitive there; new-molecule R&D remains thin at Rs 2,000 cr+ and 10-12 years to registration.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: China KSM dependence, the pending Pesticides Management Bill 2025 with data-protection uncertainty, and monsoon exposure - partly offset by an 18%-versus-35% US tariff advantage over China.

missing_critical: final shape of the Pesticides Management Bill

value_capture.basis: The highest-margin, lowest-volatility pool: innovator contracts, multi-year, with switching costs that come from qualification rather than from price.
The import leak that backward integration converts into margin: ~70% of key intermediates come from China, so whoever builds them locally prices into a shortage.
The core Indian engine and the China+1 battleground - a first-mover registration margin that decays as competitors register the same molecule.
The fastest-growing export segment (20% CAGR FY20-FY25, share of exports 31% to 37%) and a commodity spread with little pricing power.
The India-specific moat - a branded, monsoon-linked retail network that is hard to replicate - but working capital sits in the channel.
The fastest-growing pool with real pricing power and almost no scale yet; MSME-heavy and constrained by the FCO Schedule VI regulatory transition.
A large established pool where India is cost-competitive but the molecule set is mature and Chinese supply sets the price.
A toll-conversion business: low barriers, no pricing power, and the pool that any formulator can enter tomorrow.

industries.notes: First industry score on this page, 2026-11-06 (Tier-2 backfill). Market size and growth are the Rubix FY25/FY28 series already carried in the digest and now re-verified; the Statista $10.3 bn variant is a scope difference and is shown, not averaged.

industries.title: India Aircraft MRO & Civil Aerospace Components

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Airframe and line MRO is a labour-arbitrage service with thin margin and imported spares. The value sits in engines and components, which OEM shops (Safran, GE, P&W, Rolls-Royce) control, so ~80% of MRO value still flies to Singapore, Dubai and Europe.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: India MRO is ~$4.4 bn in 2025 rising to ~$5.7 bn by 2030 - a ~5.3% nominal CAGR (Alton Aviation/IBEF, Mar-2026) - against a fleet that triples to ~2,250 aircraft by 2035. Sources span $3.5-4.4 bn today to $5.7-6.9 bn by 2030, so the direction is firm and the pace is not [CONFLICTING DATA].

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Fragmented and largely unlisted at the component layer (AIESL, Air Works, Haveus, Horizon, Magnum). Engine MRO is OEM-captured and the airport/SEZ layer is a two-player rent pool (GMR, Adani).

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: The post-pandemic recovery is over; the driver now is fleet induction and shop-visit timing. Safran's Hyderabad LEAP line opens in 2026 at 300 visits a year and IndiGo's 1,000+ LEAP MoU (Jul-2026) sets the engine-visit curve.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series in the registry; the listed exposures are aerospace-component manufacturers whose multiples reflect defence and export order books rather than MRO service economics.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Engine components and aerostructures manufacturing are real domestic pools (PTC/Aerolloy, Azad, Dynamatic, Aequs, Rossell), but the MRO service layer imports its spares and loses the high-value checks abroad.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Hangars, test cells and OEM licences are capital-heavy with long payback, and the SEZ/airport landlord captures part of the return that the operator creates.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: NADCAP special processes, digital records and PMA/DER routes are the frontier. India is building from a low base, but PTC's melt-cast-forge and Azad's blade work are genuinely upstream.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Certification and skills bind hardest - the CAR-66 engine-CRS anomaly and 25-30% attrition - alongside imported spares, titanium sponge and composite prepreg.

missing_critical: segment split of MRO revenue by check type

value_capture.basis: The largest pool in the chain and the most OEM-captured: parts and data licences sit with Safran, GE, P&W and Rolls-Royce, so the Indian share only opens where an OEM builds a shop here.
The 'missing middle' that is ~100% abroad today: lower spares intensity than engines, PMA/DER routes available, and the clearest localisation gap in the whole industry.
The cleanest domestic manufacturing pool - PTC/Aerolloy's melt-cast-forge and Azad's blades - with qualification barriers high enough to keep the margin.
The deepest barrier and the worst cash profile: melt and mill capacity is capital-hungry with long qualification, which is why it is only newly domestic.
EWIS and harness work is export-strong and tariff-light (Rossell, DCX); the LRU and software layer remains imported and OEM-controlled.
Build-to-print export work at scale (Dynamatic, Aequs): real revenue, but the customer sets the price and the design stays with the OEM.
The layer India is actually competent at, and the thinnest: labour-arbitrage checks with imported spares eating the margin.
A crowded tier-3 machining layer with moderate returns and low switching costs; the barrier is accreditation, not capability.

industries.notes: First industry score on this page, 2026-11-06 (Tier-2 backfill). The market series is shown as a range across four houses rather than a point, and the opportunity score is held at mixed because the growth rate and the leak are pulling in opposite directions. Valuation stays UNAVAILABLE.

industries.title: India Ammunition & Cartridges

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: MIL's FY26 revenue of ₹10,954 cr (+33%) and a 13.3% PBILDT margin sit on cost-plus deemed contracts; private shell-body makers clear ₹20,000–26,100 a unit but face multi-year qualification, and the domestic value pool grows ~4.9–6.1% a year.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: ₹15,899 cr of import-dependent ammunition is formally under indigenisation, ~70% of defence-grade nitrocellulose is imported, and Europe's 155 mm shortage has turned India into a shell-body exporter — exports +62.66% in FY26.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Regulation still concentrates the chain: one dominant DPSU, one buyer, licensing and DGQA gates. But the body node has fragmented fast — five listed entrants in twelve months — while energetics stays an oligopoly.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Global rearmament is a genuine up-cycle: order books are 2.2× revenue at Solar, 4.04× at Premier and 3.6× at MIL, though peacetime ordering is lumpy (Nibe books ~60% of sales in Q4).

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation dataset was assembled for this run; company multiples are widely reported as elevated but were not verified here. Scored null rather than imputed.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: 91% of ammunition variants (159 of 175) are indigenised, shell bodies, brass and filling are domestic; the residue is concentrated exactly where value is highest — nitrocellulose, primers and fuze electronics.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: An energetics plant needs isolated land with water, ₹200–400 cr of imported equipment and years of approvals; of 40–46 explosives licences issued only ~15–17% of holders have built anything.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Body forging is mature and commoditising; the migration is in base-bleed and ramjet-extended 155 mm, programmable fuzes and loitering munitions — where a shell body's ₹25,000 becomes a ₹69,000 export unit.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Single-buyer concentration, a licence-and-safety regime, export controls and lumpy ordering are structural; the offsetting factor is unambiguous policy support and a record export market.

missing_critical: nitrocellulose and propellant import values by HS code
per-round cost build for a filled 155 mm round

value_capture.basis: The scarcest input: propellant prices went from under US$10/kg in 2019 to ~US$50/kg in 2025, supply is booked years ahead, and qualification is chemistry-specific.
Converts forgings into billable ammunition; gated by energetics supply and DGQA acceptance, so capacity is scarce and switching is slow, but pricing is set by a single buyer.
Value-dense hardware: a base-bleed-equipped body exports at ~₹69,000 against ₹20,000–26,000 for a plain body; thin supplier base, export-led demand.
Volume pool (~158 mn rounds/yr) but the lowest value per round and the most price-sensitive buyer; brass and primer inputs dominate cost.
Fast-growing but commoditising: five listed forgers entered within twelve months, prices are LME-indexed and DGQA approval is the only real barrier.

industries.notes: Industry-level scorecard, not a company score. Valuation unsupported in this run; coverage below 100% is shown, not imputed.

industries.title: India Battery Energy Storage (BESS)

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Developer economics are set by auction, not by product: MSEDCL cleared 2,000 MW at Rs 2.38 lakh/MW/month and GUVNL at Rs 2.32 lakh in 2026, roughly 10-25% above the same buyers' earlier rounds only because cell prices rebounded - a 15-year annuity priced against a volatile imported input.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: The requirement is 236 GWh by FY32 against 14.5 GWh operational and a 198 GWh pipeline; volume compounds at 91% a year to FY32 (Nuvama) and value at 33.7% nominal to 2032 (MarkNtel), on a policy mandate rather than on demand optimism.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Awards stay fragmented — MSEDCL’s 2,000 MW went to a long list led by Oriana at 900 MW, with BSL, ArMee, GK Energy, Stockwell and Claro taking the rest — but the operating layer is consolidating: Adani Green holds 6.63 GWh, over half the national fleet, and Pace Digitek holds ₹10,735 cr of executable orders.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: The cycle has turned from tender-led to execution-led: 8.2 GWh was added in Jan–Jun 2026 against under 100 MWh a year earlier, and Crisil expects 45–50 GWh across FY27–28, though 57% of September’s tendered volume was re-tendered and 12 GWh of under-construction capacity carries weak-return risk.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series exists in the registry; the only current data point is a single EPC/integrator trading near 10× earnings after a 29% one-year decline — a company observation, not a sector multiple.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Cells are 40–55% of system cost and still imported, BMS ≈90% and PCS largely so; what stays in India is container and pack assembly, EMS software and grid interface. The domestic cell pool only opens in 2027–28, so value-chain position is improving but still weak on the evidence available.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Grid-scale storage is a VGF-supported capital-heavy annuity: two schemes now support 43.8 GWh, VGF scheme 1 has commissioned 0.5 GWh of 12.7 GWh awarded, contracts run 15 years at 95% availability, and the balance sheet carries a 12–15 year payback on an imported cost base.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Cell chemistry, BMS algorithms and PCS topologies are largely bought in; the grid-forming mandate from Jul-2026 and the 10% co-location rule from Jul-2027 raise the technical bar faster than Indian capability is being built, though Exide, Reliance and Amara Raja have moved from drawings to commissioning.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Exposure concentrates in four gates: ≈90% cell import dependence on China, a PLI programme that has delivered 1.4 GWh of 40, a grid-forming certification barrier most domestic PCS makers have not cleared, and auction tariffs struck before the 2026 battery-price rebound.

value_capture.basis: Largest pool and the deepest barrier, but domestic economics are unproven: a 5 GWh plant runs at negative EBITDA and cell prices are set in China.
A domestic oligopoly with real pricing power; grid-forming retrofits add volume without adding a new supplier.
Same barrier as cells with a smaller pool; >90% of processing sits in China and Indian capacity is pre-revenue.
A global oligopoly with no Indian fab; the barrier is absolute but so is the distance to participating.
Whoever builds it locally sells into every gigafactory; today it is a pure import line with no Indian participant.
Highest ROIC and cash conversion in the chain, and it counts toward domestic content — the smallest pool, with no listed vehicle.
The grid-forming mandate converts a price-led import market into a qualification-led one; the barrier is certification, not capital.
Safety-critical and now certification-gated (UL 1973 Ed.3), but ≈90% imported and with no listed pure-play.
A 15-year contracted annuity with the highest switching cost in the chain, but returns are capped by auction tariffs against a volatile input.
Low capex and ROCE-accretive at ≈6–7% operating margin, but a thin, contested layer that any integrator can enter.
Incentive-backed and growing off a small base; the specialist players are unlisted.
A pass-through pool: order books are large, margins are execution-dependent, and working capital absorbs the cash.

industries.notes: Full re-analysis 2026-11-04 (previous 2026-10-09/30). Cycle raised 2 -> 3 on the commissioning inflection: 8.2 GWh added Jan-Jun 2026 against under 100 MWh a year earlier, 198 GWh pipeline at Sep-2026, Crisil expecting 45-50 GWh across FY27-28. Value and volume CAGRs come from different houses and are shown separately, never divided into each other. Valuation stays UNAVAILABLE: one listed integrator's multiple is not an industry series.

industries.title: India Battery Management Systems (BMS)

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: A capital-light design-and-assemble business with improving but thin margins: Maxwell's H1FY27 EBITDA was 6.8% (from 3.4%) on Rs 141 cr of income, and BESS integrators guide to 5-6% EBIT. Growth is real, pricing power is not.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: 308 GWh tendered against 13.7 GWh operational, a 40 GWh NGEL tender opened 4-Nov-2026 and 16 GWh of SECI bids closing 23-Nov-2026, plus 2W/3W electrification. Value series run from a 20% to a 34.5% CAGR depending on scope.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Fragmented domestic design houses and EMS players compete on assembly against integrated Chinese boards, with no IP moat at the low-voltage end; the moat that is forming is certification and cybersecurity compliance, not scale.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: The operating base multiplied 17x in nine months to 13.7 GWh and two large tenders are live this month; Maxwell's income grew 91% in H1FY27. This is the up-cycle of a policy-created market, with lumpy delivery risk behind it.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series exists for this node, and the listed proxies are diversified parents whose multiples are set by other businesses.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: The BMS is a small node (about 5% of BESS capex) sitting under a large import dependency: 30-40% of BOM cost is imported silicon, ~85% of PCB is imported, and the design layer captures margin but not volume.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Among the least capital-hungry nodes in the storage chain - SMT lines, HIL rigs and firmware teams rather than gigafactories - which is why design houses can scale on venture money and EMS players can enter on existing lines.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: India has genuine firmware, 1500 V isolation and ASIL C design capability (Maxwell, HBL, Xbattery, Vecmocon), but the silicon, the cell-level algorithms in the AFE and the security architecture IP remain foreign.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Silicon concentration in four foreign suppliers, documented firmware vulnerabilities, thin margins against Chinese price competition, an operating base still one-twentieth of the tendered pipeline, and a demand floor that depends on policy dates.

missing_critical: BMS import value and China share from official trade data (no HS line)
unit-volume series and realised per-unit BMS price

value_capture.basis: The top node in the chain and the deepest import gap: 30-40% of BMS BOM cost, a four-supplier oligopoly, 26-week catalogue lead times and no Indian fab or design house. Pricing power and cash conversion are as good as it gets in this chain. Unchanged at rank 1, and still unavailable in the NSE/BSE universe.

Same oligopoly, marginally less scarce than the AFE because safety MCUs are multi-sourced across NXP, Infineon, Renesas and TI. AEC-Q100 qualification is the barrier that keeps Indian entrants out, not price.

Moved UP two places. Two 2026 mandates turned this from a feature into a gate: MSEDCL's 4 GWh award requires indigenous EMS software with 20% local content, and AIS-156 makes cybersecurity testing mandatory for wireless BMS. Software carries high switching costs and light capital, but the revenue pool is small relative to hardware.

Moved DOWN one place. This is where India's listed exposure sits, and it is where the money is thinnest: Maxwell earned 6.8% EBITDA on Rs 141 cr in H1FY27 and is ~1.5% of Endurance's consolidated income. High growth, weak pricing power against Chinese boards, and a customer base that is itself concentrated in a handful of pack makers.

Moved UP one place above PCB assembly, because domestic integration went from announced to commissioned: 23.15 GWh/yr of disclosed capacity is running. It is the largest revenue pool in the chain and the worst cash converter - cells are imported, working capital is heavy and EBIT guidance is 5-6%.

A small but genuinely scarce pool in India: no container-scale propagation facility exists domestically, so UL 9540A evidence is imported. The MNRE import gate raises the volume of re-certification work without creating capacity to do it.

Moved DOWN one place. The most commoditised node here: ~85% of PCB is imported, barriers are low, and EMS players compete on utilisation. It captures revenue share without capturing margin, and Chinese board-level integration keeps the ceiling low.

industries.notes: Re-analysed 2026-11-06 under the daily rotation; first scoring of this page. Corrections from the prior run (2026-10-09): the page carried no scorecard, no value capture and no metric popups. '~90% of BMS units imported' is now carried as an estimate without an official HS line; Maxwell is no longer described as an unscaled start-up (H1FY27 income Rs 141 cr, 6.8% EBITDA) but is only ~1.5% of Endurance consolidated income, which the prior page omitted; the Market Research Future EV-only series was not re-verified and has been dropped. industries.title: India Chip Design & IP

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: The Indian pool is services-weighted and priced per engineer-month: MosChip 12.8% EBITDA, Sasken 7.9%, Cyient Semiconductors -US$11.2 mn EBIT on US$25.7 mn revenue in FY26. The high-margin half of the node - EDA and IP at 85%+ gross margin - is not present in India at all.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: Semicon 2.0 carries Rs 1.27 lakh crore notified 31-Aug-2026 with a design pillar; DLI 2.0 proposes ~Rs 5,000 crore; 372 design startups exist; the semiconductor vertical of India ER&D is the fastest-growing at 12.85% CAGR to 2031.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: EDA and core IP are a >85% oligopoly India cannot enter at advanced nodes; Indian design services are fragmented across nine listed firms with no pricing power. Neither structure favours an Indian entrant.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: LTTS, KPIT and Tata Elxsi posted their slowest annual growth in at least five years in FY26 (8.35%, 4.8%, 0.8%) as global auto OEMs reprioritised R&D; semiconductor GCC hiring fell 22% year-on-year in Q1. Policy money is expanding into a contracting services market.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data for an India chip-design and IP pool: the listed exposure is ER&D services equity with no comparable sector multiple series, and the fabless product businesses are loss-making at segment level.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: India captures the labour layer and a sliver of owned product; EDA, processor IP, interface IP, emulation hardware and foundry access are imported. DLI has produced 25 tape-outs, 7 fabricated chips and 140+ reusable IP cores - real progress from a very low base.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: A design centre costs US$200-500 mn against US$15-25 bn for an advanced fab, and an asset-light services model needs almost nothing. Entry capital is low, but the value-creating step - first silicon at US$3-5 mn - is where Indian venture capital is thinnest.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Three live transitions: RISC-V displacing Arm in embedded (~25% penetration by end-2025), chiplets and UCIe redefining what a chip is, and AI-assisted design automation compressing the flow. All three lower barriers, but India participates rather than owns them.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Four gates: a three-vendor EDA chokepoint already used once as an export-control lever; Arm royalty dependence; a policy regime still negotiating IP co-ownership and a 3x offshore-sale clawback; and buyer requalification cost. Concentration adds ~60% of senior VLSI talent in one city.

missing_critical: India-only chip-design and IP revenue pool (no published series)
segment-level revenue for chip design inside LTTS / Tata Elxsi / KPIT / Tata Technologies
industry-level valuation multiples for Indian design services
disbursed DLI amounts and per-company outcomes

value_capture.basis: 85%+ gross margin, 13% revenue CAGR against 7% semiconductor R&D growth, >90% share in static timing and >85% in physical verification, and multi-year switching cost from flow requalification.
Arm converts ~95% of revenue to gross profit and took US$2.61 bn of royalties in FY2026; the IP pool grows 10.2% to 2032. Cash conversion is high but royalty collection lags shipment by quarters.

40%+ gross margin is achievable on owned silicon, but Cyient Semiconductors shows the cost of getting there: -US$11.2 mn EBIT on US$25.7 mn revenue, with 120-150 weeks concept-to-samples tying up working capital.

Contract-manufacturing economics valued as capacity rather than capability, but India now has commercial capacity (Kaynes, CG Semi, SPEL) and packaging precedes fabs in every build-out, so the pool grows with domestic electronics output.
Headcount-linked revenue at 8-25% EBITDA, priced per engineer-month, with no accumulated IP. FY26 growth was the weakest in five years across the listed set.

industries.notes: Coverage 85% - valuation unscored, so the overall is provisional. Structural 58.6/100, current 40.0/100, overall 55.3/100.

industries.title: India Component MRO

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Component MRO is a spares-plus-labour business where spares are ~55% of outlay (NITI Aayog) and ~100% of components currently go overseas. Domestic shops earn labour and turnaround margin only, and the rotable pool is too thin to price power-by-the-hour.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: India component MRO is ~$1.11 bn (2026F) and ~100% of it flies abroad today, so the addressable substitution is the entire segment as the fleet triples to ~2,250 aircraft by 2035. The global component pool grows only 3.3% nominal to 2034 and no India-specific CAGR series was found [UNAVAILABLE].

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Fragmented: unlisted AIESL, Haveus, Horizon, Magnum and SA Air Works, with foreign Thales and Lufthansa Technik holding the avionics LRU work. CAR-145 C-ratings are the real gate rather than capital.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Demand tracks shop-visit intervals rather than traffic. The 2026-27 trigger is capability coming onshore - Haveus's Rs 450 cr Karnataka landing-gear and APU plant (Mar-2026) and Thales's 11-year IndiGo avionics contract.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series, and there is no listed pure-play in component MRO, so there is no sector multiple to quote.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: This is the node where the substitution gap is total and the barrier is certification rather than capital - the most independent-friendly segment, with lower spares intensity and PMA/DER routes that cut part cost 20-40%.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: A component shop is far cheaper than a hangar or an engine test cell, but tooling, OEM data licences and a rotable pool are working-capital heavy and slow to build.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Test equipment, OEM data and tooling licences and PMA/DER engineering capability are the gaps; the underlying repair technology is established rather than frontier.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: OEM data and tooling licences gate the high-end LRUs, the rotable pool is thin (long turnaround, weak PBH pricing), and the entire segment is import-dependent today.

value_capture.basis: The largest and most defensible component pool: Thales and Lufthansa Technik hold it, India is under 30% of it, and the OEM data licence is the wall.
Not a revenue pool but the tollgate on every other pool: whoever holds the C-ratings captures the work, at almost no capital cost.
High-value, high-barrier overhaul; Haveus's Rs 450 cr Karnataka plant is the first serious domestic attempt at it.
A named gap - Air India sends HGT1700s to Hamburg - and small enough that one qualified shop can take the whole domestic pool.
The 20-40% cost lever and the highest-return niche in the chain, but approval-gated and small in absolute revenue.
High-volume and established, with the best cash conversion of the component pools and the least pricing power.
A steady mid-value pool where GMR Aero Technic already does heat exchangers; moderate barriers and moderate returns.
Composite repair capability is scarce but the work is project-based and price-sensitive, with low switching costs.

industries.title: India Condenser & Heat Rejection

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Domestic build capability is real - BHEL, L&T, Thermax, ISGEC and Walchandnagar all fabricate condensers in India - but it is project business tendered on L1 price. BHEL's power segment earned a 19.7% EBIT margin in Q4 FY26 only after a turnaround from 5% a year earlier, and the one high-value material input, titanium tubing, is imported.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: India needs 86,440 MW of additional thermal capacity by FY36, with 63,545 MW already under implementation (47,545 MW under construction, 16,000 MW awarded) [REPORTED-T1: CEA National Generation Plan, Mar-2026], and every new unit carries a condenser. Dry cooling is the growth vector: India air-cooled heat exchangers USD 271.5 mn (2024) to USD 450.8 mn (2029), 10.7% CAGR [REPORTED-T3: MarketsandMarkets].

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: A qualified-supplier oligopoly - BHEL, L&T, Thermax, ISGEC, Walchandnagar - gated by ASME PTC 12.2 performance guarantees, nuclear-grade qualification for the 700 MWe PHWR fleet and utility vendor approval. The weakness is at the large end: BHEL went to a global ICB tender for the 3.2 GW Darlipali/Telangana ACC package.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Thermal ordering is at a multi-decade high - 63,545 MW under implementation against a ~242 GW installed base - so condenser demand sits in an upswing rather than at a peak. Ordering is lumpy and state-utility-led, tied to 800 MW unit awards.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series exists for condenser and heat-rejection equipment in the registry; the listed exposure sits inside diversified capital-goods and EPC companies whose multiples are not attributable to this node.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Shell, water boxes, tubesheets, ACC, pumps and aftermarket are built domestically; the titanium/stainless tube bundle and large-ACC technology are imported or globally tendered, and performance instrumentation is largely in-house at BHEL.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Heavy fabrication with moderate fixed capex (BHEL HEEP Haridwar) but a large working-capital and performance-bank-guarantee burden across 24-36 month project cycles. Affordable for an established fabricator, prohibitive for a new entrant.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Mature, incremental technology: titanium and superferritic stainless tubing, larger single units, and the shift from wet cooling towers to air-cooled condensers driven by water norms. Stable rather than disruptive.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: The gating input is imported titanium tube, with no NSE/BSE-listed maker; and the 2025 Environment (Protection) amendment that lets MoEF&CC exempt plants from cooling towers cuts both ways for forced wet-cooling retrofits.

missing_critical: India condenser market value (only a CAGR and an adjacent ACC series are published)

value_capture.basis: The core fabricated package and the largest single domestic revenue pool. Five qualified fabricators against a 63.5 GW build programme gives real pricing discipline, but L1 tendering caps it and progress payments tie up working capital.

The one genuinely scarce node: seawater-grade titanium tube (ASTM B338) is imported and has no listed Indian maker, so its margin accrues offshore. Strategic weight is high because a tube failure stops the unit, but cash conversion is poor for a project supplier.

Small revenue, excellent economics: retubing, fouling remediation and performance testing recur across a 242 GW installed base, are invoiced on completion, and carry high switching costs once a utility has qualified the crew. The most cash-generative node in the chain.

The growth pool: water norms push new units to dry cooling and the India ACC market compounds at 10.7%. It is capital-heavy, finned-tube intensive and not fully in-house even at BHEL, which tendered 3.2 GW of ACC globally in Aug-2026 - a supply gap that is also the localisation opportunity.

Tiny revenue but high margin and high stickiness - ASME PTC 12.2 performance instrumentation is specified into the guarantee and is largely developed in-house by BHEL. Value capture per rupee of revenue is the best in the chain, which is exactly why it is not a large pool.

Served by a deep domestic pump industry (KSB, Kirloskar Brothers, WPIL) with aftermarket annuity and better cash conversion than fabrication. Competitive, so pricing power is moderate and the node is substitutable across suppliers.

A qualification-gated fabrication node (thick plate drilling, seal welding, NDT) where domestic capability exists and import dependence is low. Moderate pool, protected by weld integrity and code compliance rather than by scale.

industries.title: Cryocooler (India)

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: India has no cryocooler OEM of scale. The cold head, regenerator matrix and linear compressor - the compressor alone is roughly 40-50% of system cost - come from SHI, Cryomech/Bluefors and Thales, so domestic activity is cryostat and vacuum-vessel fabrication, helium handling and integration, which earn a fraction of system value.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: Global cryocooler demand is USD 2.8-3.5 bn (2025) growing at 7.1% (MarketsandMarkets 2025-30) to 13.4% (Mordor 2026-31) [CONFLICTING DATA - scope-driven], pulled by defence EO/IR, cryogen-free MRI and quantum. India has no discrete market series [UNAVAILABLE]; the pull is programme-led - DRDO's 20 mK dilution-refrigerator TDF project (Sep-2026), the national quantum mission and indigenous IR seeker production.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: The global structure is a three-player oligopoly with certification-gated qualification. India's credible positions are RRCAT's 30 K GM cryocooler with an indigenous oil-free helium compressor (Sep-2026, transferred to industry) and Zero mK India's 20 mK development contract - a lab-to-pilot position, not a competitive one.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Demand is programme- and grant-led rather than cyclical: defence EO/IR and quantum procurement move on budget cycles and mission approvals, so volumes are lumpy but insulated from a consumer down-cycle.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No listed Indian cryocooler pure-play exists, so there is no industry valuation series to score; the nearest listed exposures are adjacent (gas handling, IR integration) rather than the node itself.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Value sits upstream in regenerator compounds, the precision compressor and the cold head, and downstream in systems integration. India captures the cryostat, helium distribution and IR/EO integration layers and imports the rest.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Precision machining, clean assembly and helium leak-test infrastructure are modest in absolute capex, but the qualification burden is heavy - MTBF demonstration runs into thousands of hours - and the Rs 500 cr TDF corpus is the main non-dilutive funding route.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: The technology is migrating on three fronts at once - GM to pulse-tube for reliability, Stirling for tactical seekers, dilution for quantum - and India is at prototype stage on each, so capability is being built against a moving target.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Helium and He-3 are imported and structurally short, the rare-earth regenerator material sits under China's export-control regime, and the Rs 7,280 cr REPM magnet scheme that would fund domestic regenerator supply has still not awarded beneficiaries.

missing_critical: domestic OEM pricing and margin data

value_capture.basis: The heart of the machine and the node with the clearest pricing power: three global suppliers, aerospace-grade qualification and no Indian producer at volume. Value capture is high on both barriers and switching costs; cash conversion is only middling because units are built to order.

Roughly 40-50% of system cost and the single largest profit pool in the chain. RRCAT's indigenous oil-free helium compressor (Sep-2026) is the first credible domestic entry, which makes this both the biggest leak and the biggest localisation prize.

The fastest-growing and most defensible node by economics: a handful of global suppliers, unit prices in crores, and demand set by quantum computing. Zero mK India's 20 mK TDF contract is the whole of the domestic position today.

A small, specialised pool with very high barriers - Ho/Er-bearing sintered spheres with tightly controlled geometry - sitting directly behind China's rare-earth export controls. Domestic supply depends on the REPM scheme, whose beneficiaries are still unawarded.
A small but strategic pool: cool-down and MTBF test capability gates every supplier, so the lab that owns it extracts rent from the whole chain. Almost entirely institutional in India today.

A commodity-like input with a genuine scarcity overlay - He-3 is effectively unavailable and He-4 is imported. Value capture is limited because it is traded rather than designed in, but its absence stops the chain, which is what makes it a bottleneck.

The one node India already serves - INOX India and similar fabricators - but it is a fabrication business with low barriers and thin pricing power. It grows with the chain without capturing its value.

industries.title: India Data Centres & AI-Compute

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Colocation economics are strong - FY26 EBITDA of 40% at Nxtra, 45% at Sify and 63% at AdaniConneX - but almost all of that capacity is unlisted. The listed domestic pool is power equipment (~40-45% of capex), which earns capital-goods margins, while compute value passes straight through to importers.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: India DC services ~USD 1.7 bn (FY26) to ~USD 6.8 bn (FY30), an implied ~41% nominal CAGR, on IT load of ~1.9 GW (FY26) to 7.0-7.5 GW (FY30) [CALCULATED from KPMG; CONFLICTING DATA on 2030 capacity - Axis Capital 2.8-3 GW, C&W pipeline 3.9 GW]. Operational capacity was ~1.8 GW in H1 2026 [REPORTED-T2: Cushman & Wakefield, Sep-2026].

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Power equipment is a domestic oligopoly with multi-year lead times and real pricing power; the compute layer is a foreign near-duopoly that India does not contest. Operator competition is intensifying as Reliance, Adani, Nxtra and Sify all build against the same pre-lease pipeline.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: A capex upcycle with a visible overbuild question: 3.9 GW of announced pipeline against an Axis view of only 2.8-3 GW operational by 2030. Growth is real, but the announcement-to-energisation ratio is the cycle risk.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series for Indian data-centre operators exists in the registry, and the largest operators are unlisted, so a sector multiple cannot be evidenced.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Roughly 40-45% of capex - power equipment, cables, cooling, EPC - is domestically sourced and stays home; up to ~90% of an AI server's value is imported silicon and memory.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Capital intensity is extreme, of the order of Rs 60-70 cr per MW of IT load, and returns depend on pre-leasing and financing cost. The offset is deep sponsor access to capital and open-access renewable power.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: The fastest-moving node in the registry: GPU generations turn over every 12-18 months, rack density has moved from 10 kW to 40-130 kW, and liquid cooling is displacing air in new builds, so installed equipment faces rapid obsolescence.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Transformer and switchgear lead times, GPU and HBM import concentration, subsea-cable landing capacity and state power availability all bind at once, and none of them is fixable by an Indian investor.

value_capture.basis: Where the money actually goes: the highest-margin, highest-barrier node in the whole map, and up to ~90% of an AI server's value. India has no presence here, which is why this node reads as a leak rather than an opportunity in an India-scoped analysis.

A three-supplier oligopoly on the critical path of every AI rack, with allocation rather than price as the rationing mechanism. No Indian exposure; the strategic weight is as high as the silicon it feeds.

The largest pool in the chain by revenue and the one that owns the customer: pre-committed hyperscale leases convert to 40-63% EBITDA margins, and land-plus-power permits are the real barrier. Capital intensity is the drag on ROIC, not pricing.

The best domestic node in the chain: an oligopoly (Hitachi Energy, Siemens Energy, GE, TBEA plus Indian makers) with 18-30 month lead times and rising realisations. Cash conversion is the weakness - long-cycle projects absorb working capital.

The fastest-growing equipment node and the clearest localisation opening, but foreign-designed today and priced against imports. Value capture is mid-chain: real margin sits in the fluids and the cold plate, not the skid.

A four-supplier global oligopoly with long lead times and consortium-based contracting. Strategically binding for India's connectivity, but the manufacturing value is offshore and the returns are project-based.

A competitive HVAC business (Voltas, Blue Star, Daikin) that grows with the market but is being displaced at the high-density end by liquid. Moderate returns, low barriers, and a structural share loss to come.

Assembly of imported silicon: revenue scales fast, margin is a conversion spread, and inventory risk sits with the integrator. The node exists in India (Dixon, Netweb) but captures little of the value it moves.
Large revenue, thin margin, completion risk and heavy working capital: L&T books the project value but earns a contractor's spread. Value capture is poor relative to the capital it absorbs.

industries.title: India Data-Centre Liquid Cooling

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: The economics are set by mix. Fluids and cold plates carry gross margins several times those of heat rejection, but the largest domestic revenue pool is chillers and dry coolers - a competitive HVAC business served by Voltas, Blue Star, Thermax and KRN. Cold plates and quick-disconnects are imported, so their margin leaves the country.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: India data-centre liquid cooling USD 207.7 mn (2025) to USD 258.7 mn (2026) and USD 1.87 bn (2035), a 24.58% CAGR over 2026-2035 [REPORTED-T3: Credence Research], inside a wider India DC cooling market of USD 2.99 bn (2026) to USD 11.38 bn (2032) at 24.86% [Mordor]. Volume driver: ~70% liquid / 30% air in new builds at 40-130 kW racks.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: The technology layer is foreign-led - Vertiv, Boyd, CoolIT, Schneider/Motivair (Bengaluru facility, Feb-2026) and STULZ (plant, Jun-2026) - while the domestic layer is fragmented HVAC and machining capacity. India's one defensible niche is two-phase fluid chemistry, via Navin Fluorine's Chemours licence at Surat.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Early in a steep adoption curve rather than late-cycle: liquid is moving from pilot to default in AI halls while the installed base of air-cooled capacity is still the majority, so the replacement pool has barely started.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series exists for data-centre liquid cooling in the registry; the listed exposures are diversified HVAC, chemicals and machining companies whose multiples are not attributable to this node.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Heat rejection and precision machining/skiving are domestic; cold plates, CDUs and quick-disconnects are foreign-designed and largely imported; fluids are the one high-margin node with a listed Indian participant.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Capex is modest against the data-centre shell - skiving, brazing, helium leak-test and clean assembly - so entry is affordable. The binding constraint is hyperscaler qualification time, not capital.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Standards are still forming (OCP cold-plate specifications, two-phase fluids under PFAS pressure) and the fluid transition is a live design risk, but the direction - direct-to-chip now, immersion later - is not in doubt.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: PFAS regulation and the 3M exit make two-phase fluid supply a single-source question, there is no Indian cold-plate standard, and leak-detection and DCIM integration capability is thin domestically.

missing_critical: India liquid-cooling value series rests on a single tier-3 forecast

value_capture.basis: The highest-margin node in the chain and the only one where a listed Indian company holds a real position: Navin Fluorine manufactures Chemours' Opteon two-phase fluid at Surat, against a global field of two or three qualified suppliers and a PFAS-driven supply retreat.

Small revenue, disproportionate margin: leak-free blind-mate connectors are a qualification-gated niche with a handful of global suppliers (Staubli, CPC, Parker). High switching costs once designed into a rack.

Integration-heavy and mid-value: pumps, plate heat exchanger and controls assembled into a skid, with foreign leaders and a credible Indian entrant set (RDP, Dynetics, Neometrix, KuhlTherm, plus Blue Star and Voltas). Real revenue, unremarkable pricing power.

High value per rack and the node every GPU platform specifies, but the design and the skived-fin process sit with foreign suppliers. The domestic machining capability exists and is not yet dedicated to data-centre cold plates - which is the opening.

Software-like economics inside a hardware chain: high gross margin, low capex, and stickiness once the hall's telemetry runs on it. The domestic capability is thin, which is why it is a localisation opportunity rather than a current pool.

The recurring annuity in the chain: coolant top-up, filtration, contamination testing and recycling recur for the life of a hall, are billed as a service, and carry almost no capex. Almost entirely unlisted today.
A real but still-small pool that depends on fluid availability and on IT vendors certifying immersion-ready hardware. Strategically interesting, economically unproven at Indian scale.

value_capture.node: Heat Rejection (Chillers / Dry Coolers / Plate HX)
value_capture.basis: The largest domestic revenue pool and the weakest economics: a competitive HVAC and heat-exchanger business (Voltas, Blue Star, Thermax, KRN) where growth comes with the market rather than from pricing. Low barriers, moderate returns.

industries.title: Defence Electro-Optics & Thermal Imaging (India)

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Prime integration earns real margin - BEL's order book was Rs 68,717 cr at 1-Oct-2026, and Paras Defence posted FY26 revenue of Rs 476 cr with an order book of Rs 986 cr - but roughly 80% of an EO/IR sight's material value is imported detectors, germanium optics and cryocoolers, so domestic margin is earned on assembly, optics and integration.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: India military EO/IR USD 1.04 bn (2025) to USD 1.19 bn (2026) and USD 1.78 bn (2030), a 10.4% CAGR over 2026-2030 [REPORTED-T2], with last-year growth of +14.4% [CALCULATED]. The pull is programme-led: the BEL GeM thermal-imager bid closed 22-Oct-2026 and night-vision, seeker and counter-drone lines are all ramping.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Structurally attractive for incumbents: BEL is the productionisation monopoly for DRDO-developed sights and BELOP holds the image-intensifier tube line, gated by DGQA acceptance and army trials. Private entrants are climbing - Paras, Data Patterns, RRP - but the qualification moat is high and the customer is a single buyer.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Defence capital outlay is in a multi-year upswing and EO/IR is a priority category, so the ordering cycle is favourable. The lumpiness is in award timing and single-buyer budget absorption, not in demand.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series exists for Indian defence EO/IR in the registry; the listed exposure sits inside diversified defence-electronics companies whose multiples are not attributable to this node.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: The deepest nodes leak: FPA dies, germanium blanks, cryocoolers, ROIC silicon and test gear are ~90-100% imported, while integration, image-intensifier tubes, optics assembly and software are domestic.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Integration, optics and electronics are affordable and the TDF and iDEX routes part-fund development; a detector fab is not, which is why the detector layer has stayed imported through decades of DRDO effort.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Migration is under way - cooled MCT/InSb toward uncooled microbolometer for volume, germanium toward chalcogenide glass, and SWIR/3D imaging for seekers - and India participates at the module rather than the die level.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Germanium is the sharpest chokepoint: China controls supply, prices are up roughly 5x since 2023 and lead times run to ~7 months, and the chalcogenide escape is early. Detector and ROIC imports are years-class exposures.

value_capture.basis: The node where the profit and the dependency both sit: cooled MCT/InSb and uncooled microbolometer dies are ~100% imported, priced by a handful of foreign fabs, and specified into every sight. Highest value capture in the chain and the largest localisation prize.

A near-monopoly inside the domestic chain - BELOP is effectively the only Indian tube line - with genuine pricing power and very high switching costs. Pool growth is modest because the volume is in sights rather than tubes.

The largest domestic pool and the one that controls the programme: BEL's DRDO productionisation role, DGQA acceptance and army trials make it very hard to displace. Pricing power is constrained by a single-buyer procurement process, not by competition.

The IDDCA is a small, high-value module that stops the whole sight if it fails, and the cooler inside it is imported from Israel and Europe. Strategic weight is high; the domestic position is assembly and integration only.

Where Indian design capability is closest to world class - Data Patterns, BEL and Zen build the boards and processing chains - but the ROIC and FPGA silicon underneath is imported, which caps the margin.

A climbing private pool - Paras Defence, RRP Defence - but the margin is squeezed by the input it depends on: germanium blanks are imported, China-controlled and up roughly 5x since 2023. Bottleneck weight is far higher than its pricing power.

The fastest-appreciating pool per rupee of revenue: fusion, ATR and tracking software carries software-like margins, near-zero capex and strong lock-in once fielded. Small today relative to hardware, and the most likely to compound.
Blackbodies, collimators, MTF benches and diamond-turning machines are ~90-100% imported, and without them nothing qualifies for DGQA acceptance. Tiny pool, disproportionate strategic weight.

The volume end of the chain - BEL's GeM thermal-imager tender is exactly this node - but it is competed on price against imports and carries the lowest margin per unit of value. Good revenue, ordinary economics.

industries.title: India Display Manufacturing

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Module assembly is 15-20% of module cost and a competitive conversion business, while array/cell processing (30-35%), glass and materials (20-25%) and driver ICs (15-20%) earn the real margin offshore. The 20% BCD on finished panels and the 5% open-cell duty protect the domestic layer, so the economics are policy-supported rather than structural.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: India display market USD 8-10 bn (2026) to USD 18-22 bn (2035) at a 9-11% nominal CAGR (IndexBox, 2026); the narrower display-module series runs USD 4.41 bn (2026) to USD 6.85 bn (2031) at 7.6% (MarketsandMarkets, Sep-2026). The ECMS 5th tranche (Rs 69,548 crore, Aug-2026) and the unclaimed display-fab scheme leave the front end as an open, large prize.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Panel supply is a Chinese/Korean/Taiwanese oligopoly (BOE, CSOT, HKC, Samsung Display, LGD); India's module layer is fragmenting fast with 106 ECMS projects approved, so domestic rivalry is destructive at the assembly end and absent at the top.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Mid-build-out: module capacity is being added ahead of demand on a duty step-change, while LCD panel prices remain cyclical and the fab window has been open since 2021 without a taker.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series in the registry - the page carries no sector multiple data, and listed exposure is too narrow (one direct module play) to read as an industry multiple.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: India captures 15-20% of module cost. Array/cell, glass substrate, polariser, liquid crystal/OLED emitters and DDICs are all imported; only module assembly and test are domestic.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: A Gen 8.6 LCD fab is USD 3-5 bn and remains unfunded despite a 50% capex subsidy; module lines are far cheaper but earn thin conversion margins.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: The LCD-to-OLED/AMOLED migration is happening offshore, and Indian lines are imported turnkey; the risk is being locked into trailing-node assembly.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Import dependence is structural (open cell 90%+ from China, DDIC and materials ~100%), offset by captive growing demand and duty protection; a China supply interruption would stop the lines.

missing_critical: capex and IRR for an Indian Gen 8.6 display fab
segment-level ROCE for Indian module assemblers

value_capture.basis: The largest pool in the chain - 30-35% of module cost - and the one India does not have. Absent since 2021 despite a 50% capex subsidy; Omdia sees no operational front-end fab before 2031, so whoever builds it faces no domestic rival and a captive duty-protected market.

15-20% of module cost, no Indian design house or fab, and 16-20 week lead times on automotive grades. A fabless design entry is plausible long before a panel fab, which makes this the cheapest route into the upstream pool.

The fastest-growing slice: OLED share of India's mobile display procurement is expected to rise from 25% (2026) to 40% (2030). ~USD 4.2 bn of AMOLED panels are imported annually, and the capital and process know-how keep the pool with Samsung Display, LGD and BOE.

Every Indian module line is built on imported equipment, so the tooling pool leaks abroad even when the assembly is domestic. A small pool, high barriers, and a genuine localisation opportunity as the installed base of lines grows.

20-25% of module cost and structurally single-sourced (Corning, AGC). The Adani-Hon Hai Gen 10.5 plan collapsed in Jan-2026 citing exactly this dependency; Vedanta's AvanStrate is the only listed Indian touchpoint, and it is a conglomerate-minor asset.
A small but ~100% imported film layer concentrated in Japan, Korea and China. Attractive margin per unit, but too small a pool to justify a standalone Indian plant at current module volumes.

The fastest-growing demand pool (12-15% CAGR, display area per vehicle rising from 8-10 to 14-18 inches by 2030) with design-in switching costs. Margin sits in qualification and integration rather than in the panel, and Indian module makers can serve it.

The layer India is actually building: 15-20% of module cost, thin-margin and competitive, but volume is compounding and duty protection (20% BCD on finished panels) hands it a widening spread. Value capture is real but shallow - it is conversion, not technology.

industries.title: India Drone Subsystems

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: OEM/assembly and DaaS carry the margin; the component layer is thin and import-gated. Defence-grade mix supports pricing, but 'white-labelling' imported parts as Made-in-India compresses the spread on commercial platforms.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: India drone (UAV) market USD 0.47 bn (2025) to USD 1.39 bn (2030), a 24.4% nominal CAGR (MarketsandMarkets, 2026); the subsystem layer is growing faster still - propulsion USD 95 mn (2025) to USD 350 mn (2030) at 29.8%. Component localisation, not platform growth, is the open pool.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Over 600 drone makers and 200+ component suppliers: fragmented at the platform end, with an import ban and PLI protecting the field. Barriers are low, so price competition is real; defence programmes favour a qualified few.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Early-growth and policy-driven: defence procurement is lumpy and disclosure-light, and the PLI has ended without a successor scheme in force.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series in the registry - listed exposure is a handful of names and the page carries no sector multiple data.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Flight controllers, ESCs, BLDC motors, optics/gimbals and RF datalinks are largely imported (IDSA puts imported components above 75%, contested by industry claims of 70-75% indigenous at the top firms); only airframes, cables and assembly are reliably domestic.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Low capital intensity at assembly and subsystem level, which is why entry is crowded; defence qualification and type certification, not capex, are the real gates.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Fast-moving (autonomy, AI, BVLOS, counter-UAS) with Indian firms designing on imported silicon; the risk is design-out when a processor or RF module is embargoed.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Component import dependence above 75% by the IDSA count, single-origin China supply for motors and magnets, lumpy defence demand, and live cybersecurity exposure on datalinks.

missing_critical: audited domestic value-addition by Indian OEMs
defence procurement pipeline beyond disclosed contracts

value_capture.basis: The drone's brain and the single hardest node to localise: autopilot, IMU and GNSS fusion, largely imported or open-source-based. Every platform needs one, it carries the certification risk, and the firmware lock-in makes switching expensive.

Datalinks and telemetry are defence-qualified, export-controlled (SCOMET 5B) and largely imported. Qualification is the moat, and the counter-UAS build-out adds a second demand pool on the same capability.

The payload decides whether a defence customer buys the platform at all, and stabilised gimbals and EO/IR sensors are almost entirely imported. High barrier, high design-in stickiness, poor cash conversion because of inventory and qualification cycles.
An imported core today with credible domestic entrants. Small value per unit, but it gates motor performance and pairs with the flight controller, so it is bundled into the same localisation push.

The fastest-growing subsystem pool (propulsion at 29.8% CAGR) and the most crowded: domestic entrants are emerging on motors and propellers, but magnets and power MOSFETs inside them are imported, so value leaks at the material layer.

Where India's domestic value already sits - and precisely because it is easy. Carbon and glass composite fabrication is competitive, low-barrier and priced as a commodity, so it captures the least value in the chain despite being the most localised node.

industries.notes: Scored during the 2026-11-09 backfill pass from the page's own evidence and the industry-data sourcing ladder; valuation left UNAVAILABLE because no industry-level multiple series exists.

industries.title: India EHV / HV Power Cables

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Cable makers are earning record margins on a richer EHV and export mix, with branded distribution supporting pricing power in LV/MV.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: HV cable (above 33 kV, land) Rs 8,038 cr (CY2024) to Rs 20,344 cr (CY2030F) at 16.7% nominal CAGR — the fastest voltage band — inside a wires-and-cables market going from Rs 1,00,000 cr (FY26) to Rs 1,57,500 cr (FY30).

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Consolidating into six or seven listed majors, but LV and MV remain crowded and price-competitive.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Capacity is being added into a rising market — Polycab's EHV line by end-CY2026, KEI Sanand Phase-II by Mar-2027 — with HV/EHV output up 10.3% in FY26.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Conductor drawing and insulation are domestic; HV/EHV XLPE and semiconductive compounds are foreign, and ~50% of EHV consumption is still imported.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: VCV/CCV lines are capital-heavy with 2-3 year lead times and no Indian equipment OEM — a genuine barrier that also slows capacity response.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: 550 kV is the domestic frontier and submarine cable is absent entirely — no plant and no repair ship.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Concentrated compound supply (Borouge/Borealis, Hanwha), imported EHV competition, and copper and aluminium price volatility.

value_capture.basis: The node that keeps the money today: record margins on a richer EHV and export mix, high-teens ROIC at Polycab and KEI, and a 16.7% segment CAGR - though the capability rests on imported lines and compounds.
Imported and concentrated, and the single input that decides whether an Indian EHV line can run at all; a qualified domestic compound would be a genuine toll.
A narrower version of the same story: no Indian maker, formulated to the cable OEM's process, requalification measured in years.
The capital good that gates entry: every new EHV plant in India is an imported CCV or VCV line, so the equipment maker earns the capex cycle rather than the cable cycle.
Accessories carry more margin per unit than the cable and are largely imported at EHV: a small pool with disproportionate pricing power.
No Indian plant and no Indian lay vessel - the pool exists only as an import, and the barrier is a ship as much as a factory.
Domestic and competitive, L1-tendered, with route and right-of-way risk: it carries the schedule but not the margin.
Copper and aluminium pass through at metal-indexed prices; Apar's scale wins volume, not pricing power.
