industries.title: India Electrical & Electronic Equipment

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: The equipment layer now earns well — CG Power's Power Systems segment made 25.1% PBIT on sales in Q2 FY27 at a 25% annualised ROCE, and Polycab earned a 10.0% PAT margin on 53% revenue growth — but the electronics half is thin-margin assembly and the trade deficit widened 33.9% in FY26, so the sector average sits mid-scale.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: Consumption of USD 59 bn in FY25 is projected at 11-13% CAGR to USD 170-205 bn by 2035, backed by Rs 9.16 lakh crore of NEP transmission capex, Rs 77,051 crore of approved ECMS projects and Rs 1,27,500 crore under Semicon 2.0 — but a rising share of that growth is currently met by imports, which caps the domestic capture.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Transformers and HV switchgear remain a four-to-five-player oligopoly with 18-24 month lead times, while cables are fragmenting as UltraTech and Adani enter and EMS stays crowded; China still supplies 45.1% of India's Chapter 85 imports, which sets the price ceiling on the component layer.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Late rather than mid-cycle: order books are at records (CG Power backlog Rs 23,646 crore, +58%; order intake +90% in Q2 FY27), transformer prices have risen for four years, and the market already pays 35x FY27 earnings for the largest cable maker.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series exists in the registry. The only datapoint gathered is Polycab at 35x FY27e and 29x FY28e EPS (Anand Rathi, 16-Oct-2026), which is one company and cannot set an industry score.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Assembly is thoroughly domestic and localisation is moving down a tier — the Aug and Nov 2026 ECMS tranches approved multi-layer PCB, copper foil, copper-clad laminate, rare-earth magnets and capacitor film — but CRGO, power-semiconductor dies, passives and the machinery that builds the plants all still arrive from abroad.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Equipment capex is modest and self-funded: Polycab spent Rs 610 crore in H1 FY27 against Rs 4,520 crore of net cash, and CG Power's 10,000 MVA transformer expansion is Rs 68 crore; the fab and OSAT layer is capital-heavy but carries 35-40% capex support under Semicon 2.0.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: The chain is mid-migration — SiC and GaN devices are growing above 30% CAGR, 765 kV and HVDC are becoming standard at the top of the range, and metering is software-led — but domestic design capability in power semiconductors and HVDC control is still partial.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Three dated exposures stack: China's rare-earth suspension lapses on 10-Nov-2026 with 85% of India's magnets sourced there, a CRGO anti-dumping duty would raise the industry's largest single material cost (25-30% of a transformer), and 59% of machine-tool consumption is imported.

missing_critical: HS-code import intensity split by component node
firm-level capacity utilisation and order-book cover by segment

value_capture.basis: MOVED TO RANK 1 (the prior page treated cables as the leading pool). 18-24 month lead times, four to five qualified 765 kV OEMs, and CG Power's Power Systems segment at 25.1% PBIT on 25% annualised ROCE make this the best returns pool in the chain. Cash conversion stays at 2 because the backlog is funded through working capital.

HV GIS grew 41.8% in FY26 while MV GIS fell 11.9%, so the value is concentrated at the top of the voltage range where few firms qualify. The LT switchgear and panel layer is the opposite case: Rs 25,706 crore of imports against Rs 12,339 crore of exports, with exports down 28%.

The largest revenue pool and the best cash conversion in the chain (Polycab net cash Rs 4,520 crore, working capital ~11 days), but barriers are thinning: UltraTech and Adani have both announced entry, and management has taken no pricing action in response. Ranked below transformers on profit capture despite earning more revenue.

Barriers moved 4 to 5: DGTR's June-2026 case treats JSW-JFE as the sole eligible domestic producer, with NLMK disqualified for its Russian links. But the entire economics rest on a duty that has not been notified, and GTRI argues a duty would not cut import dependence at 40-50 kt of domestic output against 400-450 kt of demand.

The deepest dependency and the longest runway, but almost no operating-profit share exists in India today: the domestic layer is OSAT and packaging, 5 of 12 ISM units are producing, and CG Power's semiconductor segment still ran an EBIT loss of Rs 34 crore in Q2 FY27.

~90% of PCB demand is imported and passives have no listed domestic pure-play, so the pool is real but currently offshore. Barriers ease as ECMS plants land (Kaynes HDI up to 74 layers shipping from Q3 FY27; copper foil and CCL approved), which is why the growth score is 5 and the current op-share score is 1.

Annuity-like AMISP cash flows and multi-year visibility (7.24 crore meters installed against 20.33 crore sanctioned), but price is set by discom tenders, >60% of subcomponents are imported, and the RDSS sunset date of 31-Mar-2028 puts a hard end on the visible pool.

The largest revenue pool by far (Dixon's FY25 revenue ~Rs 38,860 crore) and the weakest on every quality axis: no pricing power, 15-20% domestic value addition in mobile manufacturing, and customers who can re-tender. Value accrues only to those who integrate backwards into PCB, laminate and OSAT.

Overall = sum(category weight x score / 5) x 100, renormalised over supported categories: (3x.20 + 4x.15 + 3x.15 + 2x.15 + 3x.10 + 4x.05 + 3x.05) = 2.60; 2.60/0.85 = 3.059; overall = 3.059/5 x 100 = 61.2. Coverage 85% (valuation null). Structural group 65.7, current-opportunity group 40.0, risk lens 40.0. First scored pass for this entry (the 2026-10-09 version carried no score block). Direction changes versus the prior prose: transformers are now ranked above cables on profit capture, and machinery plus rare-earth magnets were added as first-class bottlenecks.

industries.title: India EMS / ODM

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Build-to-print margins are thin; value accrues to the customer's design.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: India EMS market ~USD 40-45 bn (FY25) to >USD 150 bn by FY30, ~27-30% CAGR — the strongest growth series in the registry.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Fragmented and competitive; scale and customer relationships decide winners.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: No cycle-position evidence on the page.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Assembly is the value-chain position; PCB demand ~90% imported, so a layer of value stays offshore.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: SMT lines are moderate capital — expandable without mega-project risk.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Build-to-print; design stays with the customer.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Consumer-linked demand and customer concentration; execution risk moderate.

value_capture.basis: Over 90% imported on passives and 90-95% on ICs; the deepest moat and the highest return per rupee of revenue in the chain, which is exactly why ECMS was designed around it. The catch is scale: Vishay, TDK, Molex and Amphenol are entering through the scheme, so an Indian entrant competes with the incumbent's own Indian plant.

The clearest toll in the chain: a ~USD 4.3 bn Indian market against ~USD 600 mn of domestic production (~90% imported), and Emkay benchmarks the business at ~35% gross margin, 15-18% EBITDA and ~16% post-tax ROCE at steady state - two to three times what box-build earns. Every major EMS player is now building here (Kaynes, Syrma, Amber, SRF), and a 30% anti-dumping duty on sub-6-layer boards from China/HK raises the switching cost.

Effectively 100% imported today and one of the largest value blocks inside a handset BOM; Dixon's 74:26 JV with HKC carries a ₹370 cr commitment for 24 mn smartphone displays a year, which is a licence-and-partner barrier rather than a capital one - and the JV trials have already slipped, so the pool is real but not yet captured.

Largely imported, with Dixon's Q Tech JV scaling 40 mn to 190-200 mn units a year for ₹6,000-7,000 cr of revenue - but management guides to sub-10% EBITDA margin on it, so this is a share-of-BOM play rather than a margin play.

The single largest slice of the domestic EMS pie (~42% of 2025 revenue) and where the HMLV specialists earn their margin: Syrma ran 11.3% operating EBITDA and 25.6% gross margin in FY26, Kaynes 15.8% EBITDA. Pricing power is thin and customer-set, but a qualified high-mix line is not trivially replicated.

Import-dominated, and the ECMS list is pulling global connector makers in directly (TE Connectivity, Molex, Amphenol) rather than through Indian partners - so the domestic share of this node is more likely to arrive as a foreign-owned plant than as an Indian business.

The biggest revenue pool in the chain and the thinnest: Dixon's FY26 operating margin was 2.1%, and its CFO put mobile assembly at ~3.5% before the 5-6% PLI benefit. Dixon's Q2 FY27 operating margin fell to 2.7% from 3.8% as material costs reached 94.9% of revenue - scale without pricing power.
Domestic and low-barrier: sheet-metal, tooling and moulding capacity already exists, so localisation here adds volume but little margin - the node is a share-of-BOM contributor, not a profit pool.

industries.title: India Engine MRO

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: A shop visit is 60-70% material (OEM-controlled), 20-30% labour and 10-20% repairs. Domestic MROs reach ~20% EBITDA margins on CRISIL's read, but the margin sits with the OEM's parts and LLP sales, not with the shop.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: India commercial MRO demand USD 4.4 bn (2025) to USD 5.7 bn (2030) at ~5.4% p.a. (Alton via IBEF, Mar-2026), with engine MRO almost half of it (~USD 2.2 bn in 2025). The prize is substitution, not growth: only ~14% of Indian carriers' MRO spend was done in India in FY24, rising to ~20% in FY26, with 75-80% still going overseas.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: A global OEM oligopoly (CFM/GE, Safran, P&W, MTU, LHT) controls parts, data and LLPs; India's domestic field is an unlisted oligopoly - AIESL, Safran SAESI, and IndiGo building in-house. No listed pure-play exists, which is itself a signal of how gated the node is.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Aftermarket demand is fleet-driven rather than GDP-driven and is compounding: the Indian fleet passes 1,800 aircraft by 2030 and global LEAP shop visits go from ~600-800 (2025) to 5,000+ (2040). The engine-recall cycle has already pulled forward shop visits.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series in the registry, and no listed domestic pure-play to derive one from.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: ~80% of engine MRO value leaves India. LLPs, airfoils, FADEC/ECUs and OEM technical data are all controlled upstream; India's natural edge is labour, the smallest line in the shop-visit waterfall.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Test cells, tooling and hangars are heavy, and critical mass needs 2,000-2,500 aircraft under a single operator base. Payback is long and the capacity decision has to precede the demand it serves.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: New-generation engines (LEAP, GTF) require OEM data and licensed workscopes, so capability migrates with the OEM partnership rather than with the shop's own R&D. Safran SAESI and the IndiGo-CFM MoU are the live routes in.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: OEM data and parts access is the binding constraint, the CAR-66 engine-CRS licence anomaly persists, and part lead times run beyond 12 months - but demand is contracted and growing, which offsets much of it.

missing_critical: India-specific engine MRO revenue (vs total demand)
shop-visit counts by engine type in India

value_capture.basis: The gate the whole chain passes through: without an engine-manual licence and OEM data an Indian shop cannot legally open a modern engine. It is not a factory but it captures the material margin, and it is why 75-80% of the work still goes overseas.

A captive, OEM-priced annuity: LLPs must be replaced at fixed cycles regardless of condition, so the revenue is non-discretionary and the price is set by the OEM. The single most attractive node in the chain and the one India cannot enter without OEM sanction.

The repair pool an independent can actually win: airfoil refurbishment and coating are DER-licensable, capital-intensive and skill-gated. PTC Industries and Azad Engineering already supply the forged parts upstream, which is the realistic Indian entry point.

Module-level exchange and repair is the intermediate step between line work and full overhaul, and the natural way to build capability without a full shop. Value per event is high; the constraint is OEM-approved module workscopes.

Where India's capacity actually sits - AIESL plus Safran SAESI's 300-LEAP-visits-a-year centre. Strategically pivotal and bottlenecked, but a low-pricing-power business: the shop competes on turnaround time against Singapore, Dubai and Kuala Lumpur on work the OEM already priced.

The independents' margin lever: used serviceable material and PMA parts cut the 60-70% material line that the OEM controls. Thin in India today, with long turnaround times, but capital-light and cash-generative where it exists.

A quiet gate: no test cell, no released engine, and slots are capacity-rationed. Small revenue pool, heavy capital, long payback - strategically decisive but financially mediocre as a standalone business.

The skills gate: licensed engine certifying staff and DGCA/CAR-145 approvals bind tighter than any material and cannot be bought quickly at any price. It captures almost no revenue itself and decides who can capture all of it.

industries.title: India EV Powertrain & Traction Systems

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Motor and controller assembly is domestic, competitive and thin-margin under OEM price pressure; gears, shafts and differentials are where Indian suppliers already earn real margin (Sona Comstar BEV revenue Rs 1,154 crore in FY26); power modules and control silicon earn the best margin and are imported.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: India's EV powertrain components and traction-motor manufacturing was ~USD 1.82 bn (2024/25 base) and is forecast to USD 7.7 bn by 2032 at 22.8% nominal CAGR (2025-2032); the narrower traction-motor series runs USD 548 mn (2025) to USD 1,766 mn (2032) at 18.2%. FY26 retail was 2.45 mn EVs (+24.6%) at only 8.3% penetration, with PMP localisation mandates pulling content onshore.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Downstream assembly is crowded - every major tier-1 and several OEMs now build motors and e-axles - while the upstream magnet, power-module and control-IC layers are a foreign oligopoly. The result is fierce rivalry on the assembly node and none where the value sits.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Early-scaling and volume-led: 6.8 mn traction units in 2025 rising to 9.27 mn motors by 2032, with penetration at 8.3% of total vehicles. The ICE price reset after GST 2.0 (Sep-2025) slowed the value mix but not the volume trajectory.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series in the registry - the page carries no sector multiple data for the component layer.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Magnets ~80% imported, power modules 60-70% imported, control ICs near-total imports, and the design IP is licensed from Gtake, Inovance, EVR Motors and AEM. A motor assembled in India can be 50-60% local by process and far less by value.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Motor and inverter lines are moderate-capex and quick to install; a sintered-magnet plant is capital-heavy and still unfunded under the REPM scheme's 6,000 MTPA target. PLI-Auto and PMP support offset part of it.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: The architecture is migrating (SiC, rare-earth-free designs, integrated e-axles) but the design IP and the silicon are licensed or imported, so Indian participants risk design-out on the next platform cycle.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: China's REPM export licensing is live with no Indian automotive licence approved as of Sep-2026, the PMP deadline has slipped three times, and under 10% of the PLI-Auto outlay has been disbursed. Magnet supply is the structural exposure.

missing_critical: per-vehicle powertrain value split by segment
traction-grade power-module capex and IRR in India

value_capture.basis: Near-total import dependence and the node that carries functional-safety qualification. Fabless design entry is the realistic Indian route, and the switching cost is set by ASIL re-certification rather than by price.

The largest single pool inside the inverter and the one India does not have at traction scale: 60-70% of module consumption is imported, with no domestic line for automotive-grade IGBT or SiC. Capital-hungry and qualification-heavy, which is exactly why the margin survives.

The vehicle OEM sets the price for every node beneath it and captures platform margin, but it is a demand node rather than a component node - included because in this chain it is the party that actually decides who earns what.

Where Indian suppliers already earn real returns: Sona Comstar's BEV revenue was Rs 1,154 crore in FY26, 35% of automotive product revenue. Integrated e-axle assembly is the migrating pool - whoever assembles motor, inverter and reducer captures the system margin.

Under ~5% of vehicle cost but it gates the entire motor - the cheapest bottleneck in the industry and the hardest to substitute. ~80% imported, no listed Indian maker, and the 6,000 MTPA REPM scheme is still at RFP stage, so the pool is a policy-created opening rather than an existing business.

Domestic, competitive and exposed to OEM price pressure. Nine listed players touch the node, which is the clearest evidence that it is not where the money stays - the growth is real, the margin is not.

A domestic materials pool that mostly stays in India - JSW Steel and the lamination converters. Top-grade thin CRNO is still imported, which is where the residual value leaks, but the node is commodity-priced.
Contract-manufacturing economics: high volume, negligible pricing power, easy substitution. It is the node most likely to be localised first and least likely to keep any of the value it creates.

industries.notes: Scored during the 2026-11-09 backfill pass from the page's own evidence and the industry-data sourcing ladder; valuation left UNAVAILABLE because no industry-level multiple series exists.

industries.title: Genomic Sequencing

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Instruments and sequencing chemistry are high-margin and almost wholly offshore; the domestic layer is clinical service, which is competitive, reimbursement-sensitive and capital-light. Value per test falls as volume rises, so the economics reward whoever owns consumables.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: India NGS was ~USD 284 mn (IMARC) to ~USD 298 mn (GrandView) in 2025 and is forecast to USD 1.34-1.43 bn by 2033-34, ~20% nominal CAGR, with the installed base going from 400-500 high-throughput sequencers (2026) to 1,000-1,400 by 2035. The clinical transition plus state genome programmes (GenomeIndia's 10,000 genomes, a proposed Rs 8,000 crore corpus) is a structural, not cyclical, driver.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: A duopoly upstream - Illumina and Thermo Fisher hold an estimated 75-85% of the Indian installed base, Illumina alone ~80% of NGS - with MGI competing on price. Indian participants are squeezed into service and kits, where differentiation is thin.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Adoption-driven rather than cyclical: sequencing cost has fallen below USD 200 per whole genome and the demand pull is clinical reimbursement and public programmes, not capex cycles.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series in the registry - listed exposure is diagnostics chains and labware, which do not price this industry.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: More than 85% of instrument and core-consumable value leaves India; kits are 70-80% imported by value. Only the clinical-service and part of the bioinformatics layer stay domestic.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Capital-light: an instrument is Rs 45 lakh to Rs 3.5 crore and a service lab can be built against contracted volume, which is why the domestic service layer grew before any domestic manufacturing did.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Sequencing-by-synthesis holds 63.4% of the market and long-read is emerging at the premium end; Indian capability is nascent (Bayosthiti's benchtop programme, domestic panels), so the technology position is dependent rather than leading.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Structural import dependence on instruments, flow cells and enzymes, single-source flow cells, foreign interpretation databases (ClinVar, gnomAD) and data-sovereignty rules - offset by a large under-served population and state backing.

missing_critical: share of India NGS revenue captured domestically
installed-base count from a primary source

value_capture.basis: The recurring toll on every run, single-sourced per platform and priced by the instrument owner. Reagents and consumables are 49.6% of India NGS value on one scope and 92.1% on another, and 70-80% of kit value is imported - the most defensible pool in the chain and the least accessible.

Effectively 100% imported, with Illumina and Thermo at 75-85% of the installed base. The instrument is the gate: it decides whose chemistry and whose kits are consumed for the next seven years, which is why placement economics are so aggressive.

The one upstream pool with a credible Indian route in: domestic kit value is ~20-30% local content today, and enzymes and panels are where Genes2Me and Decipher Genomics are building. Smaller moat than flow cells, but far lower capital.

Labour- and IP-led, capital-light and growing fastest as interpretation becomes the bottleneck rather than sequencing. Indian reference data (GenomeIndia, IndiGen) is a genuine local asset, but the global databases it is checked against are foreign.

Panel design is where local epidemiology becomes a product, and it is the cheapest way to add differentiated value without a chemistry platform. Margin depends on reimbursement acceptance, and the probes themselves are largely imported.

The pool India actually captures - Metropolis, Dr Lal PathLabs, Thyrocare, Suraksha, Krsnaa. Real revenue and real growth, but competitive, reimbursement-sensitive, and dependent on imported kits and instruments, so the margin is a service margin.

The adjacent demand pool that pulls sequencing into routine care. Large and growing, but not a bottleneck node - it competes with PCR and other cheaper modalities, so it sets the price ceiling for genomic testing rather than capturing a premium.
Price-per-run falls every year and the customer can switch labs on turnaround and price. It is the volume engine of the Indian market and the weakest place to stand in it.

industries.notes: Scored during the 2026-11-09 backfill pass from the page's own evidence and the industry-data sourcing ladder; valuation left UNAVAILABLE because no industry-level multiple series exists.

industries.title: India Green Hydrogen & Electrolyser Manufacturing

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Green hydrogen is still 2-3x grey on delivered cost, so project economics rest on subsidy, the ISTS waiver and offtake contracts rather than on the technology; stack makers and BoP suppliers earn thin, competitive conversion margins.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: Green-hydrogen market USD 1.95 bn (2025) to USD 9.75 bn (2030) at 38.0% CAGR on IMARC endpoints, with 862,000 t/yr of demand and 3,000 MW/yr of electrolyser capacity awarded against ~8,000 t/yr and ~2 GW commissioned.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Stack manufacturing is crowded — L&T, Reliance, Adani, Waaree, Advait, BHEL — but almost every one licenses stack IP from Nel, McPhy, thyssenkrupp nucera or HydrogenPro, so rivalry is on balance sheet and land, not on technology.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Earliest-stage of the three energy transitions on this registry: awards are far ahead of delivery, SIGHT Tranche-I plants slipped into 2027, and no plant was fully commissioned as of Jul-2026.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry — the page carries no sector multiple series, and the pure-play stack makers are unlisted or foreign-listed.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Balance of plant is 68-76% of electrolyser cost and already ~45% domestic, which is real Indian value capture; membranes, catalysts, PTL, bipolar plates, critical minerals and stack IP all leak offshore.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Electrolyser and project capex is heavy and front-loaded against revenue that arrives after commissioning, and viability depends on a 25-year waiver and SIGHT subsidy — a financing structure, not a market one.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Pressurised alkaline is mature and PEM is scaling, with SOEC and AEM at pilot; India can assemble and integrate both but does not own the membrane, catalyst or stack design.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Demand creation is unresolved and named as the key bottleneck by SIGHT itself; iridium (~7.5 t/yr globally) and platinum are structural constraints with no Indian reserves; and SIGHT execution has slipped once already.

value_capture.basis: Nafion (PFSA) and Zirfon are proprietary, near-100% imported and about 0% domestic; CEEW puts the Nafion membrane plus carbon cloth at roughly 60% of total stack cost. Small revenue, exceptional margin, and a five-year barrier to any Indian entrant - the purest example in the registry of a pool that leaks entirely to imports.

Iridium supply is about 7.5 t/yr globally and India has no reserves, which makes this a structural tollbooth rather than a manufacturing business. The revenue pool is tiny relative to the system, so operating-profit share is low even though pricing power and barriers are maximal.

BoP is 60-76% of electrolyser system cost and is where India is genuinely strong: pumps, vessels, power systems, heat exchangers and fabrication already exist at commercial scale, and roughly 45% is domestic today. It is also the least defensible node - many bidders, no proprietary design, and Chinese BoP sets the price.

Stack and CCM manufacturing equipment is small, specialised and largely foreign, so the revenue pool is thin - but the suppliers are few, the switching cost is high and the pool grows with every gigafactory. This is the same structural gap as cell-line machinery in the battery chain.

The stack is 24-32% of system cost (CEEW: ~40% for PEM) and the contested prize, with L&T, Reliance, Adani, Waaree, Advait and BHEL all building capacity - but most stack IP is licensed in from Nel, McPhy, thyssenkrupp nucera and HydrogenPro, and Chinese alkaline systems at USD 270-280/kW set a price floor that caps realisable margin.

Downstream molecules carry the export value and the largest revenue pool - Reliance's 15-year Samsung C&T green-ammonia SPA is worth over USD 3 bn - but green hydrogen is still 2-3x grey on delivered cost, so the economics are set by subsidy and offtake contracts rather than by the asset. Capital intensity is very high.

Round-the-clock renewable power is the largest single cost line in a green-hydrogen project and the node India can actually deliver, sitting with NTPC Green, Adani Green, Tata Power and JSW behind a 25-year ISTS waiver. Like every generation annuity it is a financing spread with no pricing power.

industries.notes: This run REPLACES the prior Market & growth block, which rested on a tier-3 source and reported 3-year and last-year splits as UNAVAILABLE. Opportunity now uses the IMARC series (USD 1.95 bn 2025 to USD 9.75 bn 2030, 38.0% CAGR) and the conflicting NITI Aayog / third-house estimates are shown as a range rather than averaged. Valuation left UNAVAILABLE — no industry valuation series. Value capture scored 2026-11-03 from this page's own BOM tree and ladder; the industry categories above are unchanged from the 2026-10-30 scoring.

industries.title: India Guns

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: DPSUs hold 76% of output on cost-plus deemed contracts with modest margins, while private entrants earn better returns but face multi-year qualification; ammunition value growth of ~4.93% a year caps the upside.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: The ammunition pool of ₹7,057 cr in 2023 growing to ₹11,981 cr by 2032 (4.93% CAGR) sits inside a defence production base growing 15.6% a year, with propellant capacity 5–6× short of demand — real but not fast-growing substitution.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Concentrated by regulation: 788 industrial licences across 462 companies, DPSUs at 76% of production and a handful of credible private players (Bharat Forge, L&T, Adani, Solar, Reliance) — barriers protect incumbents but the single buyer holds all pricing power.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Demand is at a record: ₹1.82 lakh cr of contracts concluded in FY26, exports +62.7%, private production at an all-time-high 24% share and ATAGS moving into delivery.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry — the page carries no sector multiple series.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Barrels, brass cases, energetics and assembly are substantially domestic and 91% of ammunition variants are indigenised, but propellants and primers, antimony, and barrel-forging and CNC machinery remain imported.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Capital-intensive filling, forging and proof facilities with long qualification and heavy working capital; DPSU advances soften it, private entrants carry it on their own balance sheets.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: DRDO design capability plus Bharat Forge, L&T and Reliance tooling is genuinely indigenous at platform level, but propellant chemistry and much of the production machinery are still bought in.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: A single buyer (MoD) sets price and timing, propellant and primer supply is a wartime single point of failure, and the licensing and export-control regime constrains both entry and exit.

value_capture.basis: The deepest bottleneck in the chain: propellant capacity runs 5–6× short of demand and NC/NG and primers are partly imported [REPORTED-T2]. Supply is a near-duopoly — Premier Explosives as India's first private solid-propellant maker (MRSAM, LRSAM, Astra) and Solar Industries, with Munitions India's cordite factories as the state leg. Scarcity plus qualification-gated supply is the strongest pricing position on this page, and Solar's own guidance of holding 27–28% EBITDA rests on energetics and defence mix.

The largest volume pool and the fastest-growing private one. Solar Industries did FY26 revenue of ₹9,838 cr at ₹2,622 cr EBITDA (26.7%) and 27.4% RoCE, with defence revenue of ₹2,634 cr (+94%) and a ₹21,300 cr order book of which ~₹18,000 cr is defence [REPORTED-T1: FY26 annual report and May-2026 earnings call]; Munitions India carries a ₹28,939 cr order book [REPORTED-T1]. Demand is set by the services rather than the market, so switching is slow and pricing is negotiated — strong but not commodity pass-through.

High-value, low-volume, and now majority-private: Bharat Forge holds a 60% share of ATAGS (184 guns of the ₹6,900 cr order) and L&T supplies the K9 Vajra-T (₹7,629 cr, 100 guns) [REPORTED-T2]. Value per platform is high and requalification is glacial, which protects price — but revenue is lumpy and tender-timed, which is why cash conversion and op_share are scored below the ammunition layer.

Gun-barrel metallurgy is the qualification gate: Bharat Forge is the world's largest forgings maker and the ATAGS barrel source, Yantra India is the state barrel forger, and cold-hammer forging machinery is imported [REPORTED-T2]. A small revenue pool with disproportionate strategic weight — the barrier is process know-how, not scale.

BEL and BDL sit on the integration layer with the largest absolute order books — BDL at ~₹26,176 cr as of 31-Mar-2026 [REPORTED-T1] — but cash conversion is weak against government receivables and pricing is cost-plus or L1-tender rather than proprietary. Large pool, thin retained margin.

Few qualified domestic sources: MIDHANI for special steels, superalloys and titanium, Kalyani Steels for the ATAGS barrel alloy [REPORTED-T2]. The barrier is qualification rather than volume, and defence steel is a minority share of both companies' revenue, so the pool is strategically important and economically modest.

The metal-forms layer is concentrated among unlisted players (Mittal Group: ~2 bn cups and 300 mn cases/yr at Indore) with copper and antimony import-dependent [REPORTED-T3]. No listed coverage in the selected universe, so the pool's economics are visible only through its customers' cost base — scored as a cost-bearer, not a value keeper.

Mid-value and shifting from DPSU to private integrated hubs — Adani's Gwalior LMG line (up to 100,000 weapons/yr, >90% domestic sourcing) and IRRPL's AK-203 at Korwa (601,427 rifles) [REPORTED-T2]. Several well-funded entrants chasing a modest pool is exactly the mix that compresses price, hence the low pricing-power score.

industries.notes: Opportunity uses the same series as the Market & growth digest block (KPMG ammunition market of Rs 7,057 cr in 2023 rising to Rs 11,981 cr by 2032 at 4.93%, inside FY26 defence production of Rs 1.78 lakh cr). Valuation left UNAVAILABLE — the registry carries no industry valuation data. Value capture (added 2026-11-02) scores 8 nodes taken verbatim from this page's own BOM tree and value-chain ladder, on the separate Registry Review §4 weighting (op_share 20%, pricing_power 15%, roic 15%, barriers 15%, bottleneck 10%, pool_growth 10%, cash_conversion 10%, switching 5%). It answers 'which node keeps the money' and is not blended into the industry score above.

industries.title: India Harmonic & RV Reducers

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: There is no domestic industry to have economics: ~100% of robotics-grade units are imported, and the price a new entrant would face is set by Chinese units landing at roughly half the Japanese cost.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: 10,500 robot installations in 2025 growing ~15% a year (27% CAGR over 2020–2025), with reducers at 30–40% of robot cost and 85–90% of component value imported — a real pool, but India is ~1/34th of China’s installation volume, so plant scale is hard to reach.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: A global oligopoly of Harmonic Drive Systems and Nabtesco (~75% of robot reducers) over an empty domestic field: for an incumbent the moat is exceptional, for an entrant the barrier is the same wall viewed from the other side.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Robot installations are rising 15% a year on PLI-driven electronics and auto capex, but the IFR flags a possible 2026 contraction when PLI-linked investment runs out, and demand is concentrated in one buyer group.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry, and no listed Indian pure-play exists on which to build a multiple.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: India has essentially zero presence in the node, and the layers that would make it possible — gear grinding machines, CMMs, flexspline-grade steel — are themselves imported, so there is no domestic chain to position in.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Capex is moderate but the real cost is time: sub-micron grinding, atmosphere-controlled heat treatment and 12–24 month qualification, with no revenue until a customer re-qualifies a joint.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: The 2020 patent expiry on harmonic drives genuinely lowered the legal barrier and Chinese suppliers proved the design can be copied, but the flexspline metallurgy and grinding process remain a decade-long transfer.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Chinese price competition at half the landed cost, rare-earth and export-control exposure on precision gearing, long qualification cycles and the absence of a domestic demand anchor.

value_capture.basis: The node that keeps the money in this chain, and it is not in India: Harmonic Drive Systems took ¥24.1 billion of orders in Apr–Jun 2026, up 55.7%, and lifted its operating margin from 0.9% to 11.0% — but 54% of the added sales became operating profit because the plants were already built (capex ¥4.8bn against depreciation ¥7.4bn). Robot orders were only about a quarter of that book, with surgical robots and chip tools doing the rest. Chinese competition is the live risk: Leaderdrive grew 38.6% in H1 2026 at a 20.1% net margin while pricing at a discount.

Nabtesco's franchise — about 60% of reducers in medium-to-large industrial robot joints by its own estimate — and the cleanest read on the robot cycle: reducer sales of ¥45.1 billion in H1 2026, up 23.6%, with segment margin doubling to 10.6% and the full-year plan raised to ¥94.6 billion. It is a utilisation business: incremental margin in the half was 33.3%, so the same asset earns very differently at the top and bottom of a capex cycle.

Not a revenue pool but the gate on every pool above it: Klingelnberg, Gleason, Nidec and Höfler grinders and ZEISS/Mitutoyo CMMs are imported in full, and no reducer plan can be qualified without them. Small, specialised, high-margin, and sold into every reducer plant anyone builds — the same structural position as cell-line machinery in batteries.

The sub-micron heart of the reducer and the reason a reducer plant is not a machining job: a thin-wall forged cup ground to form and a wave generator on ultra-precision bearings, both requiring heat treatment under tight atmosphere control. No Indian maker. The pool is small in revenue and enormous in strategic weight — it is the node that decides whether any domestic reducer programme can qualify at all.

The integration layer above the reducer, and the fastest-growing line in the incumbents' books: Harmonic Drive's North American mechatronics orders rose 336.2% to ¥4.4 billion with backlog up 176.2%, and mechatronics was ¥13.2 billion of its ¥59.6 billion FY26 sales. It captures the pairing of motor, reducer and encoder — which is also the layer where an Indian entrant with motor capability (Sona Comstar, Bharat Bijlee) could enter without solving the gearset first.

The demand node, included because it shows where the chain's margin actually sits: Yaskawa's robot orders rose 33% in Jun–Aug 2026 while its robot margin fell to 5.0% for the half — the assembler carries the volume and the component maker carries the margin. India's listed exposure to this chain is almost entirely here (ARAPL and adjacent precision engineers), which is precisely the wrong end of it.

industries.notes: Opportunity uses the same series as the Market & growth digest block (IFR installations of 9,120 units in 2024 and ~10,500 in 2025, 27% average annual growth 2020–2025, with imports at 85–90% of component value). No rupee market size exists at Level 1 or 2, so none is stated. Valuation left UNAVAILABLE. Value capture (added 2026-11-04) scores six nodes from this page's BOM tree and ladder on the separate Registry Review §4 weighting (op_share 20%, pricing_power 15%, roic 15%, barriers 15%, bottleneck 10%, pool_growth 10%, cash_conversion 10%, switching 5%). It answers 'which node keeps the money' and is not blended into the industry score above; with no domestic reducer maker, the scoring describes pools the incumbents hold and an Indian entrant would have to take.

industries.title: India HVDC & Power Electronics

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Attractive at project level for the few qualified bidders, but converter-station content is ~100% imported, so Indian participants capture civil works and erection rather than equipment margin.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: 32.3 GW NEP pipeline implying ~Rs 1.3 L cr of system capex [CALCULATED], with the market series at USD 15.07 bn (2025) to USD 31.06 bn (2035) at 7.5% — large, but the two market series conflict.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Valves and control code are a three-player global oligopoly; Indian participation is via JV and localisation mandate rather than independent capability.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Awards are lumpy and infrequent rather than cyclical — Barmer in Aug-2026, Khavda poles in 2028-29 — so order timing, not the cycle, drives sentiment.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Converter stations, DC XLPE compound and pre-moulded joints are all foreign; the localisation ladder (30% to FY28, 60% by FY35) is the only route in, and the first Indian converter-transformer order only landed in Dec-2025.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Project capital is enormous (Rs 24,819 cr for one 6 GW link) but borne by TBCB developers on regulated returns; equipment-level capex is modest.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: High-power thyristors, IGBT/SiC devices, converter control software and DC cable compound are all offshore — the deepest technology gap in the grid.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: The highest single-source concentration in the grid, plus Chinese component import relief running to Jul-2028 that undercuts the localisation case.

value_capture.basis: Proprietary control code is where converter-station margin is concentrated: it is software, it is specified once per link, and it cannot be reverse-engineered by the EPC. Pool growth is low because it is sold only with a converter station, but cash conversion and switching costs are the best in the chain.

The valve is the single largest equipment line inside a converter station and its IP sits with a three-player global oligopoly; Indian content is assembly at Hitachi Chennai and a GE Vernova Chennai line from 2027, so the domestic participant earns conversion margin on an imported thyristor bill. Barriers and switching are the highest in the chain: no utility requalifies a valve supplier inside a project cycle.

High-power devices carry the deepest technology gap in the Indian grid - there is no domestic high-power fab and the SiC line at Odisha is only approved. Economics are fab economics: excellent pricing power and barriers, poor cash conversion against very large sunk capital.

Custom-built and individually type-tested at 18-36 month leads, which is a genuine schedule bottleneck, but the manufacturing capability is now domestic - TARIL took the first Indian-origin private order in Dec-2025 and BHEL, CG Power and TARIL all build here. Long leads plus large advances mean working capital, not margin, is the constraint.

DC-rated cable is a global three-or-four-supplier product because the XLPE DC compound and pre-moulded joints are not made in India; Sterlite, KEI and Polycab are building capacity against the localisation mandate. Pricing power is real while capacity is short, but cable is capital-hungry and the compound stays imported.

The station is the largest revenue line and where BHEL plus Hitachi execute Khavda-Nagpur and Bhadla-Fatehpur, but it is consortium contracting priced against a regulated-return buyer, so the revenue is big and the margin is not. Local-content rules (30% to FY28, 60% by FY35) protect the position without creating pricing power.

TBCB developers such as PGCIL, Adani Energy Solutions, Resonia and IndiGrid hold a 25-35 year regulated-return annuity: predictable cash and high switching costs once the link is built, but the tariff is discovered at auction and capital cost is the whole game. This is a bond-like pool, not a margin pool.

industries.notes: Scored against 'Industry-Level Investment Parameters & Scoring Architecture'. Opportunity uses the same HVDC series as the Market & growth digest block, with the conflicting second series disclosed rather than averaged. Valuation left UNAVAILABLE. Value capture scored 2026-11-03 from this page's own BOM tree and ladder; the industry categories above are unchanged from the 2026-10-30 scoring.

industries.title: India Industrial Gases

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: One of the better economics on the registry: INOX Air Products earned a ~47% operating margin in FY26 with ~60% of revenue on annuity-like contracts and a net-debt-free balance sheet; Linde India's EBITDA margin was 28% in Q4 FY26 before compression. The merchant end is commoditised, the on-site end is not.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: Value grew 6.7% a year over 2020-25 and 7.6% last year, with forecasts clustering at 6-7.5% to 2028-31 - the same series carried in the Market & growth digest block (US$1,020m to US$1,410m, 12.4 mn tonnes in 2025). Steady GDP-plus growth rather than a step change; published sizes conflict on scope from US$1.31 bn to US$3.81 bn.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: 310 players nationally but a four-way oligopoly at scale (INOX Air Products, Linde, Air Liquide, Air Water); CRISIL calls the commodity end intensely competitive while specialty and electronic gases are qualification-gated. On-site contracts are won before a plant is built, which locks the pool to whoever commits capital first.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Steel is the anchor and steel is cyclical; argon normalised in FY26 after a supply-short FY25 spike, and INOX AP's merchant volumes actually fell 2% even as on-site grew 27%. The offsetting cycle is solar, semiconductor and data-centre demand, which is why the forecast holds at 7.5%.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry - the page carries no sector multiple series, and the market leader is unlisted.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: The strongest node mix on the page: on-site plants are built and owned domestically, cryogenic equipment is a genuine Indian export win (INOX India earns ~59% of revenue abroad at ~21-24% EBITDA), and only helium, rare gases, specialty blends and cold-box internals leak. Four of the highest-value nodes are imported or unlisted, which caps investability rather than capability.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Very capital intensive - INOX AP plans over ₹3,000 cr of capex across FY27-29 and every on-site win is a plant - but the returns are protected by take-or-pay contracts, power-cost escalation clauses in ~22% of revenue, and a net-debt-free leader. Capital is the barrier and the moat at once.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: ASU, VPSA and PFHE design still runs on foreign licences and imported cold-box internals, and electronic-grade purification is the acknowledged gap; but the operating capability, telemetry and cylinder logistics are domestic and improving.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Energy and feedstock pass-through, end-user cyclicality and import dependence on helium and rare gases - the Qatar Ras Laffan force majeure from March 2026 with a 3-5 year repair guide is the live example. Linde India's related-party and business-allocation matter adds a governance overhang at the listed leader.

value_capture.basis: Highest margin per cubic metre and the least localised pool: specialty, argon and rare gases are ~13.1% of Indian product revenue but carry the qualification burden - analytical control, container cleaning, redundancy - that turns a gas into a specification. INOX AP's ₹500 cr Dholera hub and the semiconductor fab pipeline are the demand anchor.

The annuity at the centre of the industry: 15-20 year take-or-pay contracts, ~48% of market value rising to ~52% by 2031, and ~60% of INOX AP's revenue is annuity-like. Returns are underwritten in double digits before a plant is committed, and the customer cannot switch once the pipeline is welded on.

India produces essentially none of it; supply is a handful of global fields and the Qatar Ras Laffan force majeure since March 2026, with a 3-5 year repair guide, shows how little control buyers have. Small in revenue, extreme in strategic weight - cryogenics, leak detection and semiconductor cooling all depend on it.

The rotating and heat-exchange core of every ASU, still imported as cold-box internals and large centrifugal machines. Whoever localises reliable turboexpander and PFHE manufacture captures a pool that today sits entirely with foreign licensors - and it gates the cost of every domestic ASU.

India's clearest export win in this chain: INOX India earns ~59% of revenue abroad, posted 21.3% EBITDA in Q2 FY27 and 22.3% for H1, and won a US subcooler order it will build at Savli. Engineering-led, order-book-driven and not dependent on Indian gas demand.

The production backbone and the capital sink: a 200-350 TPD ASU is a multi-hundred-crore asset with a long build, so cash conversion is poor even when margin is good. Surplus capacity above the take-or-pay minimum is sold into merchant, which is where the incremental margin comes from.

Pricing power exists only when regional supply is tight - argon in FY25 - and evaporates otherwise; INOX AP's merchant volumes fell 2% in FY26 as argon normalised. Distance-limited to roughly 200-300 km, so it is a route-density business more than a product business.

The packaged segment is the largest by customer count (~34% of the market) and the weakest by economics: a filled-cylinder logistics business with commoditised hardware, thin margin and high working capital in returns and refills.

industries.notes: Opportunity uses the same series as the Market & growth digest block (US$1,020m in 2020 to US$1,410m in 2025, 6.7% five-year CAGR, 12.4 mn tonnes). The wider IMARC (US$3.81 bn) and TechSci (US$5.06 bn) sizes are different scopes and are not blended in. Valuation UNAVAILABLE - the market leader is unlisted.

industries.title: India Inorganic Chemicals

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Commodity process economics with spreads at a cyclical low: Grasim's chemicals EBITDA fell 11% year on year in Q2 FY27 to ₹326 crore despite 15% revenue growth, on higher power costs, and Tata Chemicals' Industrial Essentials segment lost ₹120 crore of EBIT. CFR-SEA caustic at $390/t is a five-year low and soda-ash realisations stay soft on global oversupply; only contract-locked gases and integrated chlorine derivatives earn through the cycle.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: India inorganic chemicals USD 44.6 bn (2024) to USD 74.09 bn (2033) at a 5.8% nominal CAGR, with volume led by soda-ash demand at 4.5-5% a year FY27-30 and caustic demand at low-double-digit growth in FY27 on 3 mtpa of new alumina capacity  -  a mid-single-digit volume market where a ~2 mtpa caustic wave in FY28-29 and 2.169 mtpa of soda ash by FY2030 cap the upside.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Six domestic soda-ash producers and roughly 36 chlor-alkali units competing against structurally surplus Chinese, US and Turkish capacity; profitability depends on trade remedies rather than on moats  -  DGTR found imports absorbed about 85% of the incremental demand between FY23 and the most recent period, and the top six caustic producers' share is expected to fall to ~50% from 65% once the FY28-29 additions land.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Prices sit at a cyclical trough with protection arriving: CFR-SEA caustic at a five-year low of $390/t, Chinese soda-ash producer inventory at ~1.89 Mt with a US producer cutting 1.5 Mt at Wyoming, domestic caustic utilisation estimated at 85-90% in FY27, and DGTR recommending a two-year import quota. The read is [INFERENCE] from reported prices and margins, not a forecast; the risk is that the quota is not notified or is diluted.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry. Linde India's widely reported ~98x earnings is a single-company datapoint, not an industry multiple.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: The complex sits mid-chain and leaks value to feedstock: rock phosphate, potash, ammonia and sulphur are imported, and the domestic layer earns a conversion spread. Where the layer has moved up  -  Grasim's chlorine integration to ~67% by FY27 exit, smelter by-product acid, GHCL's low-cost soda ash  -  returns are visibly better, so the score stays at 3 rather than 2.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Heavy process capital: GHCL's greenfield soda-ash line is ₹6,500 crore for 1.1 MMT, chlor-alkali is of the order of ₹1 crore per daily tonne, and fertiliser working capital is heavy and subsidy-funded. Plants are long-lived and returns are set by the spread over energy and feedstock.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Mature process engineering  -  membrane cells, Solvay soda ash, DCDA acid, cryogenic ASUs  -  with little proprietary IP held in India. The genuinely technical nodes (ion-exchange membranes, ASU cold boxes, process licences) are imported, which is a dependency rather than an advantage.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Three live exposures: Gulf-sourced ammonia and sulphur moving through the Strait of Hormuz (ammonia +60%, sulphur +50% since March 2026), trade-remedy dependence for soda ash where the quota is not yet notified, and energy-cost sensitivity across a coal- and gas-based chlor-alkali fleet.

value_capture.basis: Still the most attractive pool in the complex - sold on 15-20 year take-or-pay contracts at the customer's fence, with near-total switching cost and a market growing ~6-7% a year. Linde India's Q2 FY27 revenue rose 12.3% while EBITDA fell 18%, so the growth is real but the margin is being taxed by input costs. pool_growth raised 3 -> 4 on Linde's guidance of ~7% market growth with electronics at 12-15%. The bulk of the Indian pool still sits with unlisted MNC joint ventures, so the returns exist but are largely unavailable to a listed investor.

The best-earning listed node, but the pool is policy-set rather than earned: GHCL held a 24.7% EBITDA margin with net cash in Q2 FY27 while Tata's Industrial Essentials segment lost Rs 120 crore of EBIT, and DGTR measured industry ROCE falling to an index of 71 against 100 in FY20-21. roic cut 4 -> 3 on that split. Pricing power stays at 2 - realisations are soft with Chinese producer inventory near 1.89 Mt, and the relief in train is an import quota recommendation, not a structural moat.

The binding upstream constraint. India imports it, there is no listed domestic miner, and the West Asia shock made the dependency visible again - rock phosphate and phosphoric acid rose less than ammonia and sulphur but still re-priced the chain. Small in revenue, real in pricing power, long in substitution timeline. Unchanged.

The clearest value migration in the complex. Chlorine is priced domestically and has reset from persistently negative to roughly zero - Epigral expects it never to return to negative, and Grasim reports Gujarat flat to slightly positive - which shifts cost recovery from caustic to chlorine. Grasim's integration reached 64% in H1 FY27 against ~67% guided at FY27 exit, with CPVC (50 KTPA) and ECH (50 KTPA) commissioned in Aug and Oct 2026. pricing_power 2 -> 3 and bottleneck 2 -> 3; it now outranks PVC.

A thin electricity-and-salt spread, but the trough is doing some work: Grasim's ECU held at Rs 33,587/t (+2% YoY) even with CFR-SEA caustic at a five-year low of $390/t, because domestic realisations are set at import parity and the rupee has weakened. pricing_power and roic raised 1 -> 2 on that resilience and on 85-90% utilisation in FY27; they go back down when ~2 mtpa of new capacity lands in FY28-29.

The largest single chlorine outlet and therefore the node that decides whether a chlor-alkali complex is balanced, but Indian suspension PVC is being dumped into from China, Europe and Japan and the returns show it. Barriers are capital, not technology. Unchanged: the new CPVC and ECH capacity adds volume, not pricing power.

Largely a by-product of copper and zinc smelting, which makes it a cost hedge for the fertiliser complex rather than a profit pool. pricing_power raised 1 -> 2: sulphur is up ~50% since March 2026 and smelter-acid producers get that pass-through for free, while sulphur-burners absorb it. Barriers remain minimal and the product clears at import parity.

The pool is captured by the subsidy, not the market, and in FY27 the subsidy does not cover the cost: DAP has been landing near $900-930/t CFR against a breakeven around $510/t, and NBS plus the Rs 3,500/t special package still leaves roughly Rs 23,000/t of under-recovery. op_share cut 3 -> 2 - the conversion fee is real only for producers with their own phosphoric acid. Cash conversion remains the weakest in the complex.

industries.notes: Scored against 'Industry-Level Investment Parameters & Scoring Architecture' during the 2026-11-14 full re-analysis. Opportunity uses the same India inorganic-chemicals series as the Market & growth digest block (USD 44.6 bn 2024 to USD 74.09 bn 2033, 5.8% nominal CAGR); the rupee production series, the narrower USD 16.3 bn series and the 3.95% alternative CAGR are shown beside it, not blended. Cycle is now scored (was UNAVAILABLE) because Q2 FY27 filings give a price and margin position: CFR-SEA caustic at a five-year low, Chinese soda-ash inventory near 1.89 Mt, and a pending two-year import quota. Valuation stays UNAVAILABLE - the registry holds no industry-level valuation data. Economics moved 3 -> 2 on the Q2 FY27 evidence (Grasim chemicals EBITDA -11%, Tata Industrial Essentials EBIT -Rs 120 crore).

industries.title: India Launch Vehicles & Propulsion

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Launch is a low-cadence business with one state customer, so margins come from the work rather than the market. The listed exposures show the spread: MTAR earned a 19.5% EBITDA margin on Rs 876 cr in FY26, Data Patterns 40.1% on Rs 925 cr, while MIDHANI's space segment was only Rs 93 cr of Rs 1,206 cr and HAL's space work is under 2% of Rs 32,250 cr. Value migrates to industry through fixed-price ToT fees (Rs 511 cr SSLV, Rs 860 cr for five PSLVs), which cap upside per programme.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: The forward demand signal is explicit and now contractual: three separate technology transfers in train (SSLV signed Sep-2025, full PSLV ToT offered May-2026, LVM3 EoI opened Jun-2026 with bids in Oct-2026), seven launches targeted in FY2026-27 against roughly four to six a year actually flown, 50 a year stated as the requirement, Gaganyaan-1 no earlier than 30-Nov-2026 and NGLV approved with the LME-1100 engine. Historical growth is the weak half - the whole space economy moved only ~1.6% a year between 2022 and Aug-2026 - so the opportunity is forward, programme-driven and not yet in the revenue line.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Flight heritage is a structural barrier: HAL won SSLV against an Adani-backed bidder, and only HAL, L-T and the two private entrants hold any Indian orbital launch capability. The counter-trend this run is that LVM3 ToT drew six to eight bidders including JSW, Adani, Mahindra, Solar Industries, Bharat Forge and Inox India, so the integrator pool is widening and incumbency is worth less than it was. Barriers protect qualification, not pricing - the state sets both price and schedule.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: The cycle is inflecting on dated events rather than sentiment: GSLV-F18 flew NVS-03 on 30-Oct-2026 as the 20th GSLV flight, Gaganyaan-1 is no earlier than 30-Nov-2026, SCE-200 reached 200-tonne full thrust on 5-Sep-2026, the LME-1100 methalox gas generator was ignited on 9-Oct-2026, and the LVM3 ToT bid window opened in October 2026. The counterweight is a mission count that is still single-digit.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series exists for Indian launch vehicles, and no aggregation of the listed exposures would be a valid proxy because every one of them sits inside a diversified defence or engineering business - HAL at Rs 32,250 cr of revenue, BEL at Rs 27,480 cr, L-T's space work inside a Rs 8,366 cr Hi-Tech Manufacturing segment. Company multiples are reported but one company cannot define an industry multiple.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Launch is the most indigenous node in the Indian space chain - casings, structures, tanks, engines, avionics and propellant are all made in-country and ISRO's chairman puts industry content at 80-85% of systems. Two dependencies keep it at 3 rather than 4: high-end electronics and rad-hard parts are imported, and a draft contract to procure Russian RD-191M-class semi-cryogenic engines for the LVM3 upgrade is under approval, which would put an import inside the vehicle's performance-critical path.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Development runs years before first revenue, test stands and launch pads are state-provided rather than private, and demand is anchored by one customer. The capital that is required is patient and public: NGLV, Chandrayaan-4 and the first Bharatiya Antariksh Station module were approved as government programmes, and the private entrants are venture-funded. Affordable only for large balance sheets or state backing.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: India holds a capability only a handful of nations have and is extending it on three fronts at once: cryogenic (CE-7.5, CE-20), semi-cryogenic (SCE-200 at 200-tonne full thrust, Sep-2026) and LOX-methane for NGLV (LME-1100 gas-generator ignition Oct-2026, integrated engine targeted mid-2027). Agnikul has flown a single-piece 3D-printed semi-cryogenic engine, and TDB is funding reusable-vehicle work from TRL-4 upward. Not 5 because none of the next-generation engines has yet flown.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Concentrated on one buyer, gated by two launch pads, exposed to a semi-cryogenic engine import and to imported high-end electronics, and carrying genuine execution risk - the industry PSLV has slipped from Q1 FY27 to March 2027 and PSLV-C62 lost its PS3 stage in January 2026. Offset by near-total domestic content, a stated national cadence target and a policy direction that has already transferred one vehicle outright.

missing_critical: launch-level price and cost breakdown per mission
launch volume series by vehicle type

value_capture.basis: The largest pool and the one that changed most this run: serial production moved from a state monopoly to a contestable private market with three separate transfers in train (SSLV to HAL at Rs 511 cr, full PSLV ToT offered, LVM3 ToT out for bid). Integration is asset-light because the pads and test stands are public, but pricing power is capped at a fixed ToT fee and a state-set mission price, and cash conversion is slow against a single buyer. Rank moved UP: it is now the top node, where the previous run treated vehicle production as a state activity with industry as a subcontractor.

The hardest technology on the vehicle and the tightest supplier base: LPSC owns the design, a handful of fabricators (MTAR, L-T, Godrej) execute it, and nothing substitutes for a qualified cryogenic stage. Scored below vehicle systems on operating share because the value is concentrated in few units, and marked DOWN on this run's reading of pool growth: a draft contract to import Russian RD-191M-class semi-cryogenic engines would route part of the LVM3 upgrade spend abroad, while SCE-200 and LME-1100 remain pre-flight.

Every launch consumes a full set of casings, so this pool grows with cadence more directly than any other - five SSLV missions planned in FY2026-27 alone, each with three solid stages. Barriers are forging, proof-pressure testing and qualification rather than design. Walchandnagar's Rs 30.53 cr HS200 order for Gaganyaan is the clearest evidence that the work is being placed with listed industry.

Two pads, one range and one authorising regulator make this the tightest physical bottleneck in the chain, and mission operations convert into cash quickly once a slot exists. Held back because the pool is government-owned and no NSE/BSE company operates it - BEL touches only the ground electronics.

The best cash-conversion node with real listed participation - Data Patterns at a 40.1% EBITDA margin on Rs 925 cr, BEL on range and telemetry. Scored lower on strategic weight because several qualified suppliers exist and the guidance algorithms are ISRO's, so the node is build-to-specification rather than a choke point.

Lowest score despite the highest growth expectation: Vikram-1 reached orbit on 18-Jul-2026 but commercial operations begin only in early 2027, unit economics are unproven at scale, and none of it is reachable in the NSE/BSE universe. Scored as the pool it would become, not the pool that exists - and the one node where a domestic entrant would create a genuinely new listed exposure.

industries.notes: Opportunity and Market - growth use the same scoped series: launch services US$720 mn (2022, IN-SPACe Decadal Vision) to a US$3.5 bn potential by 2033, ~15.5% nominal CAGR [CALCULATED]; the whole space economy US$8.4 bn (2022) to US$9.0 bn (Aug-2026), ~1.6% a year [CALCULATED]; volume 12 launch-vehicle missions in the three years to Jun-2026 (~4 a year), 5-6 a year per IN-SPACe, 7 targeted in FY2026-27, 50 a year stated as the requirement. Valuation left UNAVAILABLE - the registry carries no industry valuation series and no listed pure-play exists.

industries.title: India Li-ion Cell Manufacturing

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Indian cells cost Rs 8-12/Wh against Rs 6-7/Wh imported - a 30-50% premium - and a 5 GWh plant runs near -10% EBITDA with breakeven around 10 GWh. The economics are policy-made and sub-scale, not structural.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: Demand of 28 GWh in 2025 rising to ~272 GWh by FY2030 against 1 GWh installed of 40 GWh awarded, and a Rs 41,667 cr FY26 import bill growing 64% - the widest substitution gap in the registry.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Four PLI-ACC awardees and a handful of pack integrators compete at sub-scale against Chinese incumbents one to two orders of magnitude larger; domestic players are price-takers on equipment, materials and cells.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Only 1 GWh of 40 GWh awarded is installed after five years, no incentive has been claimed, the 10 GWh tender slipped from 13-Oct to 10-Nov-2026, and November cell production schedules in China fell ~5% m/m - the first monthly decline of 2026 - while lithium carbonate sits ~55% below its 2026 high.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry - the page carries no sector multiple series.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Cell making is the target node, but cathode and anode material, separator, copper foil and 55-60% of plant cost in machinery are all import-dominated; India's live value-add remains module, pack and container assembly.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Cell-line equipment is 55-60% of a 5 GWh plant's cost, EBITDA is negative below ~10 GWh and no PLI-ACC beneficiary has claimed an incentive five years in - among the most capital-hungry nodes analysed, though a 50% capex component scheme is under evaluation.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: LFP chemistry and process recipes are licensed or bought, the equipment is overwhelmingly Chinese, and India holds no proprietary cell IP; the licence layer, not the machine layer, is what stalled the 40 GWh programme.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: China's export controls on LFP technology, graphite anode and cell machinery (legal text 10-Nov-2026, political truce to 10-Jan-2027), an export VAT rebate abolished from 1-Jan-2027, sub-scale unit economics and a policy-dependent demand floor.

missing_critical: plant-level first-pass yield and realised cell cost

value_capture.basis: Still the best pool in the chain and still entirely imported: cell-line equipment is 55-60% of a 5 GWh plant's cost, over 75% of global capacity is Chinese, and the six equipment categories sit on China's dual-use list under a suspension whose legal text reads 10-Nov-2026. Suppliers carry genuine pricing power and excellent cash conversion; India has no listed pure-play, so the pool leaks in full. Unchanged rank.

CAM is 35-45% of material cost and up to 50-55% of total cell cost, and China holds about 95% of LFP CAM and precursor capacity - the largest pool and the deepest import gap. Pricing is the constraint: China LFP CAM spot ran RMB 47,500-50,500/t in mid-Oct-2026, up ~60% from the June-2025 low but still far below the level at which an Indian plant earns its guided 25-30% EBITDA. Himadri's first 2,000 tpa now lands Q3 FY27, later than the prior run implied.

Over 90% of graphitisation is Chinese and graphite anode is on China's restricted-export list. The domestic answer has firmed up: HEG Advanced Materials' 20,000 tpa reaches COD in June-2027 with 44,000 tpa by Mar-2029 under a Rs 1,606 cr plan, and Epsilon's 30,000 tpa is supported by Rs 145 cr of ECMS money. Graphitisation is power-hungry and capital-heavy, so cash conversion stays weak even where margin exists.

The biggest revenue pool in the chain and the worst current economics. Indian cells cost Rs 8-12/Wh against a Rs 6-7/Wh imported benchmark - a 30-50% premium - with Amara Raja guiding to a 15-25% gap and 10-11% EBITDA only at 8-10 GWh. The PLI record is the tell: 1 GWh installed of 40 GWh awarded and no incentive claimed. Barriers are high, but they protect a loss until scale and domestic material arrive.

Separator is near-100% imported and the most technically demanding component node, at 4-6% of cell cost on TCPL's own estimate. TCPL's Rs 125 cr / 70 mn m2 line (6-8 GWh equivalent) targets commercial production only in early 2028, so the pool stays foreign through the first wave of Indian cell volume. Film lines are capital-intensive with long qualification cycles.

Battery-grade aluminium and copper foil is the one cell input where India already has a credible listed supplier in Hindalco, but 80-85% of copper foil is still imported and the product is a rolled-metal spread with no proprietary position. Rank moved up one place: it now sits above electrolyte, whose strategic-importance score fell as domestic supply became routine.

Rank moved DOWN one place. Electrolyte is now the one component routinely sourced domestically - Neogen's 2,000 MT and Gujarat Fluorochemicals' LiPF6 since Dec-2025 - so the bottleneck score drops from 3 to 2. It remains a commodity chemical with Chinese oversupply setting the price, no pricing power, and continuous working capital against lithium swings.

The fastest-growing pool in percentage terms and the least real today: no commercial-scale Indian output is expected before 2028, black-mass recovery is licensed technology, and the economics depend on EPR rules still being framed. Low on everything except growth.

industries.notes: Re-analysed 2026-11-05 under the daily rotation. Corrections from the prior run: the 10 GWh ACC-PLI tender did NOT close on 13-Oct-2026 - it was extended to 10-Nov-2026 (technical bids 11-Nov); installed capacity is 1 GWh of 40 GWh awarded, not ~2 GWh of a working programme; Reliance's 40-to-120 GWh Jamnagar cell plan is no longer corroborated and is carried as capacity-not-disclosed with a late-2026 to 2027 production guide; HEG is now HEG Advanced Materials (HEGAM) after the demerger; Himadri's LFP plant is at a 2,000 tpa milestone, not 40,000 tpa; and the prior run's 36.5% volume CAGR was inconsistent with its own 28-to-272 GWh endpoints - the calculated figure is 57.6%. Cycle moved 3 to 2 on the PLI execution record and the first monthly fall in Chinese cell schedules of 2026. Valuation remains UNAVAILABLE. Value capture re-scored 2026-11-05; electrolyte bottleneck 3 to 2, moving it below foils.

industries.title: India Precision Machine Tools & Metrology

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Domestic builders address only about two-fifths of their own home market, with imports at ~59% of FY26 consumption, but the pool is growing ~15% a year with order bookings up ~20% — decent throughput economics behind a persistent technology gap.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: Consumption of ₹36,419 cr in FY26 against ₹21,628 cr of imports is a ~₹21,600 cr substitution pool, on a 13.7% eleven-year production CAGR, with Q1 FY27 running +26% production and +20% consumption.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: A fragmented domestic field (Jyoti CNC plus unlisted BFW and Ace) competes against a controller oligopoly (Fanuc, Siemens, Mitsubishi) and German/Japanese gear-grinding and metrology incumbents; rivalry is price-led in standard machines and closed in the precision tier.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: The industry is in a clear upcycle: FY26 consumption +15%, order bookings +20%, and Q1 FY27 production +26% YoY, with 29 capital-goods projects sanctioned to Mar-2026 feeding forward demand.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry — the page carries no sector multiple series.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: India machines and assembles the frame, but CNC controllers, spindles, precision bearings, linear guides, ball screws and CMMs — the value-dense layers — are imported, so localisation has stopped one layer short of the moat.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Moderate capex relative to semiconductors or cells, but castings, grinding capacity and a long working-capital cycle mean entry needs patient capital rather than large cheques.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: No domestic CNC controller platform and no robotics-grade ultra-precision gear grinding or metrology; five-axis and hybrid machines are bought in, so the capability is assembly and integration rather than proprietary machine design.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Controller single-sourcing, ~30% of imports from China, exposure to US tariffs on machine-tool exports and a capex-cyclical demand base — mitigated by a large protected domestic pool and a live capital-goods scheme.

value_capture.basis: Fanuc, Siemens and Mitsubishi hold the brain, and management at Jyoti puts the controller at 20-25% of an entry-level machine's cost falling to under 10% at the high end - so the foreign share of value is highest exactly where Indian builders compete hardest. High-end controllers for 5-axis are export-controlled, which makes the switching cost a licence, not a price.

Largely imported (ball screws, linear guideways, feedback elements) and the accuracy of the whole machine is set here; Jyoti makes its own spindles in Rajkot, which is the single biggest reason its gross margin sits where it does. For everyone else this is a foreign toll on domestic assembly.

The pool that exists today: Jyoti CNC did ₹2,093 cr consolidated in FY26 at a 25.2% EBITDA margin, and its 55.1% gross margin against Macpower's 38.5% is a direct read on how much of the machine a builder makes itself. Pricing power is real at the high end (40% of Jyoti's order book is above ₹2 cr a machine) and absent at the entry level, where China supplied 30% of FY26 imports.

Effectively imported with no listed Indian maker at robotics grade; small in revenue but it is the node that certifies every other node's output, so it carries pricing power out of all proportion to its size.

Partly domestic at commodity grades, effectively imported at machine-tool grades where Schaeffler, SKF and Timken set the specification; a small pool with a hard qualification gate and a long design-in cycle.

Effectively imported and a narrow niche serving gearboxes, reducers and defence drivetrains - the machine that gates the harmonic/RV reducer and gear-making chains, with volumes too small to justify a domestic line yet.

The one node where India is genuinely strong - Kennametal, Carborundum and Grindwell Norton - but it is a consumable, sold on price and availability against global brands, with no bottleneck position and a recurring but unremarkable margin.
