industries.title: India Medical Devices

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Implant gross margins are high and stents earn a real EBITDA margin (SMT 15.7% in H1 FY27, Poly Medicure 24.4% in FY26), but NPPA ceilings on stents and knee implants cap the pricing pool on the two largest value nodes.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: Ortho plus cardiac implants ran at $2.3–2.5 bn in FY24 and are forecast at $4.5–5.0 bn by FY28, with 65–70% of demand still imported and a ₹3,420 cr PLI scheme that names all implants as a target segment — the substitution headroom is the opportunity, not just the growth rate.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Two structures coexist: MNC-dominated premium orthopaedics and structural heart, where 90%+ share has only recently started to erode, and a fragmented MSME trauma segment of hundreds of makers. Stents are the one consolidated domestic pool (SMT ~31% of DES).

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Procedure volumes grow steadily rather than cyclically and the domestic makers are compounding at 28% against 12% for MNCs, but hospital capex and elective-surgery mix give the segment a soft cycle; no peak or trough signal is visible in the current data.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series in the registry. The only listed pure-play (SMT) has traded for about two weeks, so a sector multiple cannot be built without letting one company define it.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: India machines and assembles finished implants and makes stents end-to-end, but imports the mill products (Ti bar, CoCrMo, UHMWPE, PEEK), the coatings services and the metrology — localisation has reached Tier 2, not Tier 3.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: A greenfield implant plant is a ₹50–150 cr commitment plus cleanroom and certification time; working capital is heavy on hospital receivables; PLI approved projects reported ₹1,153 cr of actual investment against a ₹3,420 cr outlay.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Genuine incremental innovation exists — TiNbN and TiN coatings, Indian TAVI and drug-coated balloons, 3D-printed guides — but design IP, material specifications and the equipment behind them remain imported.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Price control is live and decision-dated: the knee ceiling runs to 15-Nov-2026, stent ceilings were revised on 27-Mar-2026, and CareEdge flags tariff, patent-litigation and regulatory-scrutiny risk alongside a 65–70% import dependence that FX shocks pass straight through.

missing_critical: segment-level import values by HS code for implants
volume series for implant procedures by type
segment ROIC for Indian implant makers

value_capture.basis: The best economics India actually owns in this chain: SMT runs a 15.7% EBITDA margin at 25% growth on a ₹1,300 cr domestic stent market. Pricing power scores 2, not 4, because the DES ceiling is ₹38,933 and a WPI revision is the only annual lever.

The deepest import dependency in the tree and a genuine qualification moat — ASTM F136/F1537 conformance plus a device master file is a two-to-three-year entry ticket. MIDHANI already holds the metallurgy; what is missing is medical-grade bar conversion at scale.

The largest revenue pool and the one price control bites hardest: primary titanium-coated knees are capped at ₹51,563 and revisions at ₹83,547, so volume growth and mix shift, not price, carry the pool. Surgeon preference gives real switching cost.

Small in operating profit but strategically gating: a coating line is what separates a machined part from an implant, and only a handful of Indian lines are qualified. TTK applies UltraCoat in-house; Shalby's TiNbN knee cleared US FDA in Jan-2025.

A tolling business with good cash conversion and modest capital, gated by validation rather than by technology. The Aug-2026 Rule 44 amendment removed the separate loan licence for outsourced sterilisation, which lowers the barrier to using third-party capacity.

A contract-manufacturing pool that does not yet exist as a listed business in India — it sits captive inside the OEMs. The opportunity is export contract work: Shalby's California plant (74,088 components in FY25) is the proof that Indian-owned machining can sell into the US.

Captures a real slice of the patient rupee but on thin, regulated margins — NPPA's trade-margin cap on stents (8%) and its repeated findings on knee-implant trade margins show how exposed this layer is. Working capital is the killer: hospital receivables run to months.

industries.title: India Missiles

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Integrator economics are thin and volatile: BDL’s FY26 EBITDA margin fell to 9.1%, its lowest on record, as revenue dropped 27% on a higher share of bought-out components, while electronics-side BEL earned a 30% EBITDA margin in FY26 — value sits in electronics and energetics, not in airframe integration.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: The missile pool grows 39.9% a year on the narrow procurement estimate (US$468.6 mn in 2025 to US$2,512.7 mn in 2030) or 6.7% on the wider precision-guided-munitions estimate (US$2,350.6 mn in 2022 to US$3,958.6 mn in 2030); either way it sits inside FY26 defence production of Rs 1.78 lakh crore growing 15.6%, with BDL’s order book at 10.6x revenue giving unusually visible forward demand.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Design IP stays with DRDO and integration is a BDL/BEL duopoly, with private entry now opening through the Aug-2026 ToT; barriers are high and durable, but the single buyer (MoD) sets price and timing, so incumbency protects volume rather than margin.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Demand is at a record and inflecting: FY26 defence production +15.6%, exports +62.7% to Rs 38,424 crore, BDL’s order book at Rs 26,176 crore, and FY27 guided back to ~Rs 4,500 crore revenue as delayed Akash and Astra deliveries clear.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series is carried in the registry; company multiples are reported (BDL at 70.5x FY27E EPS on Motilal Oswal’s estimates) but one company cannot define an industry multiple.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Around 65% of defence equipment is now produced domestically and ~91% of ammunition variants are indigenised, but seekers (Astra Mk-1), radars and specialty metals (nickel, cobalt, molybdenum, tungsten, ~Rs 8,000 crore imported) remain the imported nodes, and solid propellant is a near-duopoly.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Capital-heavy and slow: BDL is committing Rs 5 bn to a 160-acre naval systems plant plus the Ibrahimpatnam and Jhansi facilities, on receivables that took 109 days even after a 38% improvement; DPSU advances soften it, private entrants carry it alone.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: DRDO design capability is real and deep, but the GaN AESA seeker is still in development, scramjet/hypersonic propulsion is aspirational, and much of the precision manufacturing equipment is bought in.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: A single buyer sets price and schedule, the seeker and radar supply chain has already proven a delivery single point of failure, and the licensing and export-control regime constrains both entry and exit.

value_capture.basis: The best economics in the chain: Solar Industries ran a 26.7% EBITDA margin and 27.4% RoCE in FY26 with defence revenue up 94% to ₹2,634 cr and a ₹21,300 cr order book. Energetics are licence-gated, chemically hazardous and cannot be sourced on the spot market, which is precisely why a private maker earns a margin the prime does not.

The binding technology constraint on Indian missile programmes and historically imported; BDL delivered the first indigenously fabricated RF seeker for Akash-NG from its own Seeker Facility Centre, and DRDO has opened RF-seeker ToT. A small pool with the highest pricing power in the chain because the alternative is an export-control queue.

The largest pool and the highest barrier - BDL is the designated prime production agency with a ₹26,176 cr order book (10.6x FY26 revenue) and nil debt - but the economics are set by a single buyer on fixed-contract terms. FY26 revenue fell 27% to ₹2,442 cr and EBITDA margin hit a decade low of 9.1%; gross current assets above 651 days make this the worst cash conversion in the chain, which is why the score sits below the barriers it carries.

Partly imported with RLG/FOG/MEMS being indigenised; design authority sits with DRDO and the primes, so a supplier earns a qualified-part margin rather than system margin, but requalification is slow enough to protect the position once held.

Domestic with a few specialty energetic inputs imported; licensed, safety-gated and adjacent to the propellant pool, which is where the returns concentrate. Volume follows missile orders with a lag, so the pool grows later than the prime's order book.

Solid motors are domestic and increasingly contested between BDL, Solar Industries and private motor makers, so the barrier is qualification rather than capability; some specialty inputs remain imported. Case-bonding and grain design are the defensible part of the node.

Imported metals and alloys of roughly ₹8,000 cr across the programme; a fabrication node with real tonnage but commodity-like pass-through, and the most exposed to input-price and import-licence swings.

State-owned and capacity-constrained: ranges and instrumentation are a public good that gates every programme's schedule, but they generate no commercial margin - a bottleneck node that is a cost centre, not a profit pool.
Mostly domestic and structurally competitive - fabrication and hydraulics work that several private firms can bid, with no technology gate and no scarcity value.

industries.title: India Mobile Handsets & Accessories

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Final assembly is high-volume and thin-margin - Dixon's mobile and EMS business ran ~₹44,257 cr of revenue at ~3.5% operating margin - and the PLI-LSEM benefit ended 31-Mar-2026, removing 50-70 bps of support just as memory costs rose.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: Shipments are contracting rather than growing: ~153 mn in CY2025 to a forecast 125-133 mn in CY2026 (−13% to −18%), with Q3 CY2026 the weakest third quarter in a decade, so the addressable assembly pool shrinks even as value rises on a $282 ASP; the offset is accessories at a ~8.5% five-year CAGR.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Over 300 assembly units compete for the assembly step while three or four global OEMs set price, and localisation money concentrates on a handful of ECMS beneficiaries - a buyer-dominated chain with little supplier pricing power.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: The industry is in a memory-driven price shock rather than a demand collapse: memory has moved from 10-15% to 30-40% of the bill of materials on some configurations, prices rose ~16% in H1 2026, and normalisation is not expected before H1-2027 at the earliest.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry - EMS comparables are company-level and are not a sector multiple series.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Domestic value addition is ~23% against ~38% in China, and chipset, memory, display and camera - ~55-60% of the bill of materials - are imported; PCBA and battery packs are genuinely local, which is the low-value end of the chain.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Assembly capex per line is modest and heavily underwritten by ECMS (₹40,000 cr) and MPMS (₹62,500 cr), but working capital is punishing when component prices move 40% in a year and inventory is carried at the higher cost.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: SMT, display bonding and final assembly-test-pack capability are real and scaled, but there is no front-end panel fab and no semiconductor capacity; component fabs are only now starting under ECMS, so the ladder stops at module sub-assembly.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: The cost base is set outside India - a global memory shortage expected to persist into 2027-28, rupee depreciation on imported components, and a policy stack (MPMS, ECMS, the PLI phase-out) that largely determines whether assembly stays.

value_capture.node: Core Silicon & RF — SoC, Memory, PMIC, RF Front-End
value_capture.basis: The node that keeps the money and the one that is moving fastest: memory was 12–13% of a smartphone BOM and is now materially higher, DRAM/NAND are up 40–50% year on year on AI demand, and smartphone ASPs rose roughly 35–40% as a result. Dixon's management noted pass-through is automatic and immediate in EMS, which means the silicon supplier sets the price and the assembler merely invoices it. No Indian capability, no prospect of one in this cycle.

The largest localisable block in the BOM at ~13.5% and the clearest example of a pool moving onshore: Dixon's 74:26 HKC JV has ECMS and PN3 approval, ₹10bn of capex over three years, phase-1 capacity of 24 mn mobile displays (scaling to 50–55 mn) and peak revenue potential of ₹60–70bn at double-digit margins, with mobile production now expected in early FY28 after a delay. A licence-and-partner barrier, not a capital one — and the first Indian entrant is a JV, not an independent.

The largest revenue pool and the thinnest margin: Dixon did ₹48,893 crore of FY26 revenue at ₹1,887 crore of EBITDA, with mobile and other EMS at ₹9,485 crore of Q4 revenue for ₹337 crore of operating profit, and margins running ~2–2.3% on a per-piece conversion model. What it does have is capital efficiency — ROCE 44.8%, ROE 28.1%, a negative 8-day working capital cycle and OCF/EBITDA of 118% — which is why the pool is investable despite the margin. The mobile PLI's expiry on 31-Mar-2026 is a 50–70bp headwind management has already flagged.

A regulatory gate rather than a revenue pool: BIS registration and TEC–MTCTE certification decide which model can be sold at all, and accredited lab capacity sets the launch calendar. Small, defensive, high-barrier economics with no listed Indian pure-play — included because in a market where 99.2% of phones sold are made locally, the certification layer is the one domestic node every brand must pass through.

Localisation that has arrived as a share-of-BOM play rather than a margin play: Q Tech is a 51% subsidiary and India's largest camera-module plant, expanding from 70–80 mn to 180–190 mn units, but its margins fell about 450bp in FY26 because the contracts carried no forex pass-through, and management guides recovery only to 6–7%. Capacity and customer access are the assets; pricing power belongs to the brand.

Packs are 95% domestically value-added while cells are effectively fully imported — a neat illustration of the difference between assembly and manufacture. The barrier sits with the cell, the return sits with the packer, and the cell plant (ATL, Munoth-Cosmx) is an ECMS project rather than an operating business. Capital-heavy, thin, and gated on a chemistry supply chain India does not yet have.

The durable domestic pool: USD 6.86 bn (2025) growing to USD 14.66 bn (2034), a 5-year CAGR of ~8.5% calculated from USD 4.56 bn in 2020, riding a ~1 bn-device installed base and a replacement cycle that has stretched from 3.5 to 4.3 years. Low barrier, brand-led margin, and the one part of this industry where an Indian company competes on product rather than on conversion cost.

Already largely domestic (about 20% value addition) and structurally low-barrier: sheet metal, tooling and moulding capacity exists, Tata, Motherson and Hindalco are scaling it under ECMS, and Dixon is evaluating mechanicals as a backward-integration line. Volume without margin — a share-of-BOM contributor, not a profit pool.

industries.title: India Nuclear PWR Steam Generator

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: A steam generator is a two-year, milestone-billed fabrication job on a fixed-price contract inside a 60–72 month project, so the margin is earned on execution discipline rather than on design. No SG-specific margin is disclosed; the closest reported proxy is L&T's consolidated 8.7% EBITDA and 16.7% ROE in Q2 FY27 [REPORTED-T1], against a company guide of 3–3.5× nuclear-revenue growth over five years on a 55–60% share of the nuclear value chain.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: India nuclear-plant equipment is ~$2.8 bn (2026) to ~$7.4 bn (2035), an 11.4% CAGR [REPORTED-T3, MarkWide]; inside it the SG is ~7% of the ~₹19 lakh cr / 100 GW build (~₹1.4 lakh cr) [REPORTED-T2, CEA capex breakup], and each 700 MWe unit takes four SGs with 16 indigenous units sanctioned. Volume [UNAVAILABLE].

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Four qualified fabricators — L&T (above 50% SG and end-shield share), BHEL, Walchandnagar and ISGEC/Godrej — sit behind ASME N/NPT and AERB Class-1 qualification, on a component that must be qualified with the reactor it serves, so a second-source bid is a years-long qualification rather than a capex decision.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: The fleet is executing: RAPP-8 began initial fuel loading on 19-Sep-2026 and Kaiga-5&6 and GHAVP-3&4 SG deliveries are in progress [REPORTED-T2], so the order book is live; the next leg — a second fleet of ten and the ASHVINI nuclear-island package — turns on the SHANTI rules being finalised and on the ₹28,000 cr Mahi Banswara tender concluding.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series exists for steam generators: the owner (NPCIL) and designer (BARC) are unlisted and the fabricators are segments inside diversified listed companies, so a node multiple cannot be evidenced.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Every step from shell forging to hydro test is performed in India for the PHWR SG — LTSSHF forges the shell, cone, tubesheet and dished ends and NFC draws the Alloy-800 tube — so the chain is domestic at system level; the leaks are the Inconel 690 tube (PWR/VVER only, Sandvik/Valinox/Sumitomo), the fabrication machinery and primary-side SG instrumentation.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Fabrication capex is bay-and-crane scale rather than greenfield-heavy, but the model is working-capital intensive across a ~2-year melt-to-despatch cycle with a single PSU customer, and the forging shop that feeds it is a 74:26 JV carrying a ₹1,107 cr order book (Mar-2026).

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: The 700 MWe PHWR SG is proven and fully indigenised, but the PWR/VVER variant needs Inconel 690 tube, nuclear-grade Inconel weld overlay and ~11,000 tube-to-tubesheet welds to Class-1 acceptance — qualification, not design, is what gates a new entrant.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Three exposures stack: one nuclear-grade heavy-forging shop (LTSSHF) behind every shell and tubesheet, a Class-1 welder and NDT-inspector base that cannot be bought quickly at any price, and a licensing regime whose final rules were still in consultation as of 04-Sep-2026.

value_capture.node: SG fabrication — shell, heads & tubesheet assembly (A · Pressure boundary & shell)
value_capture.basis: The node that keeps the money: L&T is dominant with above 50% SG and end-shield share, BHEL, Walchandnagar and ISGEC/Godrej make up the qualified rest, and each of the 16 sanctioned 700 MWe units takes four SGs. L&T guides 3–3.5× nuclear-revenue growth over five years on a 55–60% value-chain share, but cash conversion is the weak leg — a ~2-year melt-to-despatch cycle billed against a single PSU customer.

value_capture.node: Nuclear-grade heavy forgings — shell, cone, tubesheet, dished ends (LTSSHF)
value_capture.basis: The sole domestic nuclear-grade forging shop, an L&T–NPCIL 74:26 JV at Hazira with a ₹1,107 cr order book at Mar-2026, supplying the shell, cone, tubesheet and dished-end forgings for every Indian SG. Pricing power is structural because there is no alternative source; the return on capital is diluted by heavy press utilisation and a lumpy order profile.

value_capture.node: Inconel 690 seamless U-bend tube (PWR/VVER, B · Tube bundle & heat transfer)
value_capture.basis: Sandvik, Valinox and Sumitomo hold the whole qualified supply and no Indian maker exists; the pool is narrow because it serves only the PWR/VVER fleet (Kudankulam and future LWRs) rather than the PHWR majority, but pricing power and switching costs are at the top of the chain.

value_capture.node: Tube bundle — Alloy-800 U-bend tube (PHWR, B · Tube bundle & heat transfer)
value_capture.basis: The input that decides whether an Indian PHWR SG can be built: NFC/MIDHANI now draw the Alloy-800 tube domestically on an 81-day cycle, which converted a former import into a domestic gate. Small in revenue, decisive in scheduling, and qualified only through the SG it is welded into.

value_capture.node: Logistics, installation & aftermarket — heavy transport, erection, tube inspection (G)
value_capture.basis: The recurring 60-year pool: eddy-current inspection, tube plugging and sleeving, and eventual full SG replacement on an installed base that only grows. Small per event, annuity-like across the fleet, and effectively locked to the original fabricator's design and tube layout.

value_capture.node: Fabrication machinery & consumables — forging press, welding automation, furnaces, heavy CNC (D)
value_capture.basis: Imported, and the deepest hidden dependency in a supposedly localised component: the ultra-heavy forging press, tube-to-tubesheet welding automation, heat-treatment furnaces and heavy CNC that make an SG are all foreign-sourced, so the equipment makers capture margin that Indian fabrication cannot substitute at short notice.

value_capture.node: Internals & separation — moisture separator, dryer, feedwater (C)
value_capture.basis: Fabricated domestically inside the same SG contract, so it adds revenue and absorbs shop hours without commanding separate pricing power; it is a scope extension for the SG fabricator rather than an independent pool.

value_capture.node: Testing & QA — NDT, eddy-current, hydro and helium-leak (E)
value_capture.basis: Not a revenue pool but the entry gate: ASME N/NPT and AERB Class-1 acceptance on ~11,000 tube-to-tubesheet welds is what converts steel into a deliverable SG, and accredited Class-1 inspection capacity is scarce enough to set schedule.

industries.notes: Opportunity uses the same series as the Market & growth digest block (India nuclear-plant equipment ~$2.8 bn in 2026 to ~$7.4 bn in 2035 at an 11.4% CAGR [REPORTED-T3, MarkWide], with the SG at ~7% of the ~₹19 lakh cr 100 GW build). Valuation left UNAVAILABLE — there is no node-level valuation series and the owner and designer are unlisted. industries.title: India Optical Fibre Cable

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Cable is the largest Indian revenue line in the chain and the thinnest margin: fibre is the dominant cost and its price went from Rs 300-325 to Rs 700-800 per fibre-km, so cable makers that bid BharatNet Phase III at last cycle's rates are absorbing the difference. The integrated players - STL, HFCL, Finolex, Polycab - earn the spread; pure cablers do not.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: India OFC market $550 mn in 2025 to more than $1 bn by 2031, ~11% nominal CAGR (tele.net/EY, Aug-2026); India optical-fibre exports rose 158% YoY to $483 mn in Apr-Aug FY27 (Ministry of Commerce, Oct-2026). BharatNet Phase III (about Rs 65,000 cr of BSNL tenders), FTTH, 5G backhaul and data-centre campuses are the four demand legs.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: A dozen or more Indian cable makers contest a standard product; FRP rods are the one node where India is a global hub. Differentiation is integration and certification (BSNL, MTCTE), not design, and the 2026 shortage has temporarily given everyone pricing power.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Cable follows fibre with a lag and a squeeze: demand is at a record, but fixed-price public tenders awarded before the repricing are margin-negative, and STL and Polycab have invoked force majeure on BharatNet Phase III fibre cost. Volume is strong; realised margin depends on reset clauses.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series exists in the registry. Cable makers' multiples mix wires-and-cables, EPC and fibre, and none of them is a sector series.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Value in a cable is imported fibre plus domestic polymer, armour and labour - the domestic share is real but the expensive input is not. FRP/ARP rods and the cabling line are where India adds genuine value.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Cabling capex is lighter than fibre or preform - extrusion, SZ-stranding and test - but working capital is tender-heavy and public-programme receivables are slow. HFCL and Polycab are both adding cable capacity inside larger integrated programmes.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Mature process technology: SZ-stranding, sheath extrusion and OTDR/PMD/CD test. The innovation that matters - high-fibre-count data-centre cable and ribbon - is a design and qualification exercise, not a new process.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Exposure is second-hand - germanium, helium and preform hit cable through the fibre price - plus tender and payment risk on BharatNet. Anti-dumping duties on SMOF in both directions (India to Aug-2028, China to Aug-2031) distort trade rather than secure supply.

missing_critical: India cable volume series (mn fkm) for a volume CAGR
per-km cable realisations by grade and buyer

value_capture.basis: The pool a cable maker is trying to reach: 60-70% of chain profit and 65-75% of Indian preform imported. Every Indian cable expansion is really a bet on owning this node.
Fibre is the largest single cost in a cable and its price went up 2.8-5x in 2026; whoever draws it captures the repricing, whoever buys it pays for it.
Line equipment is imported or locally assembled by a handful of firms; the pool is small but it gates every capacity addition in the country.
India is a global hub for the strength member inside every cable — a genuine export position with better returns than cabling itself.
Aramid is a global duopoly chemistry with no Indian maker; small value, but a single-source input into every ADSS and OPGW design.
The largest Indian revenue pool and a thin one: assembly of imported fibre with domestic polymer and labour, contested by a dozen makers and exposed to fixed-price public tenders.
Not a manufacturing node but the demand pool that sets the terms: public tenders with slow payment, against hyperscaler contracts that are better priced but require qualification.
Commodity polymer compounds, domestically available and priced off the petrochemical cycle; a cost line, not a moat.

industries.title: India Optical Fibre

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Drawing is the second-most profitable step in the chain, not the first: the 2026 up-cycle repriced G.652D fibre from about Rs 300-325 per fibre-km to Rs 700-800, and STL reported Q2 FY27 revenue of Rs 2,529 cr (+145% YoY) at a 27.1% operational EBITDA margin while HFCL did Rs 2,542 cr at 25.9%. The margin is cycle-made rather than structure-made - preform still takes the deeper pool, and ~100 mn fkm of Indian draw capacity against ~46 mn fkm of domestic consumption makes drawing competitive.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: India OFC market $550 mn in 2025 rising to just over $1 bn by 2031 - about 11% nominal CAGR, value only, no volume series (tele.net/EY, Aug-2026). Demand is expected to roughly triple to ~60 mn fkm a year, with data centres at 18-20% of global fibre demand in 2026 rising to 30-35% in 2027 (TrendForce, Oct-2026). The substitution gap - preform 65-75% imported - is the larger prize.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Indian drawing has consolidated to STL, HFCL, Finolex, Birla Furukawa, Polycab and Aksh, but the product is a standard and the global incumbents (YOFC, Futong, Corning, Sumitomo) are far larger. With ~100 mn fkm of Indian capacity against ~46 mn of domestic demand, the export market, not the home market, sets the marginal price.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Peak-tight. The CRU global fibre index went from 78.6 in March 2024 to 107.9 in January 2026 and 263.0 in March 2026; TrendForce puts the 2026 global deficit at 180 mn fkm, utilisation at 92%, inventory at one month and prices at 2.8-5x 2025 levels, with shortages persisting to at least 2028 and leading suppliers booked into Q1 2027.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series exists in the registry. STL, HFCL, Finolex and Polycab trade on earnings the fibre cycle has just repriced, and a company multiple is not a sector series.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: India owns drawing but not the glass: preform is 65-75% imported, so the deepest pool leaks. Integration is closing - STL is already integrated, Finolex commissioned 100 MT of preform in 2026, HFCL reaches 600 MT by Oct-2028 - but until then the Indian draw industry is a toll-taker on imported glass.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Moderate-to-heavy: STL is running about Rs 1,000 cr a year of capex from 2027 to 2029 and HFCL has approved Rs 1,800 cr across fibre, cable and preform. Working capital is heavy and price-exposed, and returns depend on the fibre price holding above preform contracts signed a year earlier.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: G.652D is a commodity made on imported draw towers (Rosendahl Nextrom, SG Controls). The frontier that matters is bend-insensitive and data-centre fibre, where India is catching up rather than leading, and coating resins, ceramic ferrules and process gases remain import-only.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Three gates: germanium, where China refines 91% of the world's primary metal and export controls are live; helium, which India imports almost entirely; and the preform contract book, which suppliers will not price beyond a year while Indian cable makers sign multi-year hyperscaler commitments. Price normalisation as 2027-28 capacity lands is the fourth.

missing_critical: India fibre volume series (fkm) to compute a volume CAGR
quarterly preform import prices by source country

value_capture.basis: The deepest moat in the chain: 60-70% of value-chain profit, 18-24 months to add capacity, germanium access gating entry, and merchant preform prices up about 600% in 2026. Two Indian makers today, three by 2028.
A handful of European and Japanese OEMs supply every Indian line. Small pool, high returns, and the customer cannot switch mid-build — the classic capital-equipment position.

Where India has world-scale capacity and where the up-cycle has just repriced output 2.8-5x; but drawing is a standard process with low entry barriers once preform is secured, so the margin is the cycle's, not the node's.
The fastest-growing fibre pool: data-centre and FTTH grades price above telco D-fibre ($25-27/km against ~$15/km) and grow with the AI build. India can draw it, but qualification takes time.
Helium and high-purity process gases are almost entirely imported and were disrupted by China's July-2026 export ban; the pool is small but the supplier holds the gate.
Zirconia ferrules are a precision-ceramics business with no Indian maker; small value, real barrier, and a connector bottleneck rather than a fibre one.
Specialty chemistry sold by a few global formulators into every draw tower; steady margin, little growth, and easy to design out only slowly.
A pass-through conversion step inside the cable plant: no pricing power, no barrier, and the first cost line a cable maker squeezes.

industries.notes: Scored 2026-11-10 in the content-backfill pass. The market figure and growth rate behind the opportunity score are the same ones carried in the digest's Market & growth block; company results are used as evidence of industry economics, never summed into an industry size.

industries.title: India Optical Fibre Preform

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: The best economics in the chain: 60-70% of value-chain profit sits in preform, and merchant preform prices rose about 600% in 2026 on non-availability (HFCL management, Oct-2026). STL, the only fully integrated Indian maker, earned a 27.1% operational EBITDA margin in Q2 FY27 on Rs 2,529 cr of revenue. A 5 is withheld only because the Indian pool is still 65-75% imported and the margin is the shortage's.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: India preform demand, at landed cost to domestic drawers, is $320-380 mn in 2026 rising to $850-1,050 mn by 2035 - roughly 12-15% nominal CAGR, with volume of 55-65 mn fkm-equivalent going to 140-170 mn (IndexBox, May-2026). The substitution case is stronger than the growth case: 65-75% of Indian preform is still imported.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Global supply is a 6-10 maker oligopoly (Corning, YOFC, Futong, Sumitomo, Furukawa, Prysmian) with 18-24 month greenfield lead times. India goes from one integrated maker to three by 2028 - STL, Finolex (100 to 200 MT) and HFCL (600 MT by Oct-2028) - so domestic competition rises exactly as the global shortage eases.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: The tightest node in the chain. Merchant preform is quoted at prices management calls insane, global fibre capacity utilisation is 92% in 2026, inventory has fallen to one month, and preform capacity cannot be dialled up inside 18-24 months - so the shortage runs to 2028 at the earliest.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series exists in the registry, and there is no listed Indian preform pure-play to proxy one: STL and Finolex carry preform inside much larger businesses.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Preform is the moat. Deposition know-how, germanium access, cleanroom glassworking and 18-24 months of lead time separate it from drawing, and it is the only node where an Indian entrant can hold price against global incumbents.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Capital-heavy and slow: HFCL's 600 MT programme is Rs 1,250 cr with capacity only in Oct-2028, and Finolex's 100 MT plant is captive. Deposition lathes and equipment are imported, and payback depends on the price holding through the build.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: MCVD/OVD/VAD/PCVD deposition plus glassworking is genuine process technology, not assembly - which is why only three Indian groups are attempting it. Specialty and bend-insensitive grades raise the know-how bar further.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Germanium is the binding constraint - China refines 91% of primary metal and its export controls are live - and helium, deposition equipment and high-purity silica are all imported. The second risk is three Indian entrants landing into a normalising price in 2028.

missing_critical: Indian preform volumes in tonnes (not fkm-equivalent)
merchant preform price series by grade

value_capture.basis: The node that keeps the money: 60-70% of chain profit, prices up about 600% in 2026, 18-24 months to replicate, and only three Indian groups attempting it by 2028.
China refines 91% of primary germanium and 40% of world output goes into fibre; the supplier sets price and allocation, and Indian buyers take what is contracted.
The process itself is the barrier — deposition chemistry and yield know-how cannot be bought with the lathe, which is why integration takes two years even after the capex is approved.
A few Western and Japanese OEMs sell every deposition lathe in the world; small pool, very high returns, and switching mid-project is impossible.
Bend-insensitive and data-centre grades are where preform value is compounding fastest, and they price at a premium to telco D-fibre.
Synthetic silica soot and high-purity feedstock are a specialty-chemistry pool with no Indian producer; the barrier is qualification, not capital.
Precision ceramics adjacent to the chain; no Indian maker, small value, real barrier, and a connector bottleneck rather than a glass one.

value_capture.node: Silica Sand & Silicon Metal — raw input
value_capture.basis: Commodity inputs several steps removed from preform economics: India has the sand, the value is created by purification, not extraction.

industries.notes: Scored 2026-11-10 in the content-backfill pass. Market size and growth are the digest's own Market & growth figures; preform prices are taken from management commentary as evidence of node economics.

industries.title: India Optical, Medical & Surgical Apparatus

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Device margins are structurally better than commodity manufacturing; approval and clinical evidence sustain pricing.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: India medical-device market USD 15.2 bn (2025) to USD 50.1 bn (2030) at a 26.9% nominal CAGR (base disputed at USD 14-17.5 bn, so the implied range is 23-29%), with 70-80% of demand imported.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Imports still dominate high-end devices; localisation is underway but uneven.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Policy support is expanding while disbursement lags, which is a mixed cycle position rather than a strong or a weak one. PLI-MD was extended to 2035-36 on 10-Nov-2026 with ~Rs 2,700 cr of its Rs 3,420 cr outlay still undisbursed (PIB, 10-Nov-2026), fresh applications opened, and CDSCO licensing has widened to 4,108 manufacturers by Mar-2026. Against that, FY26 (Apr-Dec) imports of Rs 94,664 cr ran ~3x exports of Rs 28,106 cr, imports rose ~17% in FY25 while exports stagnated, and the parliamentary committee found only ~30% local content (PIB, 13-Mar-2026) - so the demand cycle is strong and the domestic-capture cycle is not.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Assembly and component supply; design and IP sit with global device makers.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Device assembly and cleanrooms — moderate capital.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Design capability and regulatory approval are the moat.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Healthcare demand is largely non-cyclical; disruption risk low.

missing_critical: domestic value-added share by device class

value_capture.basis: The highest-ASP node in the basket, 70-80% imported; the money is in the installed base and its service contract, which is why switching costs dominate the score.
The hardest component in Indian imaging: tubes and panels are a foreign oligopoly, the Varex AMTZ line (Jul-2025) is a first local step, and nothing else in the chain gates as much value.
Import-led economics at a lower price point than MRI, and the node where Indian OEMs (Innvolution) have begun to assemble rather than to make the tube.
No Indian maker of the magnet and cryostat; it prices as a monopoly component inside an imported system and cannot be substituted at system level.
Large volume and genuine Indian share (Sahajanand, Meril), but NPPA price ceilings cap the pricing power that would otherwise sit in this node.
Same ceiling dynamic as stents: domestic manufacturing is real, but the NPPA-capped price and tender-driven hospital buying keep returns ordinary.
Strong Indian private makers (Aurolab, Appasamy) serve the volume, premium optics are imported and the lens is price-capped, so the pool is defensible rather than lucrative.
The most fragmented node, with low barriers and low switching, but it converts cash quickly and is where the listed Indian base (Poly Medicure) actually earns.

industries.notes: Scored against "Industry-Level Investment Parameters & Scoring Architecture". Delta pass 2026-11-13: cycle position filled from PLI-MD 2.0 (PIB, 10-Nov-2026) and the FY26 trade data; valuation stays UNAVAILABLE because no industry-level valuation series exists. Market size and growth are the Rubix/IBEF series already carried in the digest; value capture is scored on the page's own tree nodes.

industries.title: India Optical Transceivers

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: India assembles modules from imported engines: over 95% of high-speed module components are imported and 85-90% of consumption by value arrives finished. Local value-add is packaging, test and cable assembly, so the Indian industry earns a conversion margin on a part whose DSP and lasers it does not make.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: India optical-transceiver market $0.73 bn in 2026 to $1.73 bn by 2033, about 13.25% CAGR for 2027-33 (MarkNtel); a second scope puts India optical interconnect at $938.6 mn in 2026 to $3,569 mn by 2033 at 21% (GrandView) - the scopes differ and are not averaged. Data-centre capacity of 1.8 GW in H1-2026 rising to ~6 GW by 2029 is the volume driver.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: The module market is a Chinese-dominated oligopoly (Innolight, Eoptolink, Accelink) plus US device makers (Coherent, Lumentum, Broadcom for DSP). India's entrants are small: GX Group's SFP plant from Dec-2026, a Dixon-Gemtek JV, and CloudPhotonix, still at 100G design and targeting 400/800G test capability by 2027.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Strong but deflationary: Ethernet optics went from $16.5 bn in 2025 to $26 bn in 2026, up 60% (LightCounting), and 800G-and-above rose from 19.5% of shipments in 2024 to over 60% in 2026 - but module ASPs fall 12-18% a year, so the cycle rewards ramp speed, not installed base.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series exists in the registry, and the Indian listed exposure is thin enough that a single company multiple would not represent the industry.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: India sits at the last assembly and test step. The DSP/retimer ASIC, the EML/VCSEL/DFB laser and the photonic integrated circuit are the pools, and all three are imported; domestic content is housings, PCBs and passives.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Assembly capex is modest - die-attach, wire-bond, active alignment, burn-in - but working capital is punishing in a market with 16-18 month product generations and 12-18% annual ASP deflation, and 400/800G test equipment is itself imported.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: The frontier (800G/1.6T, silicon photonics, co-packaged optics) sits abroad; India has credible 100G design capability and is building 400/800G test. A dedicated national photonics roadmap is being argued for, not yet funded.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Three structural exposures: DSP supply concentrated in a handful of vendors, product obsolescence every 16-18 months, and bundling - switch and router OEMs tying transceiver purchase to warranty - which shuts independent Indian module makers out of the easiest channel.

missing_critical: India transceiver volumes by speed grade

value_capture.basis: The single pool that decides module economics: a handful of fabless vendors (Broadcom, Marvell, Credo) own the PAM4 DSP, and no Indian design house ships one at 400G.

value_capture.node: Light Sources: EML / VCSEL / DFB Lasers
value_capture.basis: Compound-semiconductor laser fabs are the second gate: allocation is short, qualification is long, and India has no laser fab.
The pool that grows fastest as co-packaged optics arrives; India is at design-partner stage, not production.
The OEM layer captures the system margin and controls the transceiver decision through bundling and warranty, which is why independent module makers struggle for channel access.
Coherent modules carry the highest ASPs in the category and are the hardest to assemble; Indian capability is absent above 100G.
TOSA/ROSA assembly and active alignment are the skill bottleneck in localisation — GX Group is building exactly this, and it is the realistic first rung for India.
Where India actually sits: packaging and test of imported engines, contested by Chinese ODMs at a scale India cannot match, and exposed to 12-18% annual ASP deflation.
The default Indian position today: distribution margin on imported modules, with no barrier and no pricing power, and the first layer to disappear as duty classification tightens.

industries.notes: Scored 2026-11-10 in the content-backfill pass. Two conflicting market scopes are shown side by side in the digest and neither is averaged; the opportunity score rests on the narrower, better-anchored one.

industries.title: India Organic Chemicals

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: The intermediate layer re-rated hard in Q2 FY27 — Deepak Nitrite's consolidated EBITDA rose 187% year on year to Rs 643 crore at a 21% margin, Navin Fluorine's EBITDA margin reached 34.2% and SRF's PAT grew 31% — but the commodity end is still losing money: Chemplast Sanmar posted a Rs 5 crore PAT loss with value-added chemicals under pressure and caustic soda in global oversupply. The rupee of output now earns more only where it is protected or specialised, which is why the score moves to 3 rather than 4.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: Value of output grew 11.6% a year at current prices to Rs 15.14 lakh crore in FY2023-24 inside a ~USD 220 billion sector that PIB projects at USD 300 billion by 2030, and the HS-29 import gap was Rs 42,784 crore in FY26 — but volume grew only 2.8% a year and organic-chemical utilisation has fallen to 64.3% (FY24) from 73.2% (FY19), so growth still arrives into surplus capacity.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Structurally fragmented across more than 80,000 products, so commodity grades are price-takers against Chinese imports; the moat is real only in specialty and fine chemistry, where qualification cycles bind customers. The same quarter proves the split: a 22% phenolics EBIT margin at Deepak against a PAT loss at Chemplast's commodity PVC.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: A genuine upswing is under way — Q2 FY27 was a record for Deepak, +57% revenue for Navin Fluorine and +35% for SRF — but it was driven by freight, war-related supply dislocation and trade remedies rather than by capacity closure, and China's anti-involution campaign upgrades sub-scale naphtha crackers to a 2028 deadline instead of shutting them. Recovery is cyclical, not structural: score raised from 2 to 3, not higher.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series is carried in the registry; the sector-wide re-rating is reported but no industry multiple series is available to score.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Upstream and a competitive specialty export base are genuinely domestic, and phenol-acetone is closing its import gap with Adperma's 345 kt train — but ~66% of PVC demand, over 3 MMT of methanol, ~1.2 MMT of acetic acid, nearly all catalysts and all cracker and reformer technology are still imported, and the solvent layer remains the largest leak.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Very capital-intensive with long gestation — Adani's Mundra PVC is Rs 26,000 crore for 1 MMTPA and commissions in FY28, IOCL's Paradip complex is Rs 61,077 crore for 2029 — and much of it is being added while the market still absorbs Chinese surplus and domestic utilisation sits near 60%.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Cracker and reformer technology is licensed from Linde, Lummus, KBR and Technip, catalysts are almost entirely imported, and process-chemistry skills are scarce and cannot be bought quickly; R&D intensity is structurally low outside a handful of specialty firms.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Trade-remedy outcomes are the swing factor and all of them land inside one six-month window: the S-PVC countervailing duty recommended on 26-Oct-2026 but not notified, the minimum import price expiring around 24-Jan-2027, the phenol anti-dumping case with no findings, and the Madras High Court's provisional assessment of paste-PVC imports. Add a structural Chinese surplus and Middle East feedstock volatility. Held at 2.

missing_critical: FY26 value of output (the DCPC series ends FY2023-24)
profit-pool split by node, so operating-profit share rests on segment disclosures rather than an industry account

value_capture.node: Specialty & fine chemistry (agro / pharma intermediates, CDMO)
value_capture.basis: Moved to the top of the chain: SRF chemicals revenue +25% and Navin Fluorine revenue +57% at a 34.2% EBITDA margin in Q2 FY27, with qualification cycles and USFDA/REACH registration binding customers. Segment disclosures, not an industry profit account.

Captive HF is the moat and fluorspar is China-concentrated; SRF reported robust refrigerant volumes with positive pricing momentum in Q2 FY27, and Chemplast began R-32 market seeding with capacity due by end-FY27.

value_capture.node: Licensed process technology & engineering (cracker, reformer, phenol)
value_capture.basis: Royalty and licence economics on every Indian cracker, reformer and phenol train, with Linde, Lummus, KBR and Technip as the licensors; no domestic substitute, and switching means rebuilding the plant.

The largest revenue pool and the gate on everything downstream, but a commodity spread: propylene availability was disturbed for six months and Deepak had to buy from non-traditional sources at higher prices.

RANK MOVED UP. A record phenolics quarter (Rs 2,291 crore revenue, Rs 515 crore EBIT, ~22% margin) lifted this node on import dislocation, freight and duty protection — but Adperma's 345 kt train lands in Q4 FY27 into a ~600 kt market with Deepak Chem Tech adding 300 kt by FY28, so the realised 2026 profitability is flagged to compress once the new capacity ramps.
Tiny revenue, near-total import dependence and the highest margin per tonne in the chain; no listed Indian player, so the pool is entirely offshore.
On-site take-or-pay contracts and high cash conversion; Linde India is the only listed pure-play and every new cracker, phenol train and PVC line adds a gas contract.

Large revenue pool, worst economics: commodity grade, ~66% of demand imported, remedy-dependent, and Chemplast Sanmar still posted a PAT loss in Q2 FY27 despite the MIP. Adani Mundra and RIL expansion will grow the pool while compressing the spread.
Over 3 MMT of methanol and ~1.2 MMT of acetic acid imported because domestic gas is not competitively priced; domestic producers earn a protected spread rather than a proprietary one.

Caustic soda pricing stayed under pressure through Q2 FY27 on global oversupply and weak demand, with Chemplast's Karaikal shutdown and reduced Mettur operations cutting volumes; chlorine co-product economics, not price, decide the pool.

industries.notes: Full re-analysis 2026-11-13 (daily rotation). Scores moved on new Q2 FY27 evidence: economics 2->3 and cycle 2->3 on record intermediate-layer profitability; risk held at 2 because every trade remedy that could change the picture is still unnotified or expiring within six months. Value capture: phenol/acetone moved up on realised 2026 margins and is flagged to fall back once Adperma commissions.

industries.title: Overhead Transmission Line

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: EPC margins are thin and steel, zinc and aluminium pass through; the annuity economics sit with the asset owner, not the line contractor.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: T&D EPC USD 14.68 bn (2025) to USD 35.20 bn (2035) at 9.34%, with overhead lines 81.67% of it; FY27 line target of 25,146 ckm is roughly double FY26 additions.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Fragmented EPC field with five to six scaled players; tower capacity is more concentrated (KEC ~4.8 lakh t/yr, Skipper 3.75-4.5 lakh t/yr).

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Order books at records and the FY27 target is nearly double FY26, but the 21% FY26 shortfall shows execution, not demand, is the binding constraint.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Towers and conductors are domestic and export-competitive; value leaks at OPGW fibre, composite long-rod and hollow insulators and compression hardware.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Working-capital-heavy contracting with retention and mobilisation funding; tower plants are only a few hundred crore each, so capital is not the barrier.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Mature technology; HTLS conductors and monopoles are the only real steps, and both are already commercial.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Right-of-way and forest clearance is the single binding constraint; steel and zinc price swings hit margins; four China-owned plants hold a bidding exemption to 2028.

value_capture.basis: The highest-return pool on the page because it reuses existing right of way: APAR has executed 272+ reconductoring projects and bundles HTLS supply with turnkey execution [REPORTED-T1]. Asset-light, cash-generative, and pulled by utilities that would rather avoid a new-line clearance than build one.

The premium sub-node where the margin actually sits: APAR's premium mix rose to 45.8% in FY26 from 40.6% and lifted EBITDA per tonne 17.3% [REPORTED-T1]. ACCC is made under licence from CTC Global, so the IP is licensed rather than owned — which caps the barrier — while reconductoring (272+ projects executed) is the demand engine.

The most concentrated node on the page: composite hollow (CHCI) is made by few players globally, and Aditya Birla Power Composites is India's first large-scale CHCI maker as a Grasim (51%) / MR Germany (49%) JV, with MR sharing the technology exclusively [REPORTED-T2: CARE Ratings]. Tiny pool, near-monopoly economics, and the part must be type-tested with the apparatus it insulates.

The largest listed pool in the chain: APAR's conductor division did ₹12,712 cr revenue in FY26 (+32.7%) at ₹1,040 cr EBITDA (8.2%) and ₹43,012 EBITDA/tonne, with premium (HTLS/AL59) at 45.8% of mix and a ₹7,671 cr order book [REPORTED-T1: APAR FY26 investor update]. Aluminium is commodity-linked, so pricing power is mix-driven rather than structural, and working capital is heavy against utility payment cycles.

The technology-substitution node: composite is ~43% of the Indian insulator mix in 2025 and gains where contamination performance and weight matter [REPORTED-T2], and Deccan Enterprises has qualified to 765 kV AC / 800 kV HVDC. Qualification per voltage class is the barrier, which is what separates it from commodity porcelain.

Import-linked and bottlenecked: the optical fibre inside the OPGW is the constrained input, and there is no listed OPGW/insulator pure-play in the selected universe [REPORTED-T2]. Value accrues to the qualified integrator rather than the cable assembler — which is why APAR is building the capability alongside its conductor franchise.

Fabrication is competitive and thin: KEC carries ~4.8 lakh t/yr of tower capacity and Transrail 1.84 lakh t/yr, yet the EPC layer that owns them earns 7.1% consolidated EBITDA on ₹23,506 cr of FY26 revenue [REPORTED-T1: KEC FY26 results], and Salasar's 8.1% EBITDA on ₹1,503 cr marks the pure-fabrication ceiling. Steel and zinc pass straight through.

The weakest economics on the page: Grasim's Aditya Birla Insulators did ₹479 cr of revenue in FY25 with EBITDA of just ₹7 cr against 41,727 t of capacity [REPORTED-T1: Grasim FY25 annual report], and IEEMA reports domestic overcapacity with Chinese product at ~67% of India's insulator import value [REPORTED-T2]. A necessary node with almost no retained margin, and no listed pure-play in the selected universe.

industries.notes: Scored against 'Industry-Level Investment Parameters & Scoring Architecture'. Opportunity uses the same T&D EPC series as the Market & growth digest block (Astute Analytica), cross-checked against Transrail's 2029 waypoint. Valuation left UNAVAILABLE. Value capture (added 2026-11-02) scores 8 nodes taken verbatim from this page's own BOM tree and value-chain ladder, on the separate Registry Review §4 weighting (op_share 20%, pricing_power 15%, roic 15%, barriers 15%, bottleneck 10%, pool_growth 10%, cash_conversion 10%, switching 5%). It answers 'which node keeps the money' and is not blended into the industry score above.

industries.title: India PCB & Electronic Components

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: India consumes about Rs 35,000 cr of PCB a year and makes 10-15% of it. Fabrication is small-scale and thin-margin - mid-scale shops were running gross margins below 20% as laminate landed cost rose - and the 30% anti-dumping duty on Chinese bare PCB (Mar-2024 to Mar-2029) is what keeps the domestic line alive.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: India PCB demand of about Rs 35,000 cr in FY25 rising to roughly $14 bn by FY30 on ELCINA's projection; a 15% value CAGR for 2025-34 calculated from IMARC sizes, with volume CAGR unavailable. Domestic bare-PCB output is projected to rise from ~13% of demand in FY24 to ~31% by FY29 - the substitution, not the growth, is the investable part.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Fragmented and sub-scale against Chinese and Taiwanese fabricators: ECMS has approved 9 PCB applicants and 12-14 bare-PCB units, but Kaynes' laminate capacity will cover only ~15% of projected 2027 demand. Protection is doing the work that scale has not yet done.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: A genuine supply squeeze: AI-server demand is crowding out PCB capacity, global suppliers have hiked prices over 20%, low-bromine epoxy resin rose about 70% and JUSHI 7628 glass cloth doubled in eight months (ELCINA, Aug-2026). Indian fabricators are price-takers on inputs and beneficiaries on output.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series exists in the registry. The listed Indian exposure is a handful of small bare-PCB names plus EMS majors whose PCB segment is a fraction of revenue.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: The board is the least valuable part of the board. Laminate is ~30% of the PCB bill of materials and 90% of it was imported in 2024; copper foil and glass fabric are imported too, so the pool sits upstream of the Indian fabricator.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Heavy for the return: plating and etching lines, multilayer presses, AOI and flying-probe test are imported, effluent-treatment norms are tightening, and inventory buffers for imported laminate tie up working capital.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: India is at the 4-6 layer end while demand migrates to HDI, 8-plus layer and rigid-flex; ECMS projects target that migration but commercial output is FY27-29. Photoresists are 100% imported and plating chemicals 60-80%.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Protected but exposed: the 30% anti-dumping duty and ECMS money offset Chinese scale, while laminate, foil, glass cloth and specialty chemicals are imported and their prices moved 30-70% in a year. Customer concentration in Indian EMS is a further gate.

missing_critical: India PCB volume series (sq m or panels) for a volume CAGR
domestic value-add share by board type

value_capture.basis: About 30% of the PCB bill of materials, 90% imported in 2024, and the input whose price swings decide whether an Indian fabricator makes money. Wipro's ECMS plant is the first domestic CCL line.
The layer beneath the laminate: glass cloth (JUSHI) doubled in eight months and foil rose over 30%, and India makes neither at scale — the deepest leak in the chain.
The high-value board type India does not make: ECMS HDI projects (Amber-Korea Circuit, Kaynes) are targeting it, and it carries the ASP premium that bare 4-6 layer boards do not.
Drillers, LDI, plating and AOI come from China, Taiwan, Italy, Germany and Japan; every ECMS plant is a customer, and there is no Indian equipment maker.
Consumer-electronics and automotive demand is entirely imported today; ECMS flex capacity from FY27 is the first domestic attempt.
Only about 20% domestic, and a global oligopoly in MLCC; the passives pool leaks almost entirely and gates every assembly line downstream.
The mainstream board and the largest Indian revenue pool, but thin-margin and contested by importers whose scale is ten times larger; the anti-dumping duty, not the moat, protects it.
India's real strength and its thinnest margin: Dixon, Kaynes and Syrma compete on conversion cost for global brands, and the board they populate is still imported.

industries.notes: Scored 2026-11-10 in the content-backfill pass. Market sizes conflict across scopes (Mordor's $3.31 bn 2026 bare-PCB series against HSIE's $6.3 bn CY24 total-PCB series); the digest's own figure is used for the opportunity score and neither is averaged.

industries.title: India Pharma APIs & Bulk Drugs

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Commodity APIs are China price-set with a 35-40% cost gap, so domestic viability is subsidy-determined: the bulk-drug PLI had disbursed only ₹87.7 cr against a ₹6,940 cr outlay as of Mar-2026, and a one-year minimum import price on Pen-G, 6-APA and amoxicillin was needed in Jan-2026 to stop predatory pricing.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: The market is ~$15-16 bn growing 5-7% through FY28, and the substitution pool is large and documented - $4.35 bn of API, bulk-drug and intermediate imports in FY25 of which China supplied 73.7% - but the growth rate is mid-single-digit and the addressable share is policy-gated.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Around 500 API makers across roughly 1,500 facilities compete on cost against Chinese scale with no pricing power in commodity molecules; the differentiated pool - CRDMO, HPAPI, fermentation - is where margin exists and is small against the base.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: The price cycle is imported rather than domestic: Chinese price cuts forced the MIP intervention, and Indian realisations move with Chinese KSM costs rather than with Indian demand, leaving little independent cycle signal to trade.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry - API equities are not covered by a sector multiple series in this pass.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: India holds the full synthesis chain and 38 commissioned PLI projects covering 28 products, but KSMs, advanced intermediates and fermentation inputs remain imported, and CRDMO - the premium pool - is only $3-3.5 bn of a $145 bn global market.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Fermentation capex is heavy, long-gestation and subsidy-dependent, with ETP/ZLD obligations and large water and power loads; actual investment under the PLI has already exceeded the committed ₹4,330 cr at ₹5,070 cr, which shows how much capital the state has had to underwrite.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Process chemistry is a genuine Indian strength - third-largest producer by volume with real CRDMO capability - but fermentation know-how is being re-learned after decades of import, and the equipment is largely foreign-sourced.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Single-source vulnerability defines the industry: 73.7% of a $4.35 bn import basket comes from China, the protective minimum import price runs for one year only, and the PLI scheme tenure was explicitly not extended.

value_capture.basis: Containment, cytotoxic handling and regulatory clearance make this the highest-barrier chemistry on the page, and qualification is molecule-specific so switching costs are high. Small volumes, disproportionate value per kilogram, and a pool that only a handful of Indian sites can serve.

value_capture.node: CRDMO & Biotech — CRDMO services, biologics, peptides, enzymes
value_capture.basis: The premium pool and the one that keeps its margin: India's CRDMO book is small against a ~$145 bn global market but is growing at a mid-teens rate on Western de-risking, and it is sold on capability rather than on price — the opposite of the commodity API trade. Asset-light relative to fermentation, with customer stickiness once a molecule is filed.

The choke point of the whole chain: 73.7% of a $4.35 bn API, bulk-drug and intermediate import basket comes from China, and the KSM layer sits upstream of even the domestic API makers, so an Indian producer's cost and continuity are set abroad. The pool accrues to Chinese suppliers, not to Indian balance sheets.

value_capture.node: Fermentation-based APIs & KSMs — Penicillin G, 6-APA, 7-ACA, clavulanic acid
value_capture.basis: The most strategically important and least rewarding node: fermentation was rebuilt from scratch under the PLI after decades of import, so barriers are high and the bottleneck is genuine, but the economics are capital-heavy, energy- and water-intensive, subsidy-dependent and working-capital hungry — the PLI's ₹5,070 cr of actual investment against a ₹4,330 cr commitment shows how much of the capital the state had to underwrite.

value_capture.node: Chemical-synthesis APIs — paracetamol, NSAIDs, statins, sartans, ARVs
value_capture.basis: The volume base of the Indian API industry and the largest revenue pool, but it is a price-taker: Chinese material is reported 35–40% cheaper, the DGFT minimum import price that protects the segment runs for one year only, and customers dual-source as a matter of policy. Real scale, thin and volatile margin.

Where most Indian pharma revenue actually sits, and the reason backward integration is pursued at all: FDF is crowded, tender- and brand-priced, with low barriers and no bottleneck power, but it converts API cost into a branded or regulated-market margin that the API trade alone cannot earn.

value_capture.node: Process Inputs — solvents, reagents, catalysts, industrial gases
value_capture.basis: Partly imported and largely commoditised: solvent and reagent cost is passed through to the API maker and recovered through solvent recovery rather than through price, and the industrial-gas supply is a utility relationship. A real cost line, not a profit pool.

value_capture.node: Utilities · ETP/ZLD & compliance — GMP, Schedule M, WHO maturity
value_capture.basis: A cost of entry that consumes capital rather than earning a return: zero-liquid-discharge plants, large water and power loads, and the Schedule M / WHO-maturity upgrade cycle absorb cash, and the revised Schedule M deadlines are what will thin the smaller-player base rather than reward it.

industries.notes: Opportunity uses the same series as the Market & growth digest block (~$15–16 bn growing 5–7% through FY28, and the broader-scope $14.18 bn 2025 to $22.18 bn 2031 at 7.74% CALCULATED). Valuation left UNAVAILABLE — no industry valuation series exists.

industries.title: India PCS & Power Semiconductors

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: The PCS is an 8-22% slice of BESS cost depending on scope, inside a system whose per-kWh price keeps falling. Device-integrated makers earn 27.05% gross margin on storage PCS (Sineng, H1 2026) and 32.43% on integrated systems (Sungrow) while Kehua earns 21.81%; an Indian assembler buying imported silicon and selling against Chinese cost leaders earns far less, and Hitachi Energy India guides BESS balance-of-plant margins below its portfolio average.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: 13.7 GWh operates at Sep-2026 against a 411 GWh requirement by FY31-32; the Nov-2026 VGF scheme underwrites 30 GWh of BESS with a 40% domestic content condition, and the CEA draft would put grid-forming control on 100% of BESS PCS from 01-Jul-2027. Demand is policy-anchored rather than forecast.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Unattractive structure: a foreign oligopoly on devices (Infineon, onsemi, Mitsubishi, Fuji, ST, Rohm) and Chinese cost leadership on inverters (Sungrow, Sineng and Hopewind took 84% of central-inverter shipments in Q1 2026; Chinese firms held 85.5% in the same quarter), against fragmented, largely unlisted Indian assembly. Competition is intense where margins are thin and absent where they are fat.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Delivery is inflecting - 13.7 GWh at Sep-2026 against a Dec-2025 base about one-seventeenth of it - but ordering is cooling: FY27 storage tendering down 26% year-on-year, 20% of tendered capacity cancelled, and inverter shipments down 35% quarter-on-quarter in Q2 2026. Early upswing in delivery, late peak in ordering.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series exists for Indian PCS or power-semiconductor manufacturing and none is carried in the registry. Company multiples are company facts, not an industry valuation. [UNAVAILABLE]

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Cabinet assembly, magnetics winding and the AC-side transformer are Indian; 1200-1700 V IGBT and SiC modules, isolated gate drivers, DC-link film capacitors, nanocrystalline cores and plant-level firmware are imported. India holds the volume layer and not the margin layer.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: A PCS assembly line is a low-hundred-crore asset that can run on imported silicon, so capital is not the barrier to entry - which is why entry is crowded and returns are competed away. The capital barrier sits one layer up, at a device line costing US$1-5 bn.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Two migrations run at once - silicon IGBT to SiC MOSFET, and grid-following to grid-forming control - and India follows on both: unit-level grid-forming capability (Statcon, Ador) but no device capability, with SiC module lead times of 12-16 weeks gating the transition.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Three gates: a device layer 100% imported with years-long substitution; demand resting on instruments not yet notified (CEA draft, MNRE localisation draft) plus a 40% DCR that raises input cost 18-61% on the MHI estimate; and a cost position that loses to Chinese suppliers on any unsubsidised bid. VGF underwrites volume, not competitiveness.

missing_critical: a surveyed value figure for the Indian PCS market in rupees or dollars (all estimates here are shares of a BESS envelope, not a PCS series)
segment revenue disclosure splitting PCS or inverter revenue from transformers and switchgear at the listed companies
import value of IGBT and SiC modules by HS line for India, to size the leaking device pool directly
ex-works price per kW of Indian-made versus imported central PCS at matched scope

value_capture.basis: The largest operating-profit pool in the chain and 100% imported: a five-firm oligopoly with 2,550 HHI, SiC lead times of 12-16 weeks and requalification cost on any substitute. Rated up on pricing power because the Nov-2026 DCR and the CEA mandate both increase device content per project without adding a domestic supplier.

Software and IP with almost no capital: if the CEA draft is notified, every BESS PCS sold in India needs compliant firmware and a validation report from 01-Jul-2027. Highest return on capital in the chain; the constraint is that Indian capability sits in unlisted firms.

Rated up sharply: this is the part of the PCS AC block India makes competitively, and it is where the listed pool earns. CG Power posted Q2 FY27 sales of Rs 3,802 crore (+30%) with a Rs 23,646 crore backlog and Hitachi Energy India a Rs 32,222 crore backlog - transformer and switchgear scarcity, not PCS scarcity, is doing the pricing.
Small revenue share but a genuine single-point dependency: an isolated gate driver cannot be swapped without retesting the whole power stack. Foreign oligopoly, no Indian option.
Negligible revenue share, high switching cost, and a qualification cycle that makes it sticky. A plausible first localisation for a passive-components maker.
Rated up: winding is already domestic and the DCR creates demand for documented local content, but the core material is imported and pricing power is limited by commodity copper.

Rated down: the pool grows fastest and is where the listed names sit, but the new evidence is that central-class PCS to 1.25 MW is already built in India by unlisted firms (Delta 1.1 MW, Statcon 1.25 and 1.725 MW, Ador 1.25 MW), so the barrier is lower than assumed and the price competition harder - 85.5% of central-inverter shipments were Chinese in Q1 2026.

Rated down: CG Semi G1 is in commercial production at 300 million units a year, but G2 qualification has slipped to mid-2027 with production late 2028-2029, the pool is assembly and test rather than fabrication, and the cash cycle on a Rs 7,500 crore project is punishing against a small revenue base.

industries.notes: Re-run 2026-11-07 against the 2026-10-09 entry. Three things moved the score. First, the Nov-2026 VGF scheme puts 40% domestic content on 30 GWh of BESS, replacing a 20% local-content note and the still-draft 60% MNRE proposal - a firmer demand underwriting, hence opportunity held at 4. Second, evidence that central PCS above 1 MW is already made in India (Delta, Statcon, Ador) cut the assumed barrier and pushed competitive from 3 to 2 and PCS integration down the value-capture table. Third, the order book cooled - FY27 tendering down 26%, a fifth of tendered capacity cancelled, inverter shipments down 35% QoQ - moving cycle from 4 to 3. Capital was raised from 3 to 4 because the assembly step is cheap to enter, which is a statement about barriers, not about returns. Overall falls from 64.7 to 57.6 on 85% coverage; valuation remains unscored and the score is provisional.

industries.title: India Power Semiconductors & OSAT

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Domestic build capacity ~USD 0.4 bn against ~USD 3-4 bn of demand; the industry earns on assembly today, where material is 45-50% of cost and 60-70% of that is imported.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: Discrete power semiconductor and module market USD 1.86 bn (2025) to USD 4.05 bn (2032), 12% CAGR; import substitution is the growth engine.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Global majors hold device technology and Chinese capacity sets price; India's entry point is OSAT — 9 of the 12 approved units are back-end, and 5 units in total are producing.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Split market: 8-inch MOSFET/IGBT lines at ~90% utilisation with 10-15% price increases in H1 2026, while automotive SiC is in surplus and 6-inch substrate fell from ~USD 1,500 to ~USD 500. Input inflation (components +30-35%, PCB +10-12%, 6-8 month lead times) squeezes assemblers.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry; listed proxies trade on EMS and capital-goods multiples, which are not an industry multiple.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Bottlenecks are explicit and now have named first movers: no qualified Indian leadframe, EMC or bonding wire, but Tata-Enomoto, Kinesis and Voltix have entered the frame.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Heavy fixed capital with long payback; CG Power has spent ~INR 20 bn for semiconductor EBIT breakeven only from FY28, and ~70% equipment-capex subsidy is what makes the arithmetic close.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Processes are licensed (PSMC, Clas-SiC, Renesas) and assembly-led; the first indigenous SiC epi line and a fabless 1200V SiC platform exist but are pre-scale.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Policy-dependent, qualification-gated and execution-heavy, but the strategic priority and the incentive stack are durable through Semicon 2.0.

value_capture.basis: Installed base plus service revenue and multi-year qualification; tool supply is the binding constraint on every new fab, and Semicon 2.0 Pillar 2 exists because of it. Ranked first this pass, up from second.
Highest margins and best cash conversion in the chain, and a design win locks the socket; op_share trimmed because the power-device design pool is narrower than logic. Ranked second, down from first.

Leadframe, wire and compound are qualified into a process and cannot be swapped casually; 35-40% of material cost sits in the leadframe alone. Bottleneck weight raised as localisation intent (Enomoto, Kinesis) proved how hard the layer is.
Largest absolute profit pool, but enormous fixed assets, heavy depreciation and returns that depend entirely on utilisation; Chinese capacity now sets pricing power.
Owns the customer and the brand so cash conversion is good, but it is not a bottleneck and can be served by any qualified supplier.

Added this pass as its own node. The pool grows fastest of any input, but 6-inch substrate prices collapsed from ~USD 1,500 to ~USD 500 and 8-inch is now the benchmark, so barriers and pricing power are eroding faster than volume grows.
