Where India's capacity is being built, but the thin-margin end: pricing power is weak, material is 45-50% of cost and 60-70% of it is imported, and CG Semi expects breakeven only in FY28.
Grows fastest (modules at 16% CAGR versus 12% for the market) but is the thinnest pool: dies are imported and the assembler adds process, not design.

industries.notes: Scored against 'Industry-Level Investment Parameters & Scoring Architecture'. Cycle is scored for the first time (it was UNAVAILABLE in the 2026-10-09 pass) from Yole, TrendForce and channel price data; valuation stays UNAVAILABLE, so coverage is 85%. Value capture scored per node from the review's section 4 model on the 1-5 scale.

industries.title: India Power & Distribution Transformers

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: OEM economics are strong but no longer uniformly so: CG Power's Power Systems segment earned 25.0% PBIT on ₹1,769 cr in Q2 FY27 (up 430 bps YoY), GE Vernova T&D ran a 28.6% PBT margin, TARIL 16.1% EBITDA and Hitachi Energy 16.0% in Q1 FY27 — while Voltamp, the most industrial-exposed name, lost 543 bps of gross margin and 393 bps of EBITDA margin in the same quarter on input costs and legacy fixed-price orders. Industry-wide CRISIL put operating margins at only 8–10%, so the returns are concentrated in EHV/utility-facing capacity, not spread across the sector.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: Demand visibility is the strongest part of the case and it is now measured, not projected: 1,13,013 MVA of transformation capacity was added in FY26 (90% of the CEA target) against an FY27 target of 1,58,339 MVA, power-transformer production rose 31.6% in FY26 (Q4 +58.5%), and the NEP successor plan to 2035-36 carries another ₹7.93 lakh cr for ~828 GVA. A five-year value CAGR remains [UNAVAILABLE]; the volume path (transformation capacity from 1,478 GVA in Jun-2026 to 2,345 GVA by 2032) is [REPORTED-T1].

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: The moat is qualification, not capital. Only about half of transformers pass short-circuit testing at the first attempt and 765 kV qualification needs 3–4 years of field performance [REPORTED-T2, Choice Institutional, Oct-2026]; HVDC remains a two-player contest (Hitachi Energy and GE Vernova, with BHEL in consortium). But the field is widening — Voltamp's Jarod EHV plant went live on 7-Oct-2026, CG Power's Sehore plant on 4-Sep-2026, and Atlanta's 765 kV line is running at 7–8% utilisation — so the oligopoly is being contested at 400 kV rather than at 765 kV/HVDC.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Demand sits at a cyclical high (peak demand hit a record 270.82 GW in summer 2026; 400/765 kV orders are being booked for FY29–30 execution) while ~315 GVA of announced capacity lands across FY27–FY30 — CG Power, TARIL, Voltamp, Bharat Bijlee, Shilchar and Siemens Energy India are all commissioning or expanding. FY26 TBCB ordering was thin (16 schemes vs 45 in FY25) and the HVDC pipeline of ~₹1.0 lakh cr is not yet awarded, so the risk is a margin peak in FY27–28 rather than a demand peak.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: CORRECTION from the prior run: the earlier basis quoted the listed set at 95x–167x earnings. Actual multiples on 9-Nov-2026 are two-tier — the EHV/HVDC majors at 89x (CG Power) and 109x (Hitachi Energy), and the pure-play transformer makers at 21.7x (Bharat Bijlee) to 32.4x (Shilchar), with TARIL at 30.2x and Voltamp at 30.4x [REPORTED-T2]. The industry is therefore expensive only where the HVDC optionality sits; brokers value Hitachi at 60x two-year forward and GE Vernova at 55x while Elara rates Hitachi a Sell on 60x FY28-29E — the dispersion, not the level, is the signal.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: India now performs essentially every transformer step from core slitting to impulse testing, and finished power-transformer imports have collapsed to ₹177 cr in FY26 (-60% YoY) — the system-level chain is domestic. The leaks are the same three and they are narrowing unevenly: CRGO (~90% imported, domestic capacity only from FY2028), RIP bushing cores (~95% imported, with four Indian localisers building), and vacuum OLTCs (>80% imported, no qualified Indian maker). Distribution-transformer imports, by contrast, nearly doubled to ₹2,085 cr in FY26.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Capex per MVA stays modest and brownfield-led — CG Power adds 10,000 MVA for ₹68 cr, TARIL adds ~35,000 MVA for about ₹150 cr — but the model is working-capital heavy on 18–24 month execution cycles (TARIL debt/equity 0.35x, ROCE 23.3%; CG Power annualised ROCE 27%), and the customer book is dominated by state utilities and TBCB EPCs.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: 765 kV manufacture is established across five or six makers and 1,200 kV testing exists in-house (CG Power's Sehore line covers 220–1,200 kV; TARIL runs a 1,200 kV UHV lab), but HVDC converter technology sits with two firms and design validation still queues behind scarce accredited short-circuit and impulse capacity — which is why lead time, not know-how, sets the pace.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Downgraded from 3 to 2 on evidence that arrived this quarter: record copper (LME ~US$13,950/t on 6-Nov-2026, +35% YoY) is squeezing firm-price order books — Voltamp's gross margin fell 543 bps, Atlanta's EBITDA 201 bps and Shilchar's 1,049 bps YoY — while a live CRGO anti-dumping case could raise core-steel cost without relieving import dependence, and customer mix decides who absorbs it — GE Vernova's backlog is 78% private utilities, while TARIL bids ~80% domestic with an even government/private split and the distribution-transformer makers sell to state utilities on tender.

missing_critical: FY27 industry value in ₹ cr (no published series after the FY26 projection)
measured cost shares per transformer class (only blended realisation is disclosed)
OLTC and RIP-core import value by HS code, to size the two remaining leaks

value_capture.basis: Still the node that keeps the money, and the evidence strengthened in Q2 FY27: CG Power's Power Systems segment earned 25.0% PBIT on ₹1,769 cr with backlog up 81% to ₹18,964 cr, GE Vernova T&D ran 28.6% PBT on ₹2,027 cr with a ₹21,443 cr backlog, TARIL 16.1% EBITDA on ₹709 cr and Hitachi Energy 16.0% operational EBITDA in Q1 FY27 on a ₹32,222 cr backlog. The pool is growing faster than capacity can be built, but cash conversion stays the weak leg on 18–24 month utility cycles.

Unchanged and still the highest-switching-cost node in the chain: >80% imported on a Reinhausen-led oligopoly, a moving part whose failure mode is a transformer outage, and no Indian maker qualified on vacuum OLTCs at scale. Small pool, disproportionate pricing power.

Moved DOWN one step on pricing power (5→4): JSW JFE Nashik runs at ~102% utilisation but CARE Ratings reports net sales realisations moderating through 2025-26 on rising import penetration and global capacity additions, and India's GOES price (~US$1,830/t in Sep-2026) is a discount to North America's US$4,290/t. The strategic weight is unchanged — ~90% of 4.0–4.5 lakh t of demand is imported and the DGTR case (initiated 22-Jun-2026, no finding yet) is live — but the protected-margin story is weaker than the bottleneck story.

Moved DOWN on barriers (5→4) and bottleneck (4→3): Yash Highvoltage grew revenue 95% to ₹194.5 cr in H1 FY27 at 86% RIP mix with a ₹760 cr order book, and four Indian players (Yash, CG Power, Hitachi India and MIM) are now building localised RIP capacity, so RIP supply has stabilised. What has not localised is the capacitive core — ~95% imported — and localised 420/550 kV bushings only arrive in Q4 FY28.

NEW node this run, and the one that moved into the investable set: Vilas Transcore (NSE: VILAS) has tripled CRGO lamination capacity to 36,000 MTPA, won POWERGRID approval for slitting and lamination cutting to 220 kV, and grew H1 FY27 sales volume 28.1% to 11,697 MT — but at a 7.1% PAT margin, with realisations falling as CRGO prices eased. A capital-light, low-barrier processing step between the mill and the OEM: good returns on capital, weak pricing power.

Large in revenue (winding wires and CTC are 75.3% of KSH International's FY26 revenue) but metal-indexed, so a record copper price (LME ~US$13,950/t, +35% YoY) passes straight through rather than accruing. CTC capacity is the narrower, better-priced slice, and Apar, Precision Wires, Vidya Wires and now Vilas are all adding it.

Not a revenue pool but the entry gate, and the gate is measurable: only ~50% of transformers pass short-circuit testing first time, TARIL completed dynamic short-circuit testing to IEC 60076-5 on ten units across FY26–H1 FY27, and accredited high-power lab capacity is the constraint that shows up as lead time.

Domestic, skilled-labour-bound and the step where operating leverage is actually earned — TARIL's Q2 FY27 EBITDA doubled to ₹114 cr on 66% revenue growth as utilisation improved — but it is a process inside the OEM, not a separately priced node.

Crowded, state-utility-tendered and volume-led, and the only node with a visible import leak: distribution-transformer production grew just 3.4% in FY26 while DT imports nearly doubled to ₹2,085 cr. The competitive floor of the chain.

industries.notes: Full re-analysis 2026-11-10. Corrections from the prior run: (a) EHV lead times were carried at 24-42 months from global coverage and are replaced with India-specific Ministry of Power/CTUIL figures (220 kV 11-15 months, 400 kV ~15, 765 kV 20-24); (b) the valuation basis '95x to 167x' was wrong and is replaced with measured 9-Nov-2026 multiples (CG Power 89x, Hitachi 109x, TARIL 30.2x, Voltamp 30.4x, Shilchar 32.4x, Bharat Bijlee 21.7x), which lifts valuation from 2 to 3; (c) risk moves 3 -> 2 on reported margin compression from record copper; (d) bushing localisation is later than previously stated - localised 420/550 kV lands in Q4 FY28, not H2 FY27. Market & growth uses the same series as the digest block: FY26 ~₹40,000 cr (CRISIL/Eninrac projection), 3-year value CAGR 15.5% [CALCULATED], last-year value +10-11% (CRISIL) vs +21% implied by Eninrac [CONFLICTING DATA], volume +31.6% power-transformer production and +31.4% capacity added. Value capture scores 9 nodes from this page's own BOM tree and ladder on the Registry Review §4 weighting, plus one new node (CRGO lamination & core processing) that entered the investable set with Vilas Transcore's NSE listing. Delta pass 2026-11-13: market size and growth re-confirmed against CRISIL (Aug-2025) and IEEMA FY26; CRGO anti-dumping status re-checked — no duty notified as of 11-Nov-2026.

industries.title: India Power Transmission

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Regulated and 35-year TBCB returns insulated from energy-volume risk; PGCIL earned Rs 3,867 cr of consolidated PAT at an 82% EBITDA margin in Q2 FY27, and equipment nodes now earn more per rupee of sales than a year ago.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: Rs 9.16 lakh crore of NEP capex to FY32, a further Rs 7.93 lakh crore of 900 GW-plan transmission spend to FY36 and a Rs 1.86 lakh crore GEC-III scheme — the growth is a policy commitment rather than a forecast.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Developers remain consolidated behind PGCIL plus about a dozen TBCB players, but equipment competition is loosening: ~300 GVA of transformer capacity is being added and the Ministry of Power has opened bidding to four suppliers from land-border countries.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Late rather than mid-cycle: order books are the fullest in a decade, companies are bidding for FY29-30 execution, utilisation is at maximum, transformer prices are up 70-80% since 2021 and brokerages describe valuations as no longer cheap.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry — the page carries no sector multiple series.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Lines, towers, conductors and transformers are domestically built and localisation is moving down a tier — bushings, pressboard, CTC and CRGO processing are being built by TARIL, CG and Hitachi Mysore — but CRGO, power semiconductors and HVDC control code still leak.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Very high project capital, but regulated returns plus InvIT recycling keep the developer layer financeable; equipment capex is moderate and largely self-funded (Hitachi ~Rs 720 cr FY27, CG Rs 68 cr for 10,000 MVA).

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Mature AC technology; the migration is to HVDC, synchronous condensers, SF6-free GIS, SiC devices and a planned 1,150-1,200 kV step, where domestic design capability is partial.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Right-of-way delays have already cut PGCIL's FY27 capitalisation guidance; a CRGO anti-dumping duty is pending and would raise transformer cost; land-border suppliers are re-entering; HVDC award timing is lumpy.

missing_critical: import intensity by value (HS-code share of transmission equipment)
state-wise execution slippage against NEP targets

value_capture.basis: MOVED TO RANK 1 (was 2). 18-24 month lead times, prices up 70-80% since 2021 and four to five qualified OEMs at 765 kV have turned this into the best returns pool in the chain: CG Power's Power Systems segment earned 25.0% PBIT on sales in Q2 FY27 and 27% annualised ROCE at company level. Cash conversion stays weak at 2 because the order book is funded through working capital.

MOVED TO RANK 2 (was 1). Still the largest operating-profit pool — a 35-year TBCB annuity on Rs 2.20 lakh crore of works in hand at an 82% EBITDA margin — but PGCIL cut FY27 capitalisation guidance to Rs 25,000-30,000 crore on right-of-way and land, which defers the moment capex becomes earning assets.

Held at 82/100, now joint second. One terminal supplier per corridor and 48 months to first pole; Barmer-II placed with GE Vernova T&D on 3-Nov-2026 and roughly 22 HVDC schemes are planned, but revenue is back-end loaded and requalification costs keep switching at 5.

The next constraint after transformers: domestic GIS/GIB capacity is thin, CG's switchgear lines are at peak utilisation and it is adding bays and breakers, and 765 kV breakers are short. Barriers sit below transformers because more suppliers qualify at 400 kV.

High strategic value, no domestic pool: 60-65% of STATCOM core components are imported. CEA listed 73 imported items and a SiC-MOSFET programme began in Sep-2026, but nothing is in production, so operating-profit share today is negligible.

A one-producer domestic market with a live anti-dumping case — the whole duty benefit would accrue to JSW JFE. Pricing power is scored 3 rather than higher because a duty raises transformer cost across the chain and GTRI has argued it would not cut import dependence at 40-50 kt of domestic output.

Largest by headcount and revenue volume, thinnest by margin: fragmented tower fabrication, competitive EHV EPC at roughly 13-15% margins, and no switching cost for the utility buyer. Barmer-II line packages were split across Tata Projects and Jyoti Structures on price.

industries.notes: Scored against 'Industry-Level Investment Parameters & Scoring Architecture'. Overall = sum(category weight x score / 5) x 100, renormalised over supported categories: (4x.20 + 5x.15 + 3x.15 + 2x.15 + 4x.10 + 3x.05 + 3x.05) = 3.00; 3.00/0.85 = 3.53; overall = 3.00/5/0.85 x 100 = 70.6. Coverage 85% (valuation null). Structural group 77.1, current-opportunity group 40.0. Re-scored 2026-11-08: competitive 4->3 (border-country supplier opening, ~300 GVA capacity being added), cycle 3->2 (order books fullest in a decade, prices +70-80% since 2021), risk 3->2 (capitalisation guidance cut on RoW, CRGO duty pending).

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: SECI's first PSP auction cleared Rs 1.34-1.35 crore/MW/year on a 40-year PSPPA against capex of Rs 5.4-6.0 crore/MW and 7-8 year construction; workable fixed-charge return, cleared by the 100% ISTS waiver.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: 7.43 GW operating (Aug-2026) against 26.69 GW required by FY32 and a 100 GW roadmap for FY36; 15.87 GW under construction and 10.40 GW CEA-concurred.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Developers fragmented and price-competitive; electro-mechanical equipment is a three-firm foreign oligopoly (GE Vernova, Andritz, Voith) plus BHEL capability with no PSP order.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Early upswing: 15.87 GW building against 7.43 GW operating; CEA roadmap implies about 9 GW/year of additions to FY36.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series exists for Indian pumped storage; company multiples are not an industry valuation.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Civil and hydro-mechanical (48-65% of capex) are domestic; electro-mechanical (29-38%) is imported in every flagship scheme.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Rs 5.4-6.0 crore/MW, 7-8 years to first revenue, about Rs 5.8 lakh crore cumulative capex implied by the roadmap; only balance-sheet-strong sponsors and state utilities can carry it.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Mature, stable technology; the barrier is design and manufacturing capability, not novelty. Variable-speed DFIM is the live migration and India does not build the drive.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Single-source machine from three foreign firms, thin design and model-testing pool, 7-year geology-bound execution; offtake risk partly solved by SECI, execution and equipment risk not.

missing_critical: a scope-matched historical commissioning series for a genuine 3-year growth read
segment-level revenue disclosure separating PSP from conventional hydro at BHEL
installed-price data for imported versus domestic pump-turbine packages

value_capture.basis: Site-specific machine from a three-firm oligopoly; high share of project operating profit and near-total switching cost, but long cash cycles on milestone billing.
Bundled with the turbine in the same E&M award, so it inherits the oligopoly economics; DFIM variants add a converter that no Indian plant makes.
40-year PSPPA annuity with discovered fixed charge; durable and financeable, but competed away at auction and capital-hungry.
Small revenue, high return on capital, sticky installed base; the model-testing rig is the genuine barrier.
Domestic fabrication at 8-12% of capex, several qualified fabricators, limited pricing power.
Largest revenue pool at 48-65% of capex but thin margins, geology risk and long working-capital cycles; scarcity of qualified contractors partly offsets.
Domestic oligopoly with steady returns, but a small slice of project value and not a bottleneck.

industries.title: Quantum Computing (India)

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: India's quantum activity is grant- and programme-funded, not a revenue industry: the National Quantum Mission carries Rs 6,003.65 cr over eight years and only Rs 699.5 cr of Rs 2,330.68 cr sanctioned across the four hubs had been released by Feb-2026. The commercial pool is small (India quantum computing at USD 98-121 M in 2025 depending on scope) and the hardware value - dilution refrigerator, control electronics, qubits - accrues to foreign suppliers. QpiAI reports EBITDA-level profitability at a small base [REPORTED-T3], which is the exception rather than the industry.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: India quantum computing is forecast to grow at 24.9% (P&S, USD 98.4 M 2025 to USD 465.8 M 2032) to 50.2% (MarketsandMarkets, USD 120.8 M 2025 to USD 922.1 M 2030) [CONFLICTING DATA - scope], on top of a Rs 6,003.65 cr mission whose FY2026-27 allocation rose to Rs 900 cr. The near-term demand is procurement-led: IBM's Quantum System Two at Amaravati (Feb-2027), 17 NQM startups, and defence/space quantum sensing. Growth is real but off a tiny base and dependent on public money.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: The global structure is an oligopoly of IBM, Google, Quantinuum, IonQ, PsiQuantum and D-Wave, with cryogenics and control electronics held by a handful of European and US firms. India's credible positions are early: QpiAI's 25-qubit Indus (Apr-2025) and 64-qubit Kaveri chip (Nov-2025) plus a Bengaluru foundry (Aug-2026), a 1,000 km QKD link from QNu Labs, and prototype components (Dimira cables, PrenishQ lasers, TIFR LNAs). That is a pilot position, not a competitive one.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: The cycle here is the public-funding cycle, not the business cycle. Demand moves on mission approvals, budget allocations and procurement rounds - the NQM allocation itself swung from Rs 600 cr budgeted to Rs 755 cr revised to Rs 900 cr in one year - and Gartner expects more than 50% of quantum computing startups to fail by 2030 as the market rejects losing qubit modalities. Volumes are lumpy and grant-dependent.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No listed Indian company derives material revenue from quantum computing, so there is no industry valuation series to score. The adjacent listed exposures are IT-services multiples and industrial-gas/cryogenics multiples that price entirely different businesses. Scoring them would be a scope error.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Value sits upstream in the dilution refrigerator (often the largest single line in a small system), control and readout electronics, and the qubit fab; and downstream in facility integration and applications. India captures facility EPC (L&T at Amaravati), cryostats and vacuum vessels (INOX India), helium distribution (Linde India) and the algorithms/services layer, and imports the machine itself.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Capital intensity is high relative to revenue: QpiAI has invested about USD 20-25 M in its foundry alone, on top of a USD 32 M Series A and a Rs 50 cr NCD at 13.85%. Public capital is the main non-dilutive route (NQM seed up to Rs 5 cr, scale-up up to Rs 25 cr, DRDO's Rs 500 cr TDF corpus), and a dilution refrigerator costs USD 600k-1 M before any qubit exists.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: The technology is migrating on several fronts at once - transmon to tunable-coupler and flip-chip architectures, superconducting versus trapped-ion versus photonic modalities, and the shift from NISQ to error-corrected logical qubits. India is at 25-64 physical qubits against NQM targets of 50-1,000 in eight years, and its own hardware roadmap (Ganges 128 qubits in Q1-2027) is being built against a moving target.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Four structural risks stack: helium-3 scarcity (US DOE-dominated, USD 1,000-20,000 per litre, no substitute), a cryogenics duopoly with 6-9 month lead times, export controls on lasers, vapour cells and UHV parts that Indian founders describe as tightening, and a deep dependence on imported FPGAs and microwave electronics. Any one of these can slip a programme by quarters.

missing_critical: India quantum hardware revenue split by node
capex per installed system in India

value_capture.basis: The largest single line in a small superconducting system (USD 600k-1 M) and the most concentrated supply chain in the industry - Bluefors and Oxford Instruments above 70% of the quantum market, 6-9 month lead times, and helium-3 as a hard input constraint. India's share of this pool is close to zero today.

Second-largest system cost line and the one scaling fastest with qubit count - every added qubit adds rack hardware. Zurich Instruments, Qblox and Quantum Machines hold proprietary positions; India imports FPGAs and microwave chains and is only at prototype stage on power supplies and control racks.

Essential to every non-superconducting platform and export-controlled, which supports pricing power. Ti:sapphire lasers are entirely imported into India and frequency combs come from three or four firms; the domestic entrants (PrenishQ, QuPrayog) are pre-revenue.

The highest strategic barrier and the worst cash economics: fab capex, low yields and no pricing power while modalities are unsettled. QpiAI's USD 20-25 M foundry is a national capability bet rather than a proven profit pool, and Gartner expects most startups in this layer to fail by 2030.

The pool India actually captures today: the Amaravati Quantum Computer Centre was built by L&T and the two test facilities were assembled from seven organisations' components in under eight months. Real revenue, low barriers, contract-based and not repeatable at scale.

Where six listed Indian IT firms compete. Cash conversion is good and growth is the fastest in the stack, but the pool is thin, the barriers are low, and no company discloses it as a revenue line - so it is strategic positioning rather than an earnings pool today.

industries.notes: Scored 2026-11-13 during the grounding pass for this page. Opportunity uses exactly the India series in the Market & growth digest block; valuation is null because no listed Indian exposure prices this industry. Value capture is scored from this page's own BOM tree and ladder. Company-level claims are evidence-based; all impacts are inference unless reported.

industries.title: India Railway

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: The structure is inverted: rolling-stock OEM earns 10-13% EBITDA, components earn more (Jupiter's wheelset business ~17% against a 12.4% group margin), and the richest contracted pool is the 35-year maintenance annuity held by Siemens, Alstom, Wabtec and Kinet. One buyer sets price across all of it.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: ₹2.93 lakh cr of FY27 capex, +10.5% on FY26 RE, with ₹52,108 cr earmarked for rolling stock - the same figures carried in the Market & growth digest block. The pending ~1 lakh-wagon procurement (~₹35,000-40,000 cr) and a freight target of 3,000 MT by 2030 against 1,670 MT in FY26 give multi-year visibility.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Wagon building is a three-player listed oligopoly (Titagarh, Texmaco, Jupiter) with industry capacity of 50,000-55,000 wagons against ~40,000 of annual production, so nobody needs to add capacity for the next cycle. Against that, the buyer is a monopsony, RDSO certification gates entry, and the highest-margin sub-components sit in foreign-owned plants.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: The order cycle is turning: a 30% option clause added 9,638 wagons worth ₹3,925 cr across five suppliers in early November 2026, and the ~1 lakh-wagon tender is expected in H2FY27 after slipping from H1. Capacity headroom means the upturn arrives without a capex race - favourable for returns.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry - the page carries no sector multiple series.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Rolling stock, track and structures are domestic; wheelsets are import-substituting on a dated schedule (Ramkrishna-Titagarh commercial from Aug-2026, Jupiter's Odisha plant partial by Mar-2027); propulsion design authority and the semiconductor modules stay abroad; signalling is domestic but certification-gated to three vendors.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Moderate for heavy engineering: wagon capacity already exists, working capital is heavy and the buyer pays slowly, but 20-year offtake structures (80,000 wheels a year guaranteed) and production-linked wagon demand de-risk the investment case.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Kavach, aluminium coach bodies and Vande Bharat are all migrating inside India on dated schedules - Titagarh targets end-to-end aluminium capability by FY28 - but the underlying safety electronics and propulsion modules are licensed rather than developed.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Wheelset supply, the binding constraint of FY26, is easing as three plants come up; the live risks are single-buyer policy risk (a deferred tender defers the whole chain), a certification gate that only three signalling vendors clear, and skills - Kavach alone has needed ~94,000 people trained.

value_capture.basis: The richest contracted pool in the chain and the least contested: Siemens holds 1,200 locomotives, Alstom 800, Wabtec 1,000 and Kinet 120 trainsets on multi-decade maintenance obligations. Once the fleet is delivered the service stream is near-annuity, with switching effectively impossible for the asset's life.

Small at ₹7,500 cr of FY27 capex but the most defensible node on the page: SIL-4 certification and RDSO approval leave three approved vendors (Medha, HBL, Kernex), which is why a single CLW order can be ₹2,466 cr to one company. Commissioning stands at 2,633 route km of a 21,794 km programme - the growth is committed, the gating factor is certification capacity.

A four-to-five-year-life assembly that was imported for six decades and broke the FY26 production cycle when supply failed. Jupiter's wheelset business earns ~17% EBITDA against a 12.4% group margin, and three plants (Ramkrishna-Titagarh 2.28 lakh wheels, Jupiter ~1 lakh sets) are being built at once - the clearest import-substitution pool on the page.

Safety-critical and therefore sticky, but largely manufactured in India by Knorr-Bremse, Wabtec and Faiveley-owned plants - the pool is real, the ownership is not Indian. High switching costs protect the incumbent rather than a domestic entrant.

Large revenue, thin economics: the 1,800-locomotive FY27 programme runs through IR production units and two foreign-owned private plants, so the design margin accrues abroad while Indian content is structural fabrication. Volume is policy-set and flat.

The largest visible revenue pool and the weakest economics in it: 10-13% EBITDA, and revenue fell 14-26% across the listed wagon makers in FY26 when wheelsets ran short. Capacity of 50,000-55,000 wagons against 40,000 of production means price is set by the buyer, not the builder.

The biggest single capex line after rolling stock (₹790.7 bn for new track in FY27) but it is civil contracting: rails come from SAIL, sleepers and fastenings are commoditised, and EPC margins are low. Volume grows with the network; value added per rupee is thin.

industries.notes: Opportunity uses the same series as the Market & growth digest block (FY27 BE ₹2.93 lakh cr, +10.5% on FY26 RE). Valuation left UNAVAILABLE. Freight volume growth (1,670 to 1,765 MT) is treated as the demand leg of opportunity, not as a separate growth claim. Value capture scored from this page's own 14-node tree and ladder.

industries.title: India Rare-Earth Magnets

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: The economics are hostile at entry: Chinese price cuts took unit import value down ~44% in one year (value +5% on tonnage +87%), and finished magnets are ~43% costlier to make in India than to import, so a domestic plant starts behind on cost before it starts.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: Magnet imports were Rs 1,744 crore in FY25 on 53,748 tonnes with government projecting consumption doubling by 2030 from 2025 (~15% volume CAGR), against a Rs 7,280 crore scheme targeting 6,000 MTPA from a near-zero integrated base and import dependence of 59.6–81.3% by value — a large substitution runway, on a small rupee base.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Today the market is a 93%-China import monopoly with IREL the sole domestic oxide supplier; the scheme deliberately creates a five-player domestic structure capped at 1,200 MTPA each, so concentration is being designed in rather than competed away. The 9-Nov-2026 financial bids sharpen that picture: 16 bidders chased five slots and cleared at nil to ₹505/kg against a ₹2,150/kg ceiling, so the sales-linked rent per kilogram will be a fraction of the outlay and the five winners will be competing on magnet price rather than on subsidy.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Demand is inflecting on EV, wind and robotics volumes, but the price cycle is against producers — China resumed magnet shipments to India in October 2025 under a no-re-export condition, capping the scarcity premium.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series exists for the magnet layer in the registry, and there is no listed domestic pure-play to derive one from.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: There is no integrated domestic plant until roughly Q1-2028; NdPr oxide supply is concentrated in IREL, heavy rare earths (Dy/Tb) for high-temperature grades are imported, and the strip caster, jet mill, vacuum sintering furnace and grain-boundary diffusion equipment are all imported — almost every link is missing.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: A Rs 750 crore capital subsidy against 6,000 MTPA implies heavy capex per tonne, with a two-year gestation before first sale and a five-year incentive window that must be earned back against a falling price.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Strip-casting, jet-milling to powder, field pressing, vacuum sintering and heavy-rare-earth grain-boundary diffusion are not established in India; the government states plainly that India lacks the technology and infrastructure for the oxide-to-metal-to-alloy-to-magnet steps.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: China’s April-2025 export controls already stopped Indian production lines with two to three weeks of stock, price undercutting is documented, the beneficiary award is still pending (financial bids opened, award not notified as of 9-Nov-2026), and the whole case rests on one scheme that has not yet delivered a tonne. Score held at 1 on the 2026-11-02 delta pass — it is already the floor — but the dated regime risk sharpened: the suspension of China’s October-2025 package (Announcements 55–58, 61, 62, including the 0.1% foreign-content rule) lapses on 10-Nov-2026 with no extension notice published as of 31-Oct-2026, while Announcement 18 of Apr-2025 was never suspended.

value_capture.basis: The node the whole chain exists to make and the highest-value item in a motor BOM, but India's output is zero until the first integrated plant lands around 2028, so the pool is captured abroad today. Parameters left unchanged on the 2026-11-09 delta pass: the financial bids clearing at nil-₹505/kg against a ₹2,150/kg ceiling mean the incentive transfers far less rent than the ceiling implies, so the node's economics rest on magnet pricing rather than subsidy - which the existing roic of 2 already assumes. Pricing is the weak leg: finished REPMs are about 43% costlier in India than international prices, and the scheme's sales-linked incentive (capped ₹2,150/kg, 40% of turnover) is what closes that gap rather than any market power. Demand is not the constraint — MHI's own 2030 requirement is 8,220 t against nil domestic output.

Strip caster, jet mill, vacuum sintering furnace, magnetic press and grain-boundary-diffusion kit are imported in full — the same structural gap as cell-line machinery in the battery chain. Small revenue pool, excellent pricing power, and it grows with every plant the ₹7,280 crore scheme funds; no Indian supplier in evidence, so the pool leaks entirely.

The chain's chokepoint and the reason a magnet made in India still carries Chinese exposure one stage upstream: China refined 91% of the world's rare earths in 2024, and India's separation capability sits in one state-owned miner, IREL, which allocates oxide to the three lowest REPM bidders. Small in revenue against the magnet, decisive in bargaining position. IREL's 10,000-tonne Gudur monazite plant was due to commission in 2026 — the single most consequential upstream date in this chain.

Oxide-to-metal, metal-to-alloy and alloy-to-magnet conversion is precisely the midstream gap MHI names as India's missing industrial capability — there is no domestic plant, and the ARCI pilot at Hyderabad is the only route that runs strip-cast alloy through to a finished sintered magnet. A toll on every tonne of magnet capacity the scheme creates, with the know-how rather than the capital as the barrier.

Where a listed investor actually touches this chain today. Sona Comstar ran a 23.0% EBITDA margin on ₹1,546 crore of Q2 FY27 revenue with BEV revenue up 129% and a ₹25,100 crore net order book; H1 operating cash flow was 90% of EBITDA and free cash flow ₹446 crore. Pricing power is a lagged pass-through, not a premium, and the magnet inside the motor is imported — so the node earns integration and reliability margin on someone else's scarce input.

The fastest-growing pool in percentage terms and the least real today: Takshashila estimates recycling could meet more than 35% of India's baseline REPM demand, and a six-year ₹1,500 crore critical-mineral recycling scheme is in place, but the players (Attero, Lohum) are unlisted and MeitY has only recommended that MHI fold recycling into the magnet scheme. Scored on the pool it would become, not the pool that exists.

industries.notes: Opportunity uses the same series as the Market & growth digest block (FY25 permanent-magnet imports of Rs 1,744 crore on 53,748 tonnes, government projection of consumption doubling by 2030 from 2025, and import dependence of 59.6–81.3% by value). Valuation left UNAVAILABLE — no industry valuation series and no listed domestic pure-play. Value capture (added 2026-11-04) scores five nodes from this page's own BOM tree and ladder plus the demand node, on the separate Registry Review §4 weighting (op_share 20%, pricing_power 15%, roic 15%, barriers 15%, bottleneck 10%, pool_growth 10%, cash_conversion 10%, switching 5%). It answers 'which node keeps the money' and is not blended into the industry score above.

industries.title: India Reactor Coolant Pumps & Primary Loop

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: A sole-qualified-source position on a component with 24–48 month order-to-delivery ought to earn a premium, and KSB's ₹1,235 cr nuclear order book (Jun-2026) is the evidence of it — but the pool is small against the pump business, with nuclear revenue running ~₹30–50 cr in CY25 and guided toward ~₹100–200 cr in CY26 [REPORTED-T2], so the economics are attractive per unit and immaterial per balance sheet.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: India nuclear-grade pumps are ~$460 mn (2025) to ~$980 mn (2030), a 16.3% CAGR [CALCULATED from GEP Research, T3], driven by four PCPs per 700 MWe unit across 16 sanctioned units, inside a wider nuclear-equipment market of ~$2.8 bn (2026) to ~$7.4 bn (2035) at 11.4% [REPORTED-T3, MarkWide]. Volume [UNAVAILABLE].

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: One qualified domestic supplier is the whole competitive structure today, with Kirloskar Brothers developing an indigenous PCP and Flowserve licensed under 10 CFR Part 810 to transfer technology to CORE Energy Systems — concentration that hands the incumbent pricing power and simultaneously marks it as the single point of failure the customer is trying to design out.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Orders are live but gated on test-bed capacity: GHAVP PCP testing paused on third-party test-bed equipment with resumption guided for Sep-2026, and main coolant pump order-to-delivery has run ~48 months — a delivery constraint rather than a demand problem, with new tenders (Mahi Banswara and potentially eight reactors) queued behind it.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series exists for nuclear-grade pumps; KSB is a diversified pump maker whose nuclear line is a small disclosed slice, so the node cannot be valued separately on the evidence in the registry.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: The pump, motor and pressure boundary are domestic — KSB for the PCP, BHEL for the 6 MW, 6.6 kV motors, L&T for castings and forgings, MTAR for water-lubricated bearings — while Class-1 mechanical seals, hardfacing consumables, heavy forgings and the test beds themselves still leak to imports.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Plant capex is moderate — KSB's ₹40 cr Shirwal expansion takes capacity from ~1,200 to ~1,450 pumps a year by 2027 — but qualification capex in test beds, 5-axis CNC, EDM and the seal line is recovered only across a 24–48 month order cycle.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: The 700 MWe PCP is being indigenised on a proven hydraulic design; the residual technology risk sits in the shaft seal, cobalt-free hardfacing and coastdown qualification rather than in the pump itself.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Single-source qualification cuts both ways: it protects the incumbent's position and concentrates national risk in one qualified supplier, one third-party test bed and a seal supply that is still imported.

value_capture.node: A · Reactor coolant pump (PCP/RCP) — casing, impeller, shaft, motor, flywheel
value_capture.basis: The node that keeps the money and the only one with a qualified Indian supplier: KSB is sole-source to NPCIL on the RSR 400/2, holds a ₹1,235 cr nuclear order book at Jun-2026, and is executing the first fully indigenous 700 MWe PCPs for GHAVP 1&2. Pricing power comes from qualification, not scale; cash conversion is the weak leg at 24–48 months order-to-delivery.

value_capture.node: C · Primary loop & pressure boundary — headers, feeders, piping, valves, pressuriser
value_capture.basis: The largest revenue pool in the primary loop and the one where Indian fabrication is genuinely capable — L&T and Walchandnagar supply calandria, end shields and pressure-boundary work — but it is project-tendered, milestone-billed and working-capital hungry, so a big pool converts to thin, slow cash.

value_capture.node: B · Shaft seal & bearing system — mechanical seals, thermal barrier, WLBs
value_capture.basis: The highest-consequence sub-node in the pump: a Class-1 seal failure is a reactor trip, so switching cost is near-absolute and spares are an annuity. Partly domestic now through MTAR's water-lubricated bearings, but the Class-1 mechanical seal itself remains a leak to imports and a live scheduling risk.

value_capture.node: D · Materials, forgings & fabrication machinery — forging press, 5-axis CNC, EDM, test beds
value_capture.basis: Where the schedule actually binds: shaft and casing forgings, 5-axis CNC, EDM and the dynamic test bed are all imported and all long-lead, so the equipment makers and the forging suppliers capture margin ahead of the pump fabricator while the fabricator carries the qualification capex.

value_capture.node: E · Testing, QA & certification — NDT, hydraulic, coastdown, AERB / NPCIL
value_capture.basis: Not a revenue pool but the binding gate: the GHAVP PCP test pause on third-party test-bed equipment is the single clearest illustration in the chain that a qualification facility, not a factory, sets delivery dates. Highest barrier-to-size ratio of any node here.

value_capture.node: F · Aux pumps, aftermarket & end-of-life — SDCP, ECCS, seals/bearings, spares
value_capture.basis: The steadiest cash in the chain: safety-grade aux pumps and spares across a growing installed base, sold into an owner that must keep qualified suppliers. Smaller and less glamorous than the PCP, but it converts to cash rather than to work-in-progress.

value_capture.node: Primary coolant pump motor — 6 MW, 6.6 kV (BHEL)
value_capture.basis: A captive sub-node inside the pump: BHEL supplies the 6 MW, 6.6 kV motors including the KAPS-3&4 primary circulating pump motors, so the value is real but the pricing is negotiated inside a pump package rather than set in a market of its own.

industries.notes: Opportunity uses the same series as the Market & growth digest block (India nuclear-grade pumps ~$460 mn in 2025 to ~$980 mn in 2030, a 16.3% CAGR [CALCULATED] from [REPORTED-T3, GEP Research]). Valuation left UNAVAILABLE — no node-level valuation series exists. Value capture (2026-11-05) scores 7 nodes taken verbatim from this page's own BOM tree and value-chain ladder on the separate Registry Review §4 weighting, and is not blended into the industry score.

industries.title: India Robot Software & Autonomy

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Software is the highest-margin layer available to India here, but most realised value is still services-led engineering rather than product licence, and hardware import dependence of 85–90% of component value keeps the blended economics of the systems Indian firms sell thin.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: India robot software grows from US$223.4 mn in 2023 to US$1,312.3 mn by 2030 at a 27.7% value CAGR, inside a robotics market going from US$1.1 bn in 2025 to US$4.6 bn by 2030 (~33% CAGR), with software the fastest-growing offering segment and payback down to 1.5–2 years.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: The field is fragmented — large engineering-services firms (Tata Elxsi, Cyient, KPIT) alongside a cluster of small product companies — with low switching costs on ROS2 and open-source stacks, and the differentiating platform IP (edge-AI runtimes, simulation) largely foreign.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Demand pull is strong and recent: warehouse and quick-commerce automation is compounding, payback periods have shortened to 1.5–2 years, and Indian platforms are already being deployed overseas.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series is carried in the registry for the robot-software layer; the listed comparables are diversified engineering-services firms whose multiples are not an industry multiple.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: This is India’s strongest position in the robotics chain — the deliberate counterweight to the hardware import gap — with a deep fleet-software and autonomy cluster and strong integration capability; the gap is edge-AI compute hardware, which is imported.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Asset-light: the binding inputs are engineers and compute, not plant, so incremental capacity needs little capex and working capital is short-cycle relative to hardware manufacturing.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Talent in SLAM, perception, motion planning and fleet orchestration is real and exportable, but edge-AI boards (Jetson-class) are imported and there is no unified Indian safety or interoperability standard, which slows productisation.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Talent scarcity in AI, control and integration engineering, the absence of a safety-standards framework, and dependence on imported compute and robot hardware all constrain scaling; software carries less regulatory and capital risk than the hardware layers.

value_capture.basis: Proprietary navigation engines are the defensible layer in an Indian stack that is otherwise services-like; domestic capability is strong and the pool grows with every deployed AMR.
Fleet orchestration is where recurring revenue sits - licences per robot, per site - and with 87 firms competing the moat is integration depth, not the algorithm.
The largest absolute pool in the stack, and imported: 85-90% of robotic component value including compute is foreign, so the node sets the customer's cost without leaving margin in India.
Whoever wires the robot into the customer's PLC and WMS holds the account: the highest switching cost in the stack, though the work is services-heavy and less scalable.
Perception is becoming a commodity model layer; the Indian players here are engineering-services firms (Tata Elxsi, Cyient, KPIT) earning time-and-material rather than product margin.
Sold as a service alongside deployment; low barriers and no lock-in keep it a supporting pool rather than a value pool.

industries.notes: Opportunity uses the same series as the Market & growth digest block (India robot software US$223.4 mn in 2023 to US$1,312.3 mn by 2030 at 27.7% value CAGR, inside a robotics market of US$1.1 bn in 2025 rising to US$4.6 bn by 2030 at ~33%). Valuation left UNAVAILABLE — the registry carries no industry valuation series. Delta pass 2026-11-13: software CAGR re-confirmed; last-year volume cross-checked against the IFR World Robotics 2026 India release.

industries.title: India Robotics

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Assembly and integration is the domestic activity while 85-90% of robotic component value is imported, so the industry earns an integrator's margin on a foreign bill of materials.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: Market ~USD 1.1 bn (2025) to ~USD 4.6 bn (2030), ~33% CAGR [REPORTED-T2: Avendus, Oct-2026]; warehouse automation and import substitution are the two growth engines.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Domestic structure is fragmented integrators against Fanuc/ABB/Yaskawa/KUKA hardware; ARAPL is the only listed robotics pure-play and no robotics-grade reducer, encoder or magnet maker exists.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Installations grew 7% in 2024, but IFR flags a possible 2026 pause as the electronics PLI lapses - mid-cycle rather than boom or bust.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Bottlenecks are explicit and all upstream: reducers ~100% imported, NdFeB magnets ~95%, encoders and power semiconductors absent - each is a named localisation opportunity.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Integration and software are capital-light; a component plant (reducer grinding, magnet sintering) is heavy and qualification-gated, so capital is a barrier only at the node India wants to enter.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: No indigenous core hardware or control IP; the credible capability is software, autonomy and system design layered on imported actuation.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Core inputs are import-dependent with no dedicated robotics PLI and the National Strategy on Robotics still in draft, so the domestic chain is exposed to both supply and policy timing.

value_capture.basis: Robotics-grade reducers are held by two Japanese suppliers and ~100% of India's requirement is imported, so the node sets price and lead time for every domestic robot build; OEM qualification takes years, which is the switching cost.
Frameless and servo motors are largely imported and carry good returns; cash conversion is better than in the reducer node because the product is less customised per customer.
No Indian maker of the 5-axis grinders and CMMs that cut and verify reducer gears; the node gates reducer and arm production alike, and machine qualification is the classic years-long lock-in.
China holds ~94% of sintered output and India imports ~95% of requirement; a genuine strategic chokepoint, though the magnet itself is closer to a priced commodity than a proprietary product.
Drive and controller silicon is imported wholesale; barriers are the highest in the chain but the node is capital-hungry and cyclical, which caps ROIC.
The largest absolute profit pool in the chain, but it is not the bottleneck and four global OEMs compete on price, so margins are good rather than exceptional.
Where India actually earns today: the fastest-growing pool and capital-light, but low barriers, build-to-print scope and weak pricing power keep its share of profit small.

industries.notes: Scored against 'Industry-Level Investment Parameters & Scoring Architecture'. Valuation left UNAVAILABLE - the registry carries no industry-level valuation data. Cycle scored on IFR installation growth and the 2026 PLI lapse. Value capture is a judgement on node economics from the page's own bottleneck and import-dependency evidence, not from node-level financials.

industries.title: India Room AC & White-Goods Components

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Assembly is genuinely thin: Amber's CD business earned 7.1% EBITDA and EPACK 6.0% in FY26, while value sits in compressors, condensers, blower motors and PCBs at 55-60% of cost. Compressors are 16-17% of BOM on an ex-factory basis (PL India, Sep-2026) against the page's 20-30% retail-cost estimate, a scope difference the page states rather than averages.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: India's RAC industry was worth about Rs 35,500 cr in FY26 on 11.0-11.5 mn units, a 10-15% volume decline from a record FY25; FY27 is guided up 12-14% to 12.6-12.9 mn units, and the FY26-FY30 volume CAGR is put at 10-15% [CALCULATED from ICRA, Sep-2026]. Manufacturing capacity of 28-30 mn units is planned to reach 40-42 mn by CY2030, with indigenisation rising from 60-65% to 70-75% by FY2028.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Assembly and ODM are fragmented and share-driven, with brands prioritising volume over margin; above them sit a compressor oligopoly and a refrigerant pool capped by the Kigali quota. The compressor import quota of 8-May-2026 is deliberately manufacturing a domestic competitor set.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: A recovery rather than a peak: FY26 was a reset year, H1 FY27 RAC volumes grew about 15-25% on a weak base, and ICRA expects H2 growth to moderate to 15-20%. Margins stay compressed because a 10-13% cumulative cost increase has not been fully passed through.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series exists in the registry, and the listed exposures are ODMs and diversified consumer companies, so no component-industry multiple can be evidenced.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: India captures heat exchangers, sheet metal, moulding, PCBA and ODM assembly - real but thin - and now copper and aluminium semi-fabrication; it imports the compressor, the IPM/MCU and the laminate, which is where the pool leaks.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Moderate and rising: industry capex is guided at Rs 4,500-5,000 cr across FY27 and FY28 against Rs 2,000-2,500 cr in FY26, mostly for compressor, PCB and controller backward integration, with PLI support in place until FY2028-29.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: The technology is mature assembly; the real shifts are the BEE efficiency re-rating, which forces new coil geometry, compressor and board, and the Kigali HFC freeze from 1-Jan-2028, which resets the refrigerant rather than the manufacturing method.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Policy is the main risk and it is dateable: the copper IGT QCO exemption expires 30-Nov-2026, wrought-aluminium QCOs bite 1-Dec-2026, compressor import relief expires 31-Mar-2027 and PLI ends FY2028-29. Input cost in copper, aluminium and the rupee is the second.

missing_critical: component-level import value by HS line
compressor domestic capacity utilisation by plant

value_capture.basis: The single largest value pool inside the box - 16-17% of BOM ex-factory, 20-30% on retail cost - and the one the import quota was written to localise: 7-8 mn units of capacity against about 15 mn of demand.
Every inverter AC needs an intelligent power module and an MCU, both imported; the pool grows with the inverter mix and is entirely foreign-owned.
A genuine Indian high-margin pool held by SRF and GFL and capped by the Kigali quota - the quota is what makes the margin, and the 1-Jan-2028 HFC freeze is what ends the R-32 era.
Fin presses, high-cavity moulds and helium leak detectors gate every capacity expansion and are all imported - a small, high-margin pool India has no answer to.
Hindalco's IGT and MetTube-Adani at Sanand and Mundra are the newest Indian pool; the barrier is process know-how, and the QCO regime is what protects it.
Indian coil-making is competent and increasingly integrated, but it is a cost-plus fabrication pool with several qualified suppliers.
Boards are assembled in India at thin margin with the IPM, MCU and laminate imported - the clearest example of assembly value without component value.
Fragmented, commodity and easily replicated; volume grows with units but price is set by the moulders' own competition.

industries.notes: Scored 2026-11-11 in the content-backfill pass. Market size and growth are the digest's own Market & growth figures; volume is used as the growth measure because the page shows value to be price-inflated.

industries.title: India Satellite Bus & Subsystems

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Integration is where schedule risk and strategic control sit, but the margin is thin and the buyer is effectively one government. NSIL's GSAT-7C award to a private integrator (Rs 2,563 cr, Oct-2026) is the first real commercial transfer. Domestic capture today is structures, mechanisms and build-to-spec electronics, while the highest-value items - solar cells, star trackers, reaction wheels, rad-hard silicon - are imported.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: Department of Space space-technology outlay rose from Rs 8,873.62 cr in FY22 to Rs 10,397.06 cr in FY27 BE, a 3.2% five-year nominal CAGR [CALCULATED from Union Budget 2026-27], but the commercial pool grows far faster: NSIL revenue went from Rs 321.77 cr in FY22 to over Rs 3,000 cr in FY25. India's space economy is put at $9 bn in Aug-2026 and projected at $40-45 bn over the next decade (PIB and IN-SPACe factsheet, 14-Aug-2026).

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: ISRO's integration monopoly is being deliberately broken up - NSIL procurement, IN-SPACe authorisations to 52 non-government entities and around 440 registered space start-ups - but in the subsystem nodes that matter India has one or two qualified suppliers at most, and in solar cells and ADCS none.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Launch and procurement cadence is at a multi-year high: NVS-03 flew on 30-Oct-2026 with NVS-04 and NVS-05 targeted by Sep-2027 at one launch every six months, Gaganyaan's first uncrewed mission is targeted for Q4 2026, and BAS-01's first module is due in 2028.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series exists in the registry, and the listed exposures are diversified defence and electronics companies, so no satellite-bus multiple can be evidenced.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: India captures structure, mechanisms, electronics build-to-spec and increasingly AIT; it imports the four items that decide whether a satellite works. The chain position is therefore mid-tier, and improving fastest at the integration end.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: AIT and qualification are capital-heavy - thermal-vacuum chambers, shakers, Helmholtz cages - and the capacity is concentrated inside ISRO. The Rs 500 cr Common Technical Facilities scheme and the Rs 75 cr Satellite-Bus-as-a-Service scheme exist precisely because no single private player can fund the shared infrastructure.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: III-V multijunction solar cells, flight-proven ADCS, atomic clocks and rad-hard die are technologies India has demonstrated at best in part; the gap is qualification and flight heritage, which is measured in years and cannot be bought.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Four import dependencies with years-to-structural resilience - solar cells, ADCS, atomic clocks, where imported first-generation units failed across the constellation, and rad-hard silicon - plus a qualification bottleneck concentrated in ISRO that gates every new supplier.

missing_critical: India satellite-bus market size on a published basis

value_capture.basis: The highest-value imported item on the bus: a per-watt price set by a handful of foreign suppliers, no Indian producer, and the Rs 674 cr URSC tender is the demand signal that would seed one.

value_capture.node: ADCS — Star Trackers, Reaction Wheels, Gyros
value_capture.basis: Flight heritage is the barrier, not design: Indian units exist but are unflown, and a mission will not risk an unqualified attitude sensor.
Structural dependency: imported first-generation clocks failed across the NavIC constellation, and the indigenous replacements still import key components.
Where margin and strategic control sit and where private entry is being deliberately created, as GSAT-7C shows; capital-heavy, schedule-driven and priced on capability.
A genuine Indian niche - MTAR's valves and Bellatrix's electric and green thrusters at 85-90% export revenue - small in absolute value but the fastest-growing pool on the bus.
Indian array and harness build is competent, but the value leaks to the cell rather than the panel, so this node's pool is assembly margin.
MIDHANI and L&T hold the capability; the localisation gap is mill form and grade breadth rather than tonnage, and the pool is commodity-adjacent.
L&T's SADM, RDM, bus structure and substrates are real Indian content, but fabrication and composites are contestable and priced on cost.

industries.notes: Scored 2026-11-11 in the content-backfill pass. Market size and growth are the digest's own Market & growth figures; the budget series and the NSIL commercial series are both stated on the page and both underpin the opportunity score.

industries.title: India Satellite Ground Segment

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: The chain runs on a bill of materials whose highest-margin items are imported. Nelco, the largest listed operator, earned a 9.5% EBITDA margin and a 1.0% PAT margin in FY26; Avantel's FY26 revenue fell 10.9%. Domestic value-add is civil works, integration and antennas.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: Equipment pool USD 1,014.3 mn (2026) growing 14.3% to 2031 [REPORTED-T2: MarketsandMarkets, Jul 2026] and a USD 2.5 bn 2033 policy ambition [REPORTED-T1: IN-SPACe, 2023] - but the 20% localisation clause was dropped from the 2026 authorisation rules and no commercial LEO service has launched. Downgraded from 4: the demand anchor weakened.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Fragmented domestically across L&T Smart World, BEL, Avantel, Nelco and unlisted Hughes India and Bhawani Satcom; no domestic baseband supplier of scale, and foreign vendors hold the high-performance antenna and modem tiers.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Capacity is ahead of revenue and the legacy base is contracting: 20 Starlink gateway sites are built and idle pending Cabinet and security clearance, while VSAT terminals fell 21.8% in the year to June 2026. Pre-launch, not mid-cycle.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry; the listed cohort is three small caps and one conglomerate segment, so an industry multiple would not be meaningful.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: A well-defined substitution pool rather than a diffuse gap: baseband, modems, BUC/HPA and ESA antennas are identifiable imported blocks with named foreign suppliers, and the 20% GMPCS undertaking creates a dated demand signal for whoever qualifies.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Antenna and gateway manufacturing is moderate-capex; anechoic chambers, outdoor antenna ranges and environmental qualification are the heavy items and the real entry cost. Working capital is heavy - Nelco's debtors ran at 123 days in FY26.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Antenna and RF design capability thins above Ku-band; electronically steered arrays are entirely imported; GaN module fabrication does not exist domestically. The technology frontier is moving toward ESA and software-defined gateways, both of which India does not make.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Customers are creditworthy and the security regime guarantees Indian gateways rather than displacing them, but revenue is government- and policy-timed, launch dates have slipped repeatedly, and the critical RF and baseband content is still imported.

missing_critical: timing of GMPCS security clearance and Cabinet spectrum decision

value_capture.basis: Moved up on barriers and bottleneck: the baseband platform is proprietary foreign hardware specified into a network for its life, and for LEO it is designed jointly with the constellation, so it cannot be swapped. Highest margin per rupee in the chain and almost entirely imported - the pool India does not capture. Rank unchanged at 1; score up from 76 to 84.

MOVED UP from 3 to 2. Avantel's Rs 122.58 cr NSIL order for nine Ka-ready stations and the Rs 117.88 cr DRDO ground-segment hub show this is the node where Indian listed companies actually book ground-segment work, and the pool is growing with LEO and defence TT&C demand. Barriers are still only moderate - the antenna is engineered metal, not proprietary silicon.

MOVED UP from 5 to 3. Small pool but the stickiest: mission operations are contracted for a satellite's life and cannot be re-qualified cheaply. Switching raised to 5 on that basis; pool growth held at 3 because the customer is one agency.

MOVED DOWN from 2 to 4. Pool growth cut from 5 to 4 because the largest gateway build in Indian history has already happened - Starlink's 20 sites are standing - and the Indian prime's scope inside a gateway is civil works, shelter, diversity site and integration around imported RF and baseband. Lumpy project revenue with heavy working capital.

Unchanged at 5. Fastest-growing sliver and the least defensible: IN-SPACe authorisations are not scarce, the antenna farm has to be funded before the first customer, and pricing is per pass in a market with global competitors.

Last, and worse than before: pool growth cut from 4 to 2 because the installed base is shrinking - 2,36,039 terminals in June 2025 against 1,84,579 in June 2026. Standard Ku/C terminals are commoditising with no switching cost; the replacement cycle is the only demand.

industries.notes: Scored against 'Industry-Level Investment Parameters & Scoring Architecture'. Valuation left UNAVAILABLE; coverage 85%. The score fell from 60.0 (2026-10-09) to 52.9 for two distinct reasons: opportunity was cut 4 to 3 because the 20% localisation clause was dropped from the notified 2026 authorisation rules, and the cycle category is now scored at 2 on real evidence (20 idle Starlink gateway sites, VSAT terminals down 21.8%) instead of being unavailable. Coverage rose from 70% to 85%, so part of the fall is the addition of a weak category rather than a deterioration in the others. The IN-SPACe 2022 base and 2033 target are a policy ambition, not a forecast of realised revenue, and are not used as a CAGR. Node-level financials do not exist in public disclosure; value capture is a judgement on node economics.

industries.title: India Satellite

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Upstream earns on ISRO-anchored programmes and private launch contracts, but 50-55% satellite import content means a large share of every build leaks abroad and unit margins at scale are unproven.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: USD 8.4 bn (2022) to USD 44 bn (2033) at 16% CAGR [REPORTED-T1: IN-SPACe, 2023], with downstream applications carrying ~73% of the 2033 potential.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: ISRO-anchored with 400+ startups and 133 IN-SPACe authorisations, but only a handful at commercial scale and the launch market is contested by foreign reusable providers.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: No cycle-position evidence on the page - demand-supply balance not established.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Import dependence is specific and addressable: 50-55% satellite import content, 70-80% space-grade solar cells imported, no gallium or germanium refining.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Among the most capital-hungry chains in the registry - ~USD 25 bn of investment is envisaged over the decade, with long gestation and binary mission risk.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Real indigenous capability in satellite buses, small launch and payload integration; gaps in space-grade cells, detectors and high-reliability components.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Critical inputs are imported, programmes are long-cycle and mission failure is binary; the strategic priority is durable but near-term revenue is policy-paced.

value_capture.basis: 70-80% of cells are imported and only a few global suppliers are qualified; a small pool but a hard chokepoint with qualification-driven switching costs and good incremental returns.
The largest profit pool in the space economy and recurring by nature; pricing power is capped by capacity oversupply and competing terrestrial options, but cash conversion is the best in the chain.
Software-like economics - high incremental returns and fast-growing - but the pool is still small and imagery is increasingly substitutable from foreign constellations.

Highest technical barrier in the chain and a real bottleneck, but it is the worst cash-conversion business here: heavy fixed assets, long intervals between flights and returns that depend entirely on cadence.
Real capability and a growing pool, but working capital is consumed by long build cycles and the customer set is narrow and government-weighted.
Chipset and terminal value is largely imported and adoption is policy-driven; the pool grows with mandate rather than with customer willingness to pay.
The fastest official CAGR in the plan (30% to 2033) off a tiny base; today it is integration and services work with modest pricing power and imported RF cores.

Cycle and valuation left UNAVAILABLE - the page carries no demand-supply cycle position or industry valuation data. Market sizes and segment CAGRs are the official IN-SPACe Decadal Vision figures. Value capture is a judgement on node economics, not node-level financials.

industries.title: India Satellite Payloads

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Payload economics are good where the work is design-led: Paras earned a 44% EBIT margin on its optics segment in FY26, Data Patterns a 40.1% EBITDA margin on Rs 925 cr, Centum 18-20%+ in build-to-specification against 9-10% in EMS, and Astra's management states space margins exceed defence margins. The drag is not margin but concentration: one buyer, lumpy programmes, and working-capital cycles that took Astra 374 days of cash conversion.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: The demand signal is unusually explicit: 196 transponders against a stated requirement of 500 with 300 more directed, a 12-satellite EO constellation under contract to 2029, NVS-04 and NVS-05 targeted by Sep-2027, and a space economy projected from US$9 bn to US$40-45 bn. Historical growth has been slow (~1.6% a year on the economy measure), so the opportunity is forward and programme-driven rather than a trend already in the revenue line.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Design authority sits with ISRO's SAC and flight qualification gates entry, so the qualified supplier set is small and sticky - Astra has run cumulative ISRO space orders above Rs 750 cr across two decades. Barriers protect incumbency but not pricing, because the customer is the state and it sets both price and schedule.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: The cycle is inflecting upward on identifiable events rather than sentiment: NVS-03 launched 30-Oct-2026 and restored the four-satellite constellation, the Rs 2,563 cr GSAT-7C whole-bus order went to NSIL in Oct-2026, the EO-PPP concession was signed in Jan-2026, and NSIL repriced Ku capacity 20% from 1-Apr-2026, the first revision in a decade.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series exists for Indian satellite payloads, and no aggregation of listed payload-exposed companies would be a valid proxy because the exposure sits inside diversified defence-electronics businesses. Company multiples are reported (Astra at 71.7x FY26 earnings on ICICI Securities' estimates) but one company cannot define an industry multiple.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Domestic capture is solid at the build and screening layer and has improved twice in two years - TWTA productionisation at BEL under the SAC MoU and an indigenous clock now flying on NVS-03 - but detectors, focal planes, high-grade optics and rad-hard die remain imported, and no listed company covers the navigation payload.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Payload work is materially lighter in capital than the bus: cleanrooms, bonding and RF test benches rather than vacuum chambers and shakers, and Astra funds capex of Rs 40-50 cr a year. The burden is working capital - 374 days of cash conversion at Astra, 225-350 days on Centum's build-to-specification projects.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Design capability is real and current: SAC has delivered transponders from UHF to Ka, GSAT-N2 carries 32 beams and ~48 Gbps of Ka-band throughput, GaN SSPAs substitute for TWTAs on strategic payloads, and an indigenous rubidium clock has flown. The gap is at the component level - detector and rad-hard die design and fabrication are not domestic.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: A single state buyer sets price and schedule, four of the highest-value inputs are import-dependent under export-control regimes, qualification is gated by scarce test capacity, and payload failure is mission-ending - but the domestic trend is genuinely improving on TWTA and timing.

missing_critical: volume series (payload units / transponders over time)

value_capture.basis: Highest score on the chain: the function is essential to every transponder and SAR transmitter, was historically single-sourced abroad, and now has two domestic paths (BEL's TWTA facility under the SAC MoU, Sep-2024; SAC's GaN SSPA). Barriers are the vacuum-electronics and GaN process know-how, not capital. Rank moved up this run because BEL productionisation converts an import dependency into a domestic order book.

No substitute exists for a working clock, so pricing power and switching costs are as high as anything in the chain; the pool is small in revenue terms because there are few satellites, and it is captured by SAC rather than by any listed company. The indigenous clock flying on NVS-03 (30-Oct-2026) is the first evidence that the design can be industrialised.

The richest domestic pool by margin - Paras earned 44% EBIT on its optics segment in FY26 - with the fastest-growing demand pool behind it (12-satellite EO-PPP constellation by 2029). Scored below TWTA only because the highest-value element, the detector/FPA, is still imported and therefore not yet capturable in India.

The largest operating-profit pool available to listed investors: Astra, Centum, Data Patterns, BEL and Paras all sit here, at margins above their corporate averages. Held back by a single state buyer that sets price, and by cash conversion of 374 days at Astra.

Steady, material revenue for Astra and BEL, but the least strategic node: several qualified suppliers, no export-control choke point, and apertures below the deployable-reflector class are genuinely competitive.

Lowest score despite the highest strategic weight: the pool is currently foreign, capture in India is design-only (Aelius MMIC IP inside Astra), and a fab route would be capital-heavy with long payback. Scored as the opportunity it would become, not the pool that exists.

industries.notes: Opportunity and Market & growth use the same scoped series: space economy US$8.4 bn (2022, IN-SPACe) to US$9.0 bn (Aug-2026, PIB), ~1.6% nominal CAGR [CALCULATED]; NSIL revenue Rs 321.77 cr FY22 to Rs 3,000+ cr FY25 [CALCULATED]; transponder gap 196 vs 500. Valuation left UNAVAILABLE - the registry carries no industry valuation series.

industries.title: India Satellite Services & Data

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Services carry ~68% of satcom revenue and are recurring, but spectrum and AGR charges plus leased foreign capacity take a structural rent out of the Indian operator's margin.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: Communication USD 4.19 bn (2022) to USD 14.8 bn (2033) at 12% CAGR [REPORTED-T1: IN-SPACe, 2023], with broadband-from-space still pre-revenue and therefore optionality on top.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Three licensed operators plus Starlink and Kuiper entrants competing on price, while the largest legacy pool - DTH - is in structural decline against OTT.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Current position is adverse: DTH is shrinking, broadband-from-space is not yet monetised and the 5% AGR charge was only settled in Sep-2026, so revenue is pre- rather than mid-cycle.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Indian players largely resell foreign capacity; the rent accrues to satellite operators and capacity owners upstream, leaving services with recurring but thin economics.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
