capital.basis: Gateways cost USD 10-50 mn each and licences carry fees, but the model is far lighter than owning a constellation - capex is a barrier to entry, not a moat.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Genuine strength in software, analytics and geospatial platforms; no owned constellation, no domestic user-terminal silicon.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Diversified across broadband, DTH, VSAT, EO and navigation, but regulatory timing and dependence on foreign capacity are the binding exposures.

value_capture.basis: Capacity owners collect rent before any Indian service provider earns a rupee; strong pricing power and cash conversion, but the pool is not growing and India mostly leases foreign capacity rather than owning it.
The growth pool everyone is positioning for, with licence and spectrum barriers to match - but it is pre-revenue, capital-hungry and returns are unproven at Indian ARPU.
Best incremental economics in the services layer - software margins and fast pool growth - but a small pool and imagery that is substitutable from foreign constellations.
The steady, cash-generative core: long enterprise contracts and managed-service stickiness, offset by competitive tendering and dependence on leased capacity.
Still cash-generative on a large subscriber base, but the pool is shrinking against OTT and the node is strategically irrelevant to where value is moving.
Smallest pool in the chain; adoption is mandate-driven rather than paid for by customers, and the terminal and chipset value sits with foreign silicon vendors.

industries.notes: Scored against 'Industry-Level Investment Parameters & Scoring Architecture'. Valuation left UNAVAILABLE. Two market series with different scopes are shown side by side rather than reconciled - the IN-SPACe figure is a market-potential target, the KPMG figure a service-revenue projection. Value capture is a judgement on node economics, not node-level financials.

industries.title: Semiconductor Equipment & Materials · India

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: The economics belong to the tool OEMs and to proprietary consumables, not to India. The global equipment market is $135.1 bn in 2025 heading to $229.5 bn in 2028F at tool-maker margins, while India's capture is civils, cleanroom fit-out, cryogenic tanks, gas supply and installation labour. NITI Aayog found Indian arms of global suppliers price at import parity, so localisation alone does not cut cost.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: Global equipment sales were $135.1 bn in 2025 and are forecast at $229.5 bn for 2028, a 19.3% three-year nominal CAGR [CALCULATED from SEMI, Jul-2026], with 2026 alone at $165.9 bn (+23.2%); materials were a record $73.2 bn in 2025, up 6.8% (SEMI, May-2026). India has no published equipment or materials market size [UNAVAILABLE], so the opportunity is measured as pipeline: Rs 1.64 lakh cr of committed projects and $11-12 bn of announced equipment and materials proposals.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: The most concentrated capital-goods industry there is: ASML is the sole EUV supplier, DUV is export-controlled, and deposition, etch, metrology and photoresist are each three-to-five supplier oligopolies with 2-3 year requalification. India's only present exposure is tool contract manufacturing through ASM Technologies.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Mid-cycle at worst and still accelerating: global billings rose 23% YoY to a record $40.53 bn in Q2 2026, the second consecutive record quarter, and SEMI forecasts five consecutive years of growth to 2028 on AI, HBM and advanced packaging.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series exists in the registry for equipment or materials, and the Indian exposures are contract manufacturers whose multiples say nothing about the tool market.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: India sits at the bottom of this chain - fit-out, installation, gas delivery and now precision sub-assemblies - while lithography, resist, masks and wafers are imported. The realistic entry, tool contract manufacturing, is the thinnest-margin node in the chain.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Fab-scale capital is out of reach: a leading-edge tool costs tens of millions of dollars and a fab costs billions. Even the reachable entry - an ECMS-approved contract-manufacturing plant - needs precision machining, clean assembly and years of qualification before it earns revenue.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: This is the highest technology barrier in manufacturing and India holds almost none of the process IP; what is transferable is precision manufacturing and sub-assembly, which is a genuine but narrow capability.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Three live exposures: China's gallium, germanium and rare-earth export controls, both suspensions expiring inside this quarter; the lithography chokepoint that no amount of Indian capex can bypass; and a skills bottleneck of 200-300 orbital welders per 5N/6N gas-line project, trained from scratch.

missing_critical: India equipment and materials market size on a published basis

value_capture.basis: The most valuable node in the chain: ASML is the sole EUV supplier, a tool is a multi-hundred-million-dollar sale, and export controls make the position political as well as commercial.

value_capture.node: Wafer-fab process tools (deposition, etch, clean, CMP, implant)
value_capture.basis: The bulk of the $143.9 bn 2026 wafer-fab equipment pool sits here at 45-60% gross margins for Applied, Lam, TEL and KLA; installed-base service makes cash conversion unusually good for capital goods.
KLA's near-monopoly on process control: small relative revenue, exceptional margin, and once a node is qualified on a tool it is not swapped.
A consumable that recurs every wafer and is qualified per node; the pool grows with process intensity rather than with capex, and lithography materials posted double-digit growth in 2025.
A five-supplier 300 mm oligopoly with brutal capital intensity: the barrier is enormous, the returns are cyclical, and India has no entry.

value_capture.node: Bulk & specialty process gases (N2, O2, Ar, H2, He, NF3, WF6, silane, dopants)
value_capture.basis: Recurring by nature and localisable by plant, which is why Linde and INOX are building here - but the pool splits between a commodity bulk slice and a high-purity specialty slice India does not yet make.
Consumable chamber parts recur with wafer starts and are qualified per tool; CUMI and Grindwell are the nearest Indian attempt, but the qualified pool is imported.
India's reachable layer and its thinnest pool: precision parts and sub-assemblies for foreign OEMs, priced on cost and swapped on a quote.

industries.notes: Scored 2026-11-11 in the content-backfill pass. Market size and growth are the digest's own Market & growth figures; because India has no published equipment or materials market size, the opportunity score rests on the global equipment series and the Indian project pipeline, which is stated on the page.

industries.title: India Servo Motors & Drives

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Small market with global OEMs capturing the margin; domestic players do licensed assembly.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: US$452 mn (2025) to US$642 mn by 2034 — 3.8% CAGR, the slowest growth series among the scored industries.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Predominantly served by global OEMs; limited indigenous design.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: No cycle-position evidence on the page.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Import CAGR +16.4% (2020-24) shows the value chain is still offshore-fed — a substitution runway.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Motor and drive manufacturing — moderate capital.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Applied engineering; some in-house capability.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Capex-led industrial demand; import competition.

value_capture.basis: No Indian maker of drive-grade IGBT or MOSFET, so every servo drive's power stage is an import; the barrier is absolute and the pricing power is the global device makers'. Cash conversion is the weak leg — fab and OSAT economics are capital-hungry against long qualification cycles. The India Semiconductor Mission addresses the device in general, not the drive-grade part in particular.

About 95% imported and the input that decides whether a servo motor can be built at all; heavy-rare-earth export restrictions from China are live, and Sona Comstar's management said on the Q2 FY27 call that heavy rare earths are simply 'not available', forcing a shift to light-rare-earth designs. The ₹7,280 crore REPM scheme is the only route to a domestic supply, and its award was still pending at 27-Oct-2026 — so the barrier is high while the domestic return on capital is still nil.

The smallest node with the hardest gate: a high-resolution optical or magnetic encoder sets the accuracy of the whole servo package, there is no Indian maker, and the chip inside it is a specialty semiconductor. Precision metrology and optics know-how, not capital, is the entry cost — which is why this is the node a domestic entrant is least likely to close first.

The software-shaped node: firmware, motion libraries and functional-safety stacks carry high returns on modest capital, and once a machine builder has tuned a line to a controller it does not re-tune it. Small in revenue against the motor, and in India it is mostly bundled with imported drives rather than sold as an independent product — CG Power's PLC/HMI line is the nearest listed presence.

The largest domestic slice of the chain and the least protected: Bharat Bijlee grew its motor division 12.5% in FY26 while margins were under pressure from competition, and the company's consolidated operating margin fell to 7.2% from 9.0% as commodity costs outran fixed-price contracts. CG Power's LT-motor leadership (~38–39% share) is real, but it earned that share with cumulative price hikes above 30% in twelve months — a cost-recovery story, not a pricing-power one.

More than 60% imported and assembled here under licence. Bharat Bijlee's Drives and Automation division was flat in FY26 and its margins were hit by a 17% euro appreciation — a domestic assembler carrying foreign-currency input risk with no ability to re-price. Switching costs are the one comfort: customers standardise on a drive brand for programming, spares and service, which is why CG Power can sell drives alongside its own motors.

industries.notes: Scored against 'Industry-Level Investment Parameters & Scoring Architecture'. Cycle position and valuation left UNAVAILABLE — the registry carries no cycle or valuation data for these industries. Value capture (added 2026-11-04) scores the six nodes in this page's BOM tree on the separate Registry Review §4 weighting (op_share 20%, pricing_power 15%, roic 15%, barriers 15%, bottleneck 10%, pool_growth 10%, cash_conversion 10%, switching 5%). It answers 'which node keeps the money' and is not blended into the industry score above.

industries.title: Shakti EW System (India)

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Defence-electronics economics: revenue is programme-based, lumpy and milestone-billed, and BEL — the Shakti ToT partner and dominant prime — prices on a cost-plus, margin-regulated basis rather than on proprietary margin. EW is also a thin slice of a large budget: the whole India EW market is ₹3,200 cr (FY24) inside a ₹76 lakh cr ten-year defence capital pipeline.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: India EW ₹3,200 cr (FY24) → ₹9,200 cr (FY35) committed-programme baseline, a ~10.1% CAGR [CALCULATED: (9200/3200)^(1/11)−1], with ₹15,000–22,000 cr under the report's upside scenarios [REPORTED-T3/SCENARIO]. The same series backs the Market & growth digest block. Cross-check: India defence electronics $6.85 bn (2024) → $11.35 bn (2032) at 6.18% CAGR with EW ~22.6% of it [REPORTED-T2, Fortune Business Insights, updated 05-Oct-2026]; a Fact.MR estimate puts India EW at 10.9% CAGR 2026–36 [CONFLICTING DATA — different scope, not averaged]. Volume [UNAVAILABLE].

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: High barriers and few qualified primes: BEL holds the Shakti ToT and the naval EW/CMS role, DRDO/DLRL owns design authority, and entry needs security clearance plus a proven ToT route. The subsystem layer beneath is more contested — Astra Microwave, Centum, Data Patterns, Apollo Micro — which is where private capital can actually enter.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: The strongest demand position in Indian defence electronics: Operation Sindoor (May-2025) exposed a base unable to sustain a spectrum contest, 14 EW programmes were approved under DAP 2020, and the Pragyashakti tri-service EW software framework (launched Oct-2025, 8-CSCI, 25-month timeline) is funded. Procurement velocity, not demand, is the constraint.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: Directional [INFERENCE]: Indian defence-electronics names have re-rated well above their own history since 2022, so expectations are already demanding. No industry-level valuation series exists for EW; what would settle it is a sector EV/EBITDA and P/E series against its ten-year mean.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: India captures ~85% of system value at prime integration, but every decisive input leaves the country: GaN/GaAs MMICs ~75% imported, SiC substrate ~95%, MOCVD reactors ~100%, RF test gear and BAW/SAW filters ~90–100%. Deep domestically in software and integration, hollow at the chip.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Two very different profiles: integration and software are asset-light and working-capital-led on milestone billing, while a commercial GaN-on-SiC fab — the node that would close the import gap — is a multi-hundred-crore commitment with a 2028–29 volume timeline.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: A catch-up position, not a lead: GaN-on-SiC design is cracked but DRDO's GAETEC output (~100 wafers/month) is far below need, and cognitive EW sits at TRL 4–5 against China's 6–7. Technology is the binding gap, which is why this sits below the industry's demand fundamentals.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Resilience is low on the inputs that matter: MMIC, FPGA/ADC, RF test gear and filters are 75–100% imported with years-long requalification, and acceptance-to-delivery averages ~9.5 years (2.4x peer countries).

value_capture.basis: The largest pool and the one that books the programme: ~85% of system value is captured domestically at integration, and the prime controls the ToT, the acceptance route and the customer relationship. Pricing is negotiated rather than tendered, cash conversion is weak on milestone billing, and switching costs are effectively total once a navy has standardised a suite.

value_capture.node: EW Software, Cognitive EW & Threat Library
value_capture.basis: The highest-margin, fastest-appreciating pool on the page and the one with the best economics: software and threat libraries are near-zero marginal cost, update on a cycle rather than a build, and lock a customer in permanently once fielded. Small in revenue today, which is why op_share is low — but this is where value migrates as Pragyashakti moves the industry from hardware to algorithms.

The second-largest and most technically gated node: digital RF memory jammers are the decisive capability in a spectrum contest, are held by very few suppliers worldwide, and are procured on performance rather than price. Barriers and bottleneck power are high; the cash profile is the same milestone-billed defence profile as the rest of the suite.

The binding constraint and the best-priced node — ~75% imported, SiC substrate ~95%, MOCVD reactors ~100% — so the offshore fab houses set both price and schedule for every T/R module India builds. A small pool with disproportionate leverage, and the worst cash profile on the page: a fab is a long-dated capex bet with no revenue until 2028–29.

The fastest-climbing private pool and the layer where listed private capital actually participates (Astra Microwave, Centum, Apollo Micro). It carries real qualification barriers, but it sells into a prime that sets the price, so it captures scope without capturing the programme margin.

Imported, export-controlled and non-substitutable in the near term: the FPGA and high-speed ADC behind every receiver are bought from a handful of US and European vendors, so the node earns an offshore oligopoly rent that India pays rather than collects.

Necessary and defensible but not a margin pool: acceptance, sea trials and DGQA certification gate every delivery and take ~9.5 years end to end, so the capability is scarce — but it is a service to the prime rather than a product with pricing power.

Real revenue and a genuinely domestic capability — antenna and array fabrication is the most localised hardware layer in the suite — but several qualified fabricators compete for it and the design authority sits upstream, so it captures volume without pricing power.

industries.notes: Opportunity uses the exact series in the Market & growth digest block (India EW ₹3,200 cr FY24 → ₹9,200 cr FY35 baseline, ~10.1% CAGR [CALCULATED]; ₹15,000–22,000 cr upside scenarios [SCENARIO]). Value capture scores 8 nodes taken verbatim from this page's own BOM tree and value-chain ladder on the separate Registry Review §4 weighting, and is not blended into the industry score.

industries.title: India Shipbuilding & Ship Repair

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Sharply split: newbuild earns 5-12% PBIT while repair and refit earns 34-44%, and the defence yards convert that into 19.0% (MDL), 14.3% (CSL) and 10.7% (GRSE) PAT margins in FY26. Commercial newbuild economics remain uncompetitive without the subsidy, and revenue is delivery-lumpy.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: Order book of 1.1 mn CGT, 0.5% of the global total and rank 12, with deliveries scheduled for 2026-30 nearly double the 2021-25 tonnage - the same figures carried in the Market & growth digest block. The ₹69,725 cr package and a 4.5 mn GT target by 2047 set the runway; no consistent 3- or 5-year value CAGR exists for India, so growth is quoted as GT and revenue only.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: India is a price-taker in a market where China holds 64% of the order book, Korea 19% and Japan 6%, and where 94.2% of 2025 delivered tonnage came from those three. Domestically the order book is concentrated in four listed yards, but their competition is with Korean and Chinese yards on cost, not with each other.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: The global cycle is at a record: order book of 203.2 mn CGT on 1-Sep-2026, up 13% year-on-year and above the 2008 peak, with the newbuilding price index at 185.15 in Jun-2026 (+33% on Jun-2021). Chinese yards are full through 2028, which is precisely the window in which a new entrant can win work.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry - the page carries no sector multiple series.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Equipment and materials are ~65% of a warship's cost and propulsion is largely imported (MAN ES, Wartsila, MTU); deck machinery, marine valves and switchboards are genuinely domestic and exportable; Alang's recycling base and the 40%-of-scrap credit note are a structural advantage no competitor has.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Among the most capital-hungry industries on the registry: dry docks, shiplifts and cranes are decade-lived assets, working capital is consumed for years before a hull is delivered, and yard land needs waterfront access. The SBFAS/MDF/SbDS package exists precisely because private capital will not carry it alone.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Design authority, naval architecture and classification sit abroad, and the green transition - dual-fuel, methanol/ammonia, electric propulsion - is the next capability gap. The India Ship Technology Centre is the institutional answer and is only now being stood up.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: The execution record is the risk: 57,637 GT delivered in 2025 is 0.075% of global output and output has oscillated between 21,251 and 72,137 GT since 2020. Add a demand base that is Navy-concentrated, no commercial order pipeline beyond the 437-vessel fleet plan, and a cost gap that subsidy only partly closes.

missing_critical: commercial newbuild cost benchmark versus China/Korea

value_capture.basis: The cleanest pool in the industry: 34-44% PBIT against 5-12% in newbuild, cash collected on delivery rather than over a build cycle, and recurring by nature. India repaired 418 vessels in FY23-24 across ~42 dry docks and holds under 1% of the global repair market while 7-9% of world maritime traffic passes within 300 nautical miles - the gap is capacity, not demand.

The highest-barrier content in a warship and the reason MDL earns a 19.0% PAT margin on naval newbuild while commercial yards struggle. Customer switching is effectively nil inside a Navy programme, and DRDO/BEL/BDL supply chains keep most of the value in India - but it is a single-buyer pool.

value_capture.node: Propulsion — Main Engines, Gearboxes, Shafts, Propellers
value_capture.basis: A licensed, oligopolistic pool (MAN ES, Wartsila, MTU) with real pricing power and certification lock-in, and the single largest imported content block in an Indian hull. India assembles engines under licence; the design royalty and the high-value rotating parts leave the country.

Pure IP economics - no capital, near-total margin, and classification societies hold a statutory gate that cannot be competed away. Small in revenue, decisive in who is allowed to build; the India Ship Technology Centre is the first domestic attempt to own part of it.

The forward pool: ~7% of the global fleet is alternative-fuel-capable and roughly 50,000 vessels may need replacement or retrofit, yet alternative-fuel conversions are under 1% of repair activity today. Almost no Indian capability yet, which is why the growth score is high and the current profit share is near zero.

A pool no other shipbuilding nation has in this form: Alang is a global-scale recycling base, and the shipbreaking credit note worth 40% of fair scrap value, redeemable against a new build, converts end-of-life steel into newbuild demand. Small, fast-cycling and directly subsidised.

value_capture.node: Hull & Steel Fabrication (block assembly, erection, launch)
value_capture.basis: The largest single cost block and the weakest economics: welding and block assembly are labour-and-steel conversion with 5-12% PBIT, priced against Chinese yards that build at a scale India cannot match. It is where the jobs are, not where the money is.

SAIL and MIDHANI supply the plate and the alloys, so the tonnage stays domestic - but plate width and armour-grade capability are the gaps, and steel is a pass-through cost with commodity returns. Strategic, not lucrative.

industries.notes: Opportunity uses the same figures as the Market & growth digest block (1.1 mn CGT order book, 0.5% global, deliveries 2026-30 ~2x 2021-25, GT output 57,637 in 2025). 3-year and 5-year value CAGRs are left UNAVAILABLE because revenue is delivery-lumpy and no consistent India series exists. Valuation UNAVAILABLE.

industries.title: Silver Paste & Metallisation

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Formulation IP and qualification lock-in give the paste makers real pricing power, and the cost base is a pass-through metal price; the economics are strong — but they accrue to Chinese-owned producers, not to any Indian entity.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: India silver-paste imports US$184.33 mn in FY26, up 64.51% YoY from an implied US$112.05 mn in FY25, tracking cell capacity toward ~103 GW by Dec-2026 — fast growth on a small pool whose per-watt silver intensity is being thinned by substitution.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: An effective duopoly-plus: China is 90-92% of global PV paste output and the top three Chinese-owned producers hold close to 70%, but customers are price-sensitive and subsidy-distorted, and Chinese paste is optimised for Chinese cell lines.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Per-unit demand is in a substitution down-cycle even as Indian cell volumes rise: PV silver demand fell 6% in 2025 and is forecast down 19% in 2026, and spot silver at ~$61/oz is roughly half its Jan-2026 record, so revenue is volume-led and price-deflating.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry — the page carries no sector multiple series, and the leading paste makers are not NSE/BSE listed.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: India captures only the upstream metal (Hindustan Zinc, Vedanta); powder, frit, vehicle, formulation, screens and printers are all imported, so domestic value addition at this node is close to zero.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Paste plants are formulation-led rather than capital-led — modest mixing and milling capex against a high-value product — so capital is not the barrier; IP, qualification and silver access are.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: The node is on the wrong side of the transition: LECO, seed-and-plate copper and full copper metallisation all reduce silver per watt, and ITRPV sees HJT silver-based metallisation falling from ~75% of production in 2025 to ~10% by 2036.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: DGFT silver-bar restrictions and a 15% duty, 90-92% Chinese concentration, a technology roadmap explicitly designed to remove the product, and no domestic supplier to fall back on.

value_capture.basis: Where the IP and the margin sit: global PV paste is concentrated — the top three hold ~68% of revenue and China is ~92% of output [REPORTED-T2: QY Research] — while TOPCon paste gross margins run roughly 5–20% [REPORTED-T3], making the pool a formulation spread rather than a metal spread. India buys it rather than makes it: imports of US$184.33 mn in FY26, +64.5% YoY, 65% from China [REPORTED-T1: DGFT via CSE].

The smallest and most defensible node: Solamet's 229 active patents centre on the Pb-Te-O frit system that underpins PERC and mainstream TOPCon pastes, and DKEM paid CNY 696 mn for a 60% stake specifically to absorb that IP [REPORTED-T2: pv magazine, Jun-2025]. Tiny revenue, near-monopoly economics, and effectively impossible to substitute without reformulating the entire paste.

The substitution play: DKEM's pilot replaced 60–80% of silver with copper cores at 98.7% of pure-silver conductivity, cutting metallisation cost by ~US$0.012/W [REPORTED-T3: Mordor]. No revenue at scale yet — 2–3 ppt fill-factor loss after damp-heat ageing still restrains adoption — so op_share is 1 and pool_growth 5: the optionality is the value.

The plating route is the structural threat to the whole paste pool, because it removes silver rather than thrifting it; the same ITRPV trajectory that erodes paste demand is what makes plating the beneficiary [REPORTED-T2]. Value shifts to plating chemistry and equipment suppliers, none of them Indian-listed.

A process node with real leverage: fine-mesh screens and printers set line width and therefore silver consumption per cell, and the printers and screens are imported. Recipes are qualified to the printer, so switching is slow — but the value is captured by the equipment vendor, not by the Indian cell maker that operates it.

Silver is priced off the metal with no formulation margin, and high-purity PV-grade powder is the constrained step; India's listed exposure is Hindustan Zinc's by-product silver [INFERENCE]. DGFT silver-bar restrictions from 16-May-2026 and a 15% duty raise the landed cost of the input without creating domestic value — the metal flows through the chain, it does not stay in it.

The shrinking half of the stack: aluminium rear paste loses share as TOPCon dual-layer metallisation displaces Al-BSF, and per-cell Ag/Al pad content falls with silver thrifting — ITRPV sees HJT silver-based metallisation falling from ~75% of production in 2025 to ~10% by 2036 [REPORTED-T2, cited on this page]. A pool in structural decline rather than a pool under pressure.

Commodity chemistry bundled into the paste recipe: the formulator captures the value and the vehicle supplier is a cost line. Low barriers and easy substitution are why it scores at the bottom of the chain on every structural parameter except cash conversion.

industries.notes: Opportunity uses the same series as the Market & growth digest block (DGFT silver HS-category imports: US$184.33 mn FY26 vs an implied US$112.05 mn FY25, +64.51%). Valuation left UNAVAILABLE — no industry valuation series, and the pure-plays are foreign-listed. The CSE import line is an HS proxy, so it overstates paste narrowly and understates it if paste enters under a different code. Value capture (added 2026-11-02) scores 8 nodes taken verbatim from this page's own BOM tree and value-chain ladder, on the separate Registry Review §4 weighting (op_share 20%, pricing_power 15%, roic 15%, barriers 15%, bottleneck 10%, pool_growth 10%, cash_conversion 10%, switching 5%). It answers 'which node keeps the money' and is not blended into the industry score above.

industries.title: India Smart Meters

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Meter manufacturing still earns money but less of it: Genus ran a 19.1% EBITDA margin in Q1 FY27 against 21.2% a year earlier on a 44.8% revenue jump, HPL's metering EBIT margin fell to 12.28% from 17.59%, and Salzer's PAT halved to ₹8.33 cr on a 6.29% EBITDA margin. Fixed-price contracts with no raw-material pass-through turn every input shock into a margin event; Genus's FY27 guidance is ₹6,000-6,500 cr at ~18-20% EBITDA. The AMISP annuity is the better structure and the worse cash cycle.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: RDSS sanctions 20.33 crore meters, of which 5.73 crore were installed by 30-Jun-2026, leaving ~14.6 crore in the 21 months to the extended 31-Mar-2028 deadline - a ~8.3 crore/year requirement against ~1.0 crore a quarter achieved recently - and CRISIL puts the meter-maker revenue opportunity at ~₹90,000 cr. The same figures sit in the Market & growth digest block. No published value CAGR exists, so committed volume, not a growth rate, carries this score.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Assembly is fragmented and tender-driven, and the price evidence is now explicit: on KSEBL's Phase II base scope the lowest bid was ₹1,399.79 cr against ₹3,568.06 cr from the largest AMISP - a 2.5x spread on identical work. Genus alone can build 1.8 crore meters a year against a ~8.3 crore/year national requirement, the customer is a cash-strapped discom, and pricing power sits with the imported metering IC. The one consolidating layer is the AMISP concession, where Adani's IntelliSmart purchase was cleared on 30-Oct-2026.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Execution, not demand, is the swing factor and the clock is short: 28% of sanctioned meters were in at 30-Jun-2026 with 21 months left, the deadline has already slipped once from Mar-2026, and Tamil Nadu - 3.05 crore sanctioned, 9,746 installed - re-floated 1.77 crore meters in Oct-2026 after two cancelled rounds. Capacity is not the constraint (HPL ran at ~70% utilisation), so a tendering recovery converts straight into volume.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series is carried on this page - no sector multiple, EV/EBITDA or P/E band was gathered for the meter-making industry in this pass. Company multiples are not a substitute for an industry multiple.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: The meter is assembled domestically but the metering front end, MCU, communication baseband and relays are imported; ~88% of PCB demand is imported too. The Ministry of Power's 13-Jul-2026 order - 100% India-made mechanical relays and India-designed chipsets from 1-Jun-2028 - converts the gap into a dated domestic opportunity, and the Power Secretary has said fabricate-in-India will follow.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Working capital, not plant, is the binding constraint, and the evidence got worse this run: Genus expects positive operating cash flow only from FY28 after a 50-75 day working-capital improvement, Salzer carried ₹12 cr of quarterly finance cost against ₹498 cr of revenue, and AMISPs fund the whole rollout before collecting. Capex per meter of capacity is modest; the balance sheet is the barrier.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: The product is mature and the migration is in components - RF mesh to NB-IoT/PLC communications, and imported silicon to India-designed chipsets. That migration is now real rather than aspirational: MosChip's VIDYUT100 taped out in Q1 FY27 and completed initial silicon bring-up on 17-Sep-2026, and Cyient-backed Azimuth's 40nm SoC is production-ready at 20-30% claimed local value addition. Nothing here is frontier; everything is qualification-gated.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Two risks moved in opposite directions. Resolved: the Adani-IntelliSmart consolidation, which the CCI approved on 30-Oct-2026 after an incomplete-filing pause. Worsened: the input-cost and execution risks actually landed - the West Asia disruption and a weaker rupee compressed gross margins across the listed OEMs, and Tamil Nadu scrapped two tender rounds. Live: the 1-Jun-2028 localisation deadline, discom payment cycles of 90-180 days, and consumer pushback in some circles.

missing_critical: published value CAGR for meter making

value_capture.basis: Unchanged and still the top of the chain: the metrology front end carries accuracy class, tamper detection and certification, and is supplied by ADI, TI, NXP and Renesas with no commercial Indian alternative. The 1-Jun-2028 design-in-India rule creates an addressable domestic pool but does not yet shift any of it - MosChip's VIDYUT100 completed silicon bring-up only on 17-Sep-2026.

Moved UP on bottleneck (4->5): the Power Secretary has confirmed design-in-India is mandated from mid-2028 with fabricate-in-India to follow, which makes the MCU/SoC the single component the entire domestic meter industry must replace on a fixed date. The pool is real; the capture is still foreign.

Unchanged: licensed or SaaS, capital-light, and extremely sticky once a discom's head-end system is integrated - the best cash conversion on the page. Genus guides O&M revenue of ₹600-700 cr from FY28 rising to ₹1,100-1,200 cr, which is where this pool becomes visible in a P&L.

Moved UP on barriers (4->5): the CCI's 30-Oct-2026 approval of Adani's ₹3,050 cr purchase of IntelliSmart leaves two large platforms (Adani and the Genus-GIC platform, 3.61 crore meters) holding most of the concession layer, and a 93-month annuity is not something a new entrant can bid its way into quickly. Cash conversion is still the weak leg - financed up front, collected late.

Moved UP on pricing power (3->4), barriers (3->4), bottleneck (3->4) and switching (3->3->4): the 13-Jul-2026 order makes 100% India-made mechanical relays a procurement condition from 1-Jun-2028, which protects domestic capacity (AEW's 5 million units a year, Salzer backward-integrated) against imported 90 A relays. Still a small rupee pool per meter.

value_capture.node: Communication module / NIC (RF mesh / NB-IoT / PLC)
value_capture.basis: Unchanged: a standards-based module business with several qualified suppliers and no pricing power; the value sits in the reference design rather than the assembly. India has module and gateway capacity but not the baseband silicon inside it.

Moved DOWN on ROIC (3->2): the margin evidence turned this year - HPL's metering EBIT margin fell to 12.28% from 17.59%, Genus's EBITDA margin to 19.1% from 21.2%, and Salzer's PAT halved - on fixed-price contracts with no raw-material pass-through. Volume is enormous and growing; price is set by tender and the spread between the lowest and highest bid on identical scope was 2.5x.

Unchanged and still the most commoditised node: conversion-fee EMS work on single-digit margins, exposed to imported bare PCBs (~88% of demand imported on a ₹35,000 cr FY25 base) and to the same input-cost shock that hit the OEMs. It grows with the rollout and keeps little of the upside.

industries.notes: Opportunity uses the identical figures as the Market & growth digest block (20.33 crore sanctioned, 5.73 crore installed at 30-Jun-2026, ~₹90,000 cr meter-maker opportunity per CRISIL Jun-2025). A value CAGR is deliberately left out because no published series exists - the score rests on committed volume, not an invented rate. Valuation UNAVAILABLE. Re-scored 2026-11-11: capital 3->2 and risk 3->2 on the realised margin compression and working-capital evidence; economics, opportunity, competitive, value_chain, cycle and technology held.

industries.title: India Small Modular Reactor

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Nothing is yet earning: the demonstration units are sanctioned projects, not products, and per-MW cost of Rs 27.1 cr for BSMR-200 and Rs 63.6 cr for the twin SMR-55 is well above large-PHWR economics, so viability depends on financing terms rather than on unit margin.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: Nuclear capacity 8.78 GW (Oct-2026) to ~22 GW by 2031-32 and 100 GW by 2047 (~16.5% and ~12.3% CAGR) on a Rs 15 lakh cr investment frame, but SMR-specific revenue is limited to three demonstration units worth Rs 13,280 cr by 2033 — a large build-out with a very thin near-term SMR order book.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Design and heavy forging are single-source (BARC/NPCIL; the L&T-NPCIL JV) and reactor C&I is ECIL alone, which is highly concentrated — but with no commercial order book the concentration buys incumbents position, not pricing power.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: The earliest point on any curve in the registry: DPRs released, AEC/ETG clearance obtained, but administrative and financial sanction for BSMR-200 still pending and no construction start.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry — the page carries no sector multiple series, and the core value-chain participants (NPCIL, BARC, NFC, ECIL) are unlisted.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: The nuclear island and fuel cycle are indigenous and capture the deepest moats; turbine island is BHEL-dominated; reactor C&I is high-margin but unlisted; EPC is thin-margin. Localisation is real, unlike in most of the registry.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Rs 20,000 cr of mission funding against a Rs 15-25 lakh cr requirement, 60-72 month construction from financial approval, and a liability regime still being amended — capital is the binding constraint, not engineering.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Heavy forging and steam generators are PHWR-proven and ApuRVA alloy is a genuine indigenous material step, but SMR module integration is early-commercial and the 5 MWth HTGCR is a pilot.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Licensing and liability (SHANTI Act implementation), a single nuclear-grade forging shop, Class-1 skilled-trade shortages, public acceptance, and a financing framework that still excludes nuclear from green-finance rules.

value_capture.node: B · Nuclear island — SG, containment, pumps, forgings
value_capture.basis: The node that will keep the money if SMRs are ever built at scale, and the one with an existing qualified supply base — L&T (steam generators, forgings, the LTSSHF forging shop), BHEL, Walchandnagar and KSB (pumps). Barriers are ASME N/NPT and AERB Class-1, growth is the whole 100 GW-by-2047 frame, but cash conversion is the weakest leg: demonstration projects are milestone-billed over 60–72 months against a state owner.

value_capture.node: A · Reactor core & fuel — fuel, cladding, control
value_capture.basis: The scarcest capability in the chain and the one that cannot be imported around: fuel fabrication sits with Nuclear Fuel Complex and heavy water with the Heavy Water Board, both unlisted, and the ApuRVA alloy cladding is an indigenous material step. Enormous strategic leverage, but the pool is state-owned, capital-hungry and closed to listed investors.

Small revenue, the best economics per rupee in the chain: reactor C&I is ECIL alone domestically, safety-class software qualification is a years-long gate, and once a design is licensed the switching cost is effectively infinite. The pool is limited by being tiny and held by an unlisted PSU.

value_capture.node: F · Fuel cycle front-end — uranium → UO2 → cladding
value_capture.basis: A monopoly in everything but name: uranium from UCIL, conversion and fuel fabrication at NFC, heavy water at HWB, with no private participation in evidence and the SHANTI Act only now opening the door. Strategic value is near-total; investable value is nil within the NSE/BSE universe.

value_capture.node: C · Power conversion — turbine, generator, electrical
value_capture.basis: Domestic and BHEL-led for nuclear steam turbines, with L&T-MHI developing 700 MW and 220 MW nuclear sets under the Make-in-India BSR scheme — so a second source is arriving. Real revenue, moderate barriers, and the best cash conversion among the hardware nodes because the technology is conventional.

The annuity at the end of the chain: spent-fuel management, waste conditioning, decommissioning and the inspection and spares market across a 60-year operating life. Small today because almost nothing is operating, recurring and cash-generative once it is, and gated by regulatory custody rather than by capital.

The largest revenue line in a conventional island and the least defensible: civil works, cooling towers, water systems and balance-of-plant EPC are competitively bid by many contractors, so the pool scales with the build-out while the margin stays at EPC levels.

industries.notes: SMR-specific revenue is UNAVAILABLE — no unit is under construction and no commercial price exists, so opportunity is scored on the nuclear build-out frame and the three sanctioned demonstration projects rather than on an invented SMR market size. Valuation left UNAVAILABLE — no industry valuation series and the core participants are unlisted.

industries.title: Solar Cell Fabrication

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: ALCM/DCR premiums give domestic cells a protected realisation and early movers ran 50-60% utilisation at 4-5 year payback; CRISIL expects payback to stretch 1-2 years as capacity doubles, so the return is policy-made rather than structural.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: Cell demand of 60-65 GW in FY27 against 36.6 GW of capacity, with imported cells at US$3.06 bn in FY26 (+86% YoY, 28.6% two-year CAGR) and ALCM shifting ~half of demand to domestic supply — a large, policy-locked substitution pool.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Concentrated in roughly fifteen players with Premier at 10.6 GW, Adani 10 GW and Waaree 5.4 GW, but capacity rising from 26.4 GW in Jan-2026 to ~103 GW by Dec-2026 means rivalry is about to intensify sharply.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Capacity is being commissioned into a demand pool that is growing slower than capacity, with CRISIL flagging utilisation and realisation pressure and possible ALCM exemptions that would remove protected demand.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry — the page carries no sector multiple series.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: The conversion step is now genuinely Indian; the wafer (>99% imported), polysilicon, silver paste (~90% imported), screens and >90% of cell-line equipment are not, so the localisation has moved one step up the chain rather than closing it.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Rs 470 cr/GW of capex, long qualification cycles and rising working capital, with payback stretching as capacity lands; only PLI-backed and backward-integrated balance sheets can carry the next wave.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: India executed the PERC-to-TOPCon transition in-country and TOPCon now dominates listed capacity, with HJT lines already qualified — but the process recipes and tools are bought in, so the capability is operational rather than proprietary.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: US AD ~123% / CVD ~126% on Indian cells in force since 9-Nov-2026, >99% wafer dependence on China, and a demand floor that rests on ALCM thresholds, the 31-Dec-2026 net-metering cut-off and exemption decisions.

value_capture.basis: The node that decides an Indian cell's cost and the one India does not have: wafers are ~97% Chinese, and ALMM-III from 1-Jun-2028 makes domestic wafer supply a condition of listing [REPORTED-T2: Mercom]. Scored on the economics of the node rather than on Indian revenue — monopoly-like pricing and switching, but op_share is set at 2 because the value leaves India entirely.

The largest listed pool and currently the most profitable: Premier Energies did FY26 revenue of ₹7,824 cr at 30.4% operating EBITDA and 33.5% ROCE [REPORTED-T1: Q4 FY26 investor presentation], against Waaree's 22.3% FY26 operating EBITDA and 18.5% in Q4 FY26 [REPORTED-T1]. Pricing power is eroding as capacity compounds — 36.6 GW in Jun-2026 heading to ~103 GW by Dec-2026 — and module oversupply at 217 GW against 55–60 GW of installations drags cell realisations down [REPORTED-T2: ICRA, Aug-2026].

~93% Chinese polysilicon: the highest-barrier, most capital-hungry node, and the one Indian entrants have only announced — Premier's 10 GW ingot-wafer (5 GW by Dec-2027, 5 GW by Dec-2028) and Waaree's 10 GW at ₹6,200 cr by FY28 [REPORTED-T1/T2]. No Indian revenue yet, so op_share is 1; the score is a statement about the pool's structure, not about a business that exists.

Metallisation is up to ~12% of cell manufacturing cost and the qualified-supplier list is short: the global PV paste top three hold ~68% of revenue and China is ~92% of output [REPORTED-T2: QY Research]. Value leaks out of India entirely — domestic paste production is near zero and imports were US$184.33 mn in FY26, +64.5% [REPORTED-T1: DGFT via CSE].

The equipment layer is imported and concentrated: every listed Indian cell expansion — Premier's 7 GW Naidupeta, Waaree's 10 GW — is a machinery order booked abroad [REPORTED-T1], and Emmvee's 1.4 GW TOPCon line was ramped on German equipment. Process recipes are qualified to the tool, so switching is slow and the vendor captures value before the Indian cell earns any.

A gate rather than a pool: ALMM List-II listing — mandatory for utility bids after 31-Aug-2025 and in force from 1-Jun-2026 — is what converts capacity into revenue, and testing and sorting is the instrument [REPORTED-T2]. Small revenue, high strategic leverage, and the qualification record is itself the asset.

Silver is priced off the metal, so the pool is a refining spread rather than an IP margin; high-purity PV-grade powder is the constrained step. India's listed exposure is upstream metal only — Hindustan Zinc's by-product silver [INFERENCE] — and DGFT silver-bar restrictions from 16-May-2026 plus a 15% duty raise landed cost without adding domestic value.

industries.notes: Opportunity uses the same series as the Market & growth digest block (CRISIL demand of 60-65 GW FY27; Commerce/TradeStat imported-cell value US$3.06 bn FY26 with a 28.6% two-year CAGR). Valuation left UNAVAILABLE — the registry carries no industry valuation data. Value capture (added 2026-11-02) scores 7 nodes taken verbatim from this page's own BOM tree and value-chain ladder, on the separate Registry Review §4 weighting (op_share 20%, pricing_power 15%, roic 15%, barriers 15%, bottleneck 10%, pool_growth 10%, cash_conversion 10%, switching 5%). It answers 'which node keeps the money' and is not blended into the industry score above.

industries.title: India Solar PV

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Module assembly is a competitive, thin-margin conversion business; the cell layer earns policy-protected premiums that CRISIL expects to compress as capacity quadruples; the developer annuity is contracted but capital-heavy.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: India solar market USD 10.4 bn (2023) to USD 24.9 bn (2030) at 13.4% nominal CAGR, with FY26 installations up 87.2% to 44.61 GW and a 262 GW module base sitting on a 36.6 GW cell base — committed growth with an upstream gap as the prize.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Module capacity of 262 GW against ~40 GW of annual demand implies 35-40% utilisation and commodity pricing; upstream cells, wafers and polysilicon are Chinese-concentrated, so domestic rivalry is destructive at the assembly end and absent at the top.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Late-expansion, early-glut: module capacity is far ahead of demand, cell capacity is compounding toward ~103 GW by Dec-2026, and the US AD/CVD determinations of Oct-2026 remove an export outlet.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry — the page carries no sector multiple series.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Modules, BoS and EPC are domestic; cells are about half domestic and rising; wafers are ~100% and polysilicon ~100% imported, and paste, glass, encapsulant and cell-line equipment leak value offshore.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Cell capex of ~Rs 470 cr/GW plus heavy working capital and a 4-5 year payback that CRISIL expects to stretch 1-2 years; the Rs 24,000 cr PLI offsets part of it and module assembly remains low-capex.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: PERC has been displaced by TOPCon inside India and HJT is next, so the migration is being executed locally — but on imported turnkey lines, so process capability sits with the equipment vendor.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: US AD ~123% / CVD ~126% on Indian cells and modules now in force from 9-Nov-2026 at AD 123.04% / CVD 126.09%, Chinese curbs on equipment and wafer technology, and a demand mix that depends on ALMM/ALCM thresholds and net-metering exemptions.

value_capture.basis: The scarcest node in the chain and where the profit currently sits: Premier Energies earned a 30.5-31% EBITDA margin in Q2 FY26 with cell realisations up 29% year-on-year, against 37.8 GW of ALMM-II cell capacity behind 262 GW of module capacity. ALMM List-II from 1-Jun-2026 converts that scarcity into pricing power, but the position is protected by policy rather than by IP.

About 70% of solar glass is imported and Borosil Renewables is the lone listed domestic maker, protected by anti-dumping duty. Pricing power is duty-derived rather than structural, and a glass furnace is a large, continuous, energy-intensive asset.

Inverters are Chinese-led (Sungrow ~26% share) and India is entering by acquisition rather than by development - Premier bought 51% of KSolare, Waaree is building 4 GW. The node is electronics, so working capital is light and returns can be decent, but pricing power sits with the import and ALMM for inverters is only proposed.

Wafers are effectively 100% imported and the node has no listed Indian player, which is exactly why ALMM-III (wafers, 1-Jun-2028) creates a protected pool. It is also the most capital-hungry step in the chain with technology that China restricts, so returns depend on whether the mandate arrives before the capital does.

The 25-year PPA annuity held by Adani Green, NTPC Green and Tata Power is the largest pool by revenue in the chain, but tariffs are discovered at auction, capital intensity is extreme, and the return is a financing spread. Switching costs are high once a plant is built; pricing power is nil.

Polysilicon is the deepest upstream node and the one with the worst economics to enter now: global capacity is in oversupply, prices are set by Chinese producers, and a CVD plant is the largest single cheque in the chain. India makes none of it; the mooted VGF scheme is the only reason the pool exists at all.

EPC is a pass-through business: the contractor books the project value but earns a thin, competitive margin and carries the completion risk. Returns come from asset turns and working-capital discipline, not from pricing.

Module assembly is the most crowded node in the chain - 262 GW of nameplate against a domestic cell base of 36.6 GW - and management at Waaree puts sustainable margin on a normal module at 18-19% EBITDA, falling to single digits in oversupplied quarters. Barriers are close to zero and customers switch on price and warranty alone.

industries.notes: Opportunity uses the same series as the Market & growth digest block (PS Market Research, base 2023, 13.4% nominal CAGR 2024-2030). Valuation left UNAVAILABLE — the registry carries no industry valuation data. The panels-only Grand View series (9.4%) is a different scope and is not blended into the score. Value capture scored 2026-11-03 from this page's own BOM tree and ladder; the industry categories above are unchanged from the 2026-10-30 scoring.

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: The global pool is small and pre-scale: US$233.8m in 2026 heading to US$935.8m in 2030 on the most-cited forecast, and the published forecasts disagree by nearly 4x at 2030. Within that pool, 30-40% of BOM value is SiC modules made abroad, and the integrator's layer is the thinnest. An Indian assembler would buy imported silicon, certify through a foreign body and sell against Eaton, Delta, Sungrow and TBEA — the same structural position as PCS assembly, in a much smaller market.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: The demand step is policy- and architecture-anchored rather than forecast: India's data-centre capacity moves from about 1.5 GW in 2025 to 8-10 GW by 2030 (Deloitte), the Ministry of Power told Parliament on 27-Jul-2026 that AI data centres add 26.3 GW of load by FY32, and 800 VDC is the architecture hyperscalers are specifying. Add the HVDC local-content roadmap (30% FY28 to 60% FY35), megawatt charging and rail. The opportunity is real but it accrues to whoever has a product; India has pilots.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Unattractive in the direction that decides returns: a foreign device oligopoly upstream, a commercial field downstream that consolidated fast in 2026 — Eaton, Delta with Chindata, Sungrow, TBEA at 200 units a year, Zhiguang, Siemens with Reinhausen — and three well-funded pure-plays (Amperesand US$80m, DG Matrix US$60m, Heron Power US$140m). India's participants are pre-product and unlisted. Competition is absent where the margin is and brutal where the volume is.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: A genuine inflection point rather than a peak: five named commercial milestones landed between 02-Jul-2026 and 28-Sep-2026, UL opened a certification programme on 24-Sep-2026 and volume production is targeted for Q1-2027. India is at the start of that curve with no revenue, while its adjacent cycle - transmission and data-centre equipment - is at its strongest in a decade with 18-24 month lead times. Early-cycle technology inside a late-cycle equipment market.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series exists for SST manufacturing, in India or globally, and none is carried in the registry. The listed proxies are T&D equipment makers trading at 54-66x FY27 earnings on Jefferies estimates from June 2025 - company facts, not an industry valuation. [UNAVAILABLE]

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: India can build the enclosure, the busbar, the PCBA, the winding and the assembly labour, and can engineer the control firmware. It cannot make the SiC module, the gate driver, the DC-link film capacitor, the nanocrystalline core, the DSP or the MFT insulation system, and it has no SST certification route. The domestic share of the bill of materials is real; the margin is not.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Two very different capital problems. An SST integration and test line is a low-hundred-crore asset and is not the barrier - which is why entry is crowded elsewhere. The device layer costs US$1-5bn a fab, and the test layer needs a megawatt-class MV bay that nobody in India has built. Capital is available for the middle, scarce for both ends.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Two migrations run at once and India follows on both: 1200 V SiC to 2.3 and 3.3 kV SiC modules, and line-frequency transformation to a DC-native architecture. India's own capability is a 2 kV module using 3.3 kV SiC devices at IIT Bombay with a 200 kW prototype under way, a 1.2 kW prototype at IISc with Delta, and one commercial-scale demonstration. The gap is engineering depth and field hours, not theory.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Four gates. Devices 100% imported with years-long substitution. No Indian certification route, so approval is foreign and slow. A 3-4x price premium that only DC-native applications justify. And no field record anywhere, in a market where utilities and insurers buy decades of history. The policy tailwind - local content, Semicon 2.0, SiC pilot procurement - is real but aimed at HVDC and semiconductors, not at SSTs by name.

missing_critical: any India-specific SST revenue or unit series (none exists; the domestic pool is inferred as pilot-scale)
an ex-works price per kW for an Indian-assembled SST at matched scope, against an imported unit and against a 50 Hz transformer
segment disclosure splitting power-electronics or converter revenue from transformers at the listed T&D companies
the import value of SiC MOSFET modules by HS line for India, to size the leaking device pool directly
whether the MeitY-MoP-POWERGRID SiC module programme extends to SST-duty devices or stays HVDC-only

value_capture.basis: 30-40% of BOM, an oligopoly on the device, and the whole cost curve of the industry tracks this line. Capital intensity is brutal - a fab is US$1-5bn - so ROIC and cash conversion stay poor even where pricing power is real.

No Indian facility can type-test an SST today. Capital-light relative to a fab, high switching costs once a vendor's design is qualified on your bay, and it monetises every adjacent industry - PCS, HVDC valves, chargers, drives.

8-12% of BOM, contestable, and the component where an Indian winding and insulation base could hold a defensible position. Returns are ordinary; the strategic value is that it feeds four markets at once.
10-15% of BOM and imported in full. A small-ticket line that would serve inverters, chargers and drives alongside SSTs, so the pool is larger than the SST market alone.

The layer India could enter first. Low capital, high growth, real switching costs once a unit is type-tested into a customer's design - but no pricing power against an imported cabinet and no operating-profit share worth defending yet.
Box-build is competed to cost. It grows with the pool and earns nothing distinctive; the value is in the design and the devices above it.

industries.title: India Steam Turbine (Turbine Proper)

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: BHEL is the dominant utility turbine maker and earns a thin margin on a 48-60 month turnkey cycle: an outstanding order book of Rs 2,57,571 cr at 30-Sep-2026 and Q2 FY27 revenue of Rs 9,300 cr, but boiler-turbine-generator contracts are fixed-price EPC and Chinese EPC bidders discount by up to 20% (Mordor Intelligence, Jan-2026). The money in the chain sits with rotor forging and design, not with Indian assembly.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: India steam turbine market ~$3.33 bn (2022) to ~$4.38 bn (2030), a ~3.5% nominal CAGR [CALCULATED from Grand View Research], with the scope conflict shown on the page (IMARC $0.97 bn in 2025 at 4.15%; TechSci $0.83 bn at 7.61%). Headline growth is modest, but the order pool is not: 47,545 MW of thermal capacity under construction at 30-Jun-2026, of which 44,020 MW supercritical and 34,500 MW ultra-supercritical (CEA), plus the 700 MWe PHWR fleet and AUSC optionality.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Five credible Indian suppliers behind rotor-forging and qualification barriers - BHEL, Toshiba JSW, L&T-MHI, Triveni and Siemens Energy India - but a single state-dominated buyer and discounted Chinese EPC keep pricing contestable; the AUSC demonstration and the nuclear tranches are the swing orders.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: The order cycle is at a high: BHEL's order book rose 17.3% YoY to a record and 47,545 MW is physically under construction, though Q2 FY27 inflow slowed to about Rs 4,000 cr, which suggests the peak in awards may be behind rather than ahead.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series exists in the registry, and the only listed pure exposure - BHEL - carries steam turbines inside a much larger EPC business, so no industry multiple can be evidenced.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: The chain's value sits in large rotor forgings and hot-stage blading, both partly imported; India's position is design plus assembly of the turbine proper, with foreign forging vendors on the critical path - NTPC's approved HP/IP/LP forging list is entirely foreign.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Very capital-heavy and slow: 48-60 month turnkey execution, heavy fabrication and balancing/overspeed rigs, and large customer working-capital lock-in. BHEL's Rs 500 cr Haridwar thermal and nuclear turbine-generator expansion (14-Oct-2026) is small against the installed base it must fund.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Supercritical and ultra-supercritical design is licensed rather than owned, and the indigenous step - AUSC at 310 bar and 710 C on Alloy 617(M) - is unproven: the 800 MW demonstration still awaits final government approval.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Two structural exposures: imported large rotor forgings and superalloy blade stock, where NTPC-approved forging vendors are all foreign and resilience is measured in years; and a technology step (AUSC, dissimilar-metal-weld rotors) that is not yet commercial. Coal-transition policy is a third, slower risk.

missing_critical: India steam-turbine market size on one consistent scope (utility vs industrial)

value_capture.basis: The node that keeps the money. Rotor forging is the gating input, NTPC's approved forging vendors are all foreign, and a qualified rotor cannot be resourced inside a project schedule - so price is set by the forgemaster, not by the turbine assembler.
Hot-stage blading in Ni-superalloy is the second import-gated item; the cooler rows are domestic, so the pool splits between a high-margin imported slice and a competitive domestic one.
Steady and cash-generative, growing with the installed base rather than with awards; Triveni already books 38% of orders from aftermarket. Switching costs are high because the OEM holds the design.

value_capture.node: Heavy Machinery: Forging Press, CNC & Furnaces
value_capture.basis: A small, concentrated pool of ultra-heavy press, heavy CNC, heat-treatment and balancing-rig builders; India buys rather than builds, and a delayed press gates a whole programme.
MIDHANI and the special-steel mills supply grade and form; the barrier is metallurgy and qualification rather than scale, and AUSC raises it further.
Precision valve work with genuine qualification behind it, but small absolute value and several qualified suppliers.
Large fabrication and machining that Indian shops can do; real volume, thin margin, easy substitution.
Commodity scrap economics several steps removed from turbine value; volume rises with retirements but the pool is priced off steel scrap.

industries.notes: Scored 2026-11-11 in the content-backfill pass. Market size and growth are the digest's own Market & growth figures, so the opportunity score rests on exactly the figures shown there.

industries.title: Substation Equipment

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Order books beyond a year of sales and utilisation above 80% have restored pricing power to transformer OEMs; CRISIL expects healthy cash flows and stable credit.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: Transformer market Rs 33,000 cr (FY25) to over Rs 40,000 cr (FY26) at 10-11%, with a Rs 70,000-75,000 cr opportunity across FY26-FY27 and switchgear at 7.7% to 2035.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Concentrated at EHV among four to five qualified OEMs, but new capacity is entering and four Chinese OEMs may bid at 50-60% localisation.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: Clearly in up-cycle: power transformer output +31.6% and HV GIS +41.8% in FY26, against a NEP MVA target only ~30% achieved by FY25 — a multi-year runway remains.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Winding, tanks and assembly are domestic; CRGO ~90% imported, EHV bushings short globally, OLTC over 80% imported and IED design IP foreign.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Moderate to heavy — shed height, crane capacity and HV test bays gate entry, and a new entrant needs two to three years to become bid-eligible.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: Design IP sits abroad in IEDs, vacuum interrupters and HVDC valves; the SF6-free GIS mandate is a forced migration rather than an earned capability.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: CRGO anti-dumping outcome, the global EHV bushing shortage, Chinese OEM re-entry, and certified winding and test-bay manpower.

value_capture.basis: The centre of gravity: Rs 33,000 cr (FY25) to over Rs 40,000 cr (FY26) at 10-11%, 9-18 month lead times and a five-OEM qualified field; order-book working capital is what holds ROIC below the margin.
A three-player global oligopoly supplying every Indian HVDC scheme; the pool is large per project and effectively closed to new entrants.
A domestic oligopoly with HV GIS output up 41.8% in FY26 and a bus-duct gap that keeps some value abroad; better cash conversion than transformers.
Automation content per bay rises with digital substations, and the system stays with the asset for the life of the substation.
Imported at the high end and firmware-defined; the qualified-supplier list is short and the device outlives the project.
An imported precision sub-assembly replaced through the transformer's life, giving aftermarket recurrence on top of the OEM fit.
The chain's cost-setting import at ~90% dependence with an anti-dumping probe live; the value is captured abroad and the domestic share is only 10-12%.
Domestic, competitive and schedule-bound: it books revenue on every project but earns a thin, tender-set margin.

industries.notes: Scored against 'Industry-Level Investment Parameters & Scoring Architecture'. Opportunity uses the same CRISIL transformer series as the Market & growth digest block; the switchgear series is reported separately and never added to it. Valuation left UNAVAILABLE. Delta pass 2026-11-13: transformer series re-confirmed (CRISIL Aug-2025, IEEMA FY26); CRGO duty status re-checked, still unnotified.

industries.title: India Telecom Chipsets

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Chip design carries up to about 50% of value-add and 20-50% of handset BOM cost, but Qualcomm, MediaTek and Unisoc hold roughly 75-80% of India smartphone SoC value, so Indian participants earn design-service and packaging margin. Kaynes' OSAT is the exception that proves the rule: FY26 consolidated revenue of Rs 3,626 cr, up 33%, with packaging guided to 30% of group revenue in four to five years.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: India's semiconductor market is $62 bn in 2026 rising to $155 bn by 2031, a ~20% nominal CAGR (Kotak Mahindra Mutual Fund, Aug-2026), with a second scope at ~$64 bn to $200 bn by 2035 (EY-IESA, Sep-2026) shown rather than averaged; telecom is the second-largest end-segment at about $13.2 bn by FY30. The chipset slice grows faster still: India RF power semiconductors for wireless infrastructure were $1.99 bn in 2025 at an 11.7% CAGR to 2034 (Semiconductor Insight, Oct-2026).

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Two chokepoints sit above everything Indian - a baseband and modem oligopoly, and an EDA duopoly of Synopsys, Cadence and Siemens plus Arm. Below them the RF front-end is a filter-and-substrate oligopoly with no Indian line, so competition inside India happens only in OSAT and design services, where it is fragmented.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: The global chip cycle is in an AI-led upswing, but India's handset volume is moving the other way: smartphone shipments fell about 20% YoY in Q3 2026 to a decade low on memory prices, so unit demand and market value are diverging.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation series exists in the registry, and the Indian exposures are conglomerate segments or loss-making design houses, so no industry multiple can be evidenced.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: India's reachable layers are OSAT and design services; the value sits in the baseband SoC, the RF front-end module and the filter, all imported. OSAT costs in India run 20-30% below peers, which is a real cost edge but a thin pool.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: A fab is out of reach, but OSAT is not: the Sanand, Surat and Mohali lines were built for hundreds of crores rather than billions, and Semicon 2.0's Rs 1,27,500 cr carries 50% capex support. The binding constraint is customer qualification, not capital.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: India holds about 20% of the world's chip-design engineers and has taped out 25 designs under the Design Linked Incentive, so design capability is real; what is missing is compound-semiconductor epitaxy, filter and fab process technology, which is a decade of process learning rather than a hiring problem.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: Structural exposures: no commercial fab until Dholera in 2028, no GaAs/GaN substrate or SAW/BAW line, EDA and core IP held abroad, and a design-to-revenue gap in which 24 DLI projects and 25 tape-outs have produced almost no commercial silicon revenue.

missing_critical: India telecom-chipset market value on a published basis
Indian OSAT revenue and capacity utilisation by player

value_capture.basis: The node that keeps the money: Qualcomm, MediaTek and Unisoc hold roughly 75-80% of India smartphone SoC value, the design is the product, and switching a platform means re-qualifying a handset.
Content per handset rises with band count and 5G carrier aggregation, and the module integrates filters, switches and amplifiers that India does not make.
A duopoly plus Arm collecting licence and royalty revenue with almost no capital; India hosts the engineers but owns neither the tools nor the cores.
The tightest component in the front end: a handful of suppliers, patent-gated, and filters were the largest RF component segment in India in 2025.
Compound-semiconductor epitaxy and device design, priced on performance at backed-off power; India has neither a GaAs nor a GaN line.
An upstream crystal-growth pool of very few suppliers, extremely capital-intensive and priced on scarcity - the deepest import dependency in this chain.
India's reachable layer: 20-30% below peer cost and scaling from 15 mn to 48 mn chips a day by CY28, but packaging is a cost-plus business with heavy capex and thin margin.
A service attached to the OSAT line: real volume, little pricing power, and easily replicated once the testers are bought.

industries.notes: Scored 2026-11-11 in the content-backfill pass. Market size and growth are the digest's own Market & growth figures; both published India scopes are shown rather than averaged, and the RF power semiconductor series is used only as evidence of the chipset slice.

industries.title: India Telecom

economics.name: Industry economics & value creation
economics.basis: Equipment manufacturing is an assembly-weighted business: average domestic value addition is ~27.8% and the 4G/5G RAN bill of materials is only ~4% localised, so gross margin sits with imported silicon and RF. The operator side is consolidated and monetising (gross revenue ₹4,04,067 cr FY26, +8.59%) but absorbs $3-4 bn of annual capex per large operator. Mixed, not poor.

opportunity.name: Market opportunity & structural growth
opportunity.basis: India telecom & network equipment (TANE) market $25 bn (FY25) to $50 bn (FY32) at ~10% nominal CAGR [REPORTED-T3, NITI Aayog / KPMG, Oct-2026] - the same series carried in the Market & growth digest block. Committed demand from 5G densification, fibre and data-centre interconnect; NITI Aayog puts the export prize at $50 bn by 2035.

competitive.name: Competitive structure & moat
competitive.basis: Almost no pricing power at the assembly end: ~98% of equipment demand comes from private operators who prefer established global OEMs, Indian makers carry a 26-29% fiscal disability, and localisation is below 15% in several product categories [REPORTED-T3, NITI Aayog, Aug-2026]. Anti-dumping duty protects single-mode fibre, which is the exception rather than the rule.

cycle.name: Current opportunity & cycle position
cycle.basis: The operator capex peak is behind the industry: Bharti guides to $3-4 bn a year with 5G rollout largely complete, India Ratings expects capex intensity to moderate in FY27, and tower additions have slowed to a sub-1% quarterly growth rate. Telecom PLI 1.0 ends 31-Mar-2027 with PLI 2.0 still awaiting Cabinet.

valuation.name: Valuation & market expectations
valuation.basis: No industry-level valuation data in the registry - the page carries no sector multiple series, and listed exposure is a handful of mid-cap equipment names plus the operators.

value_chain.name: Value-chain position & bottlenecks
value_chain.basis: Optical fibre preform is being pulled home (HFCL ~₹1,800 cr programme, Finolex 100 to 200 MT) and transceiver assembly is starting (Dixon-Gemtek, GX Quantum Photonics), but baseband and RF-front-end silicon, high-speed optical DSPs and test equipment remain import-only. Towers and services are genuinely domestic.

capital.name: Capital intensity & financial quality
capital.basis: Operator capex runs at 15-20% of revenue even in the steady state and spectrum is a separate multi-billion-rupee outlay; equipment plants are less capital-hungry but R&D-intensive, and the ₹12,195 cr PLI has drawn only ~₹5,200 cr of investment across 22 units.

technology.name: Technology & innovation
technology.basis: The transition is being executed locally but not owned locally: 5G is complete, 5G-Advanced and 6G work is starting, and BSNL's indigenous stack plus 23 approved design projects under C2S/TTDF prove capability - yet design authority for radios and silicon sits abroad.

risk.name: Risk & resilience
risk.basis: More than 80% of critical components (4G/5G antennas, signal processors) come from China; China extended its own anti-dumping duty on Indian single-mode fibre for five years from 14-Aug-2026; every product is gated by MTCTE and trusted-source (NSCS) approval; and the PLI cliff lands in March 2027.

value_capture.basis: The highest-value content in a 5G radio and the node with the widest moat anywhere in this chain - and India captures almost none of it: there is no listed pure-play, and NITI Aayog reports >80% of critical components including antennas and signal processors are sourced from China. Scored on the node's economics, not on domestic capture.

Preform holds roughly 70% of the optical-fibre chain's profit and only 6-10 companies worldwide make it; 65-75% of Indian requirement is imported and global fibre is short as AI data centres absorb supply, lifting fibre and preform prices 20-25%. HFCL's ~₹1,800 cr programme and Finolex's 100-to-200 MT expansion are the first real domestic entries.

~$0.6 bn a year imported (USA ~50%, Taiwan ~25%, China ~15%) and the fastest-growing node on the page as 400G/800G optics are pulled through by data-centre demand. Dixon-Gemtek and GX Quantum Photonics are building the first Indian base, so the pool grows faster than domestic capture.

By far the largest pool - ₹4,04,067 cr of gross revenue in FY26 and ARPU of ₹187.12 - but traffic grows ~17% a year against ~2.7% revenue growth, so the pool expands slowly relative to the capital it absorbs. Three-player structure gives real barriers and high switching costs; returns are still recovering from the 5G build.

Software economics inside a hardware industry: minimal capital, high cash conversion and sticky once integrated into an operator's stack. Small in revenue, but it is where the AI-network and autonomous-operations layer will be monetised.
